azd provision creates the foundation and configures its services; it does not build or publish application images. azd deploy uses that foundation to build and publish the selected application. azd up runs both stages. Reprovisioning must preserve application images and revisions already published by deployment. Infrastructure ownership does not extend to resetting those application-managed values.

The root azure.yaml selects the native azd Terraform provider, infra/terraform path and main module. Shared PowerShell and shell hooks configure services and deploy the application. Use the selected provider for provisioning, updates and removal.

docs.title: Repository-owned AVM composition
docs.text:
The Terraform root composes Azure Verified Modules (AVM) with explicit inputs, dependencies and outputs. Complementary AzureRM or AzAPI resources cover requirements not met by the selected modules. The composition lives in infra/terraform/ alongside the product's configuration and lifecycle hooks.

Operators use documented environment inputs and root main.parameters.json. Preprovision resolves the shared topology and generates typed infra/terraform/main.tfvars.json; generated inputs are not operator-edited. The environment records its provider and application binding. The adapter derives matching provider, storage and backend cloud settings for public, usgovernment or china; operators do not edit the generated azureCloud context.

All flat infrastructure outputs feed azd and the shared configuration hooks automatically. The hooks publish runtime settings and platform outputs under the agent-lz App Configuration label, with secrets referenced from Key Vault. The platform-output document is part of the integration contract, not a replacement for every lifecycle output. Foundation settings and declared additional values retain their labels and content types. Shared defaults fill only missing keys; runtime-owned values follow the declared ownership contract.

docs.title: Versions, state and ownership
docs.text:
• manifest.json pins the coordinated application component sources.
  • Every direct and transitive provider version is pinned exactly. The committed infra/terraform/.terraform.lock.hcl records provider selections and checksums for Windows and Linux. Module versions are pinned separately.
  • Native azd initialization uses -upgrade. Exact pins constrain provider selection; read-only lock-file validation runs separately in CI.
  • Azure Storage holds remote state with an environment-specific key and identity-based access. Backend storage, permissions, network access and recovery controls are prerequisites outside every workload resource group. The workload uses an existing backend and leaves it outside azd down.
  • Immutable private backend/group records bind the state address and ownership. Terraform teardown uses that recorded state across owned or bring-your-own group layouts; it does not use a bulk group-deletion hook.
  • With azd 1.37.1, plan and apply run without native backend state locking. Individual environments can use local azd. Shared and production operations use one authorized executor and a non-canceling queue per actual backend state identity, not per branch. Follow the single-writer policy.
  • State, saved plans, generated inputs and local .azure/ data can expose sensitive values. Do not commit them. Review dependency updates deliberately, rather than upgrading providers to repair an unrelated deployment failure.

See the Terraform infrastructure runbook for backend readiness, updates and removal boundaries.

docs.title: Validation scope
docs.text: Verification includes offline tests and an Azure-authenticated plan of the public foundation, using in-memory test state without applying resources. Native backend operations, full-stack and private deployments, runtime RBAC and recovery were not exercised in Azure. Validate your deployment with the foundation and application runbook checks.

docs.title: Related reference
docs.text: The AI Landing Zone Terraform foundation reference is for composing a foundation directly from the shared AVM pattern. For Agent Landing Zone service configuration and application deployment, use the product runbooks above.

docs.title: Objective
docs.text: Find the first failing stage and its exact error, then use the matching section below. Deployment proceeds through resource provisioning, service configuration, image preparation and application deployment. Runtime checks confirm the application can authenticate and use its dependencies.

docs.title: When to use
docs.text:
Use this runbook after a provisioning, configuration, deployment or runtime failure. Diagnose the failing stage before retrying or changing inputs.

What you see Start here Multi-group setup reports a missing target or denied access Resource group destination checks azd down is blocked for split resource group destinations Split-group cleanup safety check Hosted deployment asks for preparation Hosted handoff Private endpoint or build-pool failure Private prerequisites, package installation Configuration stops after provisioning Post-provision diagnostics Deploy reports success but the application fails Revision health, startup authentication Chat, history or authorization fails Runtime diagnostics

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. Run diagnostics from the platform repository root. Confirm the intended environment with azd env list and the Azure CLI subscription with az account show. Verify the identity used by azd separately from the CLI identity; each tool can use a different account.
  2. Record the failing command, time, stage, source revision and relevant non-secret settings, such as NETWORK_ISOLATION, BUILD_MODE and DEPLOYMENT_TOPOLOGY.
  3. For private environments, use a host with the required VPN/VNet connectivity. Inspect DNS, TLS and authorization separately.
  4. Preserve local work, data, environment bindings and security controls while investigating. Use the recovery steps below for the failed stage.

The default hosted-no-panel layout runs the orchestrator in Foundry, with maf_lite and Foundry IQ. Confirm the recorded layout before recovery. Do not switch runtimes or weaken authentication to diagnose a failure.

Share useful, redacted diagnostics

Hooks write to the terminal. Agent Application Container App component deployments also write child logs under <component>/.logs. Share the exact error and relevant log excerpt, not the full output of azd env get-values. Remove private environment names, user identifiers, document contents, signed URLs, tokens, cookies and credentials.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Capture the first error and match it to a diagnostic entry below.
  2. Check the named source, identity, endpoint and selected environment.
  3. Apply only the entry's scoped correction, then run its verification.
  4. Complete Validation before reopening access or promotion.

docs.title: Resource group destination checks
docs.text:
For Agent Bicep/azd deployments, compare the selected environment's AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP, AZURE_APP_RESOURCE_GROUP and AZURE_NETWORK_RESOURCE_GROUP with the approved destination mapping. New environments initialize separate application and network destinations; existing single-group environments retain their mapping.

With CREATE_RESOURCE_GROUPS=false, have the owner pre-create missing additional groups. Enabling creation instead requires explicit authorization and subscription-level Microsoft.Resources/subscriptions/resourceGroups/write. An authorization failure is not evidence that the group is absent. Check the actual identity and denied action; do not grant subscription Owner or bypass the failure.

After partial creation, keep the same destinations, repair the cause and retry. Do not delete created/shared groups as rollback, change destinations to evade a binding check, or move existing resources through these inputs. Verify resource IDs and scoped permissions in every destination before continuing.

docs.title: Split-group cleanup safety check
docs.text:
For Bicep, the predown hook blocks azd down when the workload destinations span distinct resource groups. This is an intentional safety check, not a provisioning or permission failure. No automatic deletion or bypass option is provided; do not bypass the hook or change the destination mapping to make teardown proceed.

Inventory resources in every destination and identify shared dependencies, retained data, locks and ownership. Additional groups created by the feature do not receive the azd-env-name tag, so tag-based discovery is not a complete inventory. Arrange separately authorized, itemized manual removal with the owners. Confirm retained/shared resources remain intact afterward. The normal single-group azd down path is unchanged; its deletion review still applies.

For Terraform, split groups use recorded state-scoped ownership. Missing original group/backend records or changed destinations block teardown; restore the original environment metadata instead of recreating bindings. Follow Terraform removal for the required records, preview and explicit destruction approval.

docs.title: Hosted deployment is not prepared
docs.text:
Symptom: Deployment reports missing hosted foundation prerequisites or automatic image preparation fails.

Diagnose: Provision creates prerequisites and records HOSTED_AGENT_PREPARED=true. Deployment builds or reuses the immutable image, records its application handoff and creates the running agent version. A missing digest before deployment is normal; it does not require another provision.

Correct: Provision if the foundation is missing. Otherwise review the failed build, pinned source, registry access and private ACR Tasks pool, then retry azd deploy. A foundation project or registry binding mismatch must be resolved against the intended environment, not bypassed by editing output flags. Follow the Deploy full stack runbook. For an unchanged, compatible image, use the redeployment guidance. Let the workflow generate its output flags.

Verify: Deployment targets the intended digest and routed agent version. Then test authenticated task execution and the retrieval/authorization features you use.

docs.title: Hosted agent deployment returns an agent permission denial
docs.text:
Symptom: HTTP 403 names Microsoft.CognitiveServices/accounts/AIServices/agents/read.

Diagnose: Compare the denied object ID with the actual deployment principal. Foundry data-plane permission is granted separately from ARM provisioning access.

Correct: Have an authorized administrator review the minimum project-scoped agent authoring role for that principal. A runner creating/updating agents needs Foundry User or the appropriate equivalent custom role. Azure AI Developer targets different hub/workspace scenarios. Allow role propagation before retrying, keeping grants scoped to the project.

Verify: The same principal can perform the previously denied operation. Test delegated-user/OBO access separately.

docs.title: Application definition does not match the environment
docs.text:
Symptom: Application definition binding check failed. No changes were made. with exit code 2. An invalid definition instead exits with code 1.

Diagnose: Compare the selected definition's application ID with the existing AGENTLZ_APP_ID binding. The application ID identifies the application selected for that environment; orchestrator topology is a separate choice.

Correct: Restore the matching definition. For a different application ID, use a separate environment and select the definition before first provision. Retain the original environment's binding and topology.

Verify: Definition validation and binding checks pass for the intended environment. See Custom applications.

docs.title: Custom hosted image pull fails
docs.text:
Symptom: A custom azure.ai.agent service cannot activate its private image, although Foundry project and registry outputs exist.

Diagnose: Check the Foundry project identity's registry pull grant and the exact image/registry. Custom hosted components require hosted foundation preparation regardless of where any other component runs.

Correct: Preserve the environment, definition and immutable image, then rerun the custom application workflow. Provisioning applies the declarative pull grant; refreshing outputs alone cannot. For an external registry, review its supported pull-role mode and resource scope separately.

Verify: Image activation succeeds and the actual runtime principal receives the declared capabilities. Check the routed version before testing the agent. Keep registry authentication identity-based, grants narrowly scoped and delegated-user/OBO authentication intact.

docs.title: Private deployment prerequisites failed
docs.text:
Symptom:

Private deployment prerequisites failed. Use a VPN/VNet-connected host; RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX is not a connectivity bypass.

Diagnose: With NETWORK_ISOLATION=true, the host cannot resolve or establish TLS to App Configuration, or to the Foundry project endpoint for hosted topologies. The gate allows up to 20 seconds per endpoint.

Correct: Move to the approved jumpbox, VPN or peered-VNet runner and inspect the private connectivity path. The RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX input requests a connectivity check from that host.

Verify: Resolve and reach each required endpoint from that runner, then retry the failed stage. If it returns an authorization error, check the requesting principal and its permissions next.

docs.title: ACR Task agent pool is missing
docs.text:
Symptom:

Run 'azd env set DEPLOY_ACR_TASK_AGENT_POOL true' and 'azd provision', or set BUILD_MODE=local on a VNet-connected host with Docker.

Diagnose: The private environment has no ACR_TASK_AGENT_POOL output and BUILD_MODE is not local. This guard also applies to a custom service with a prebuilt digest.

Correct: Select the pool intentionally and run the foundation workflow:

azd env set DEPLOY_ACR_TASK_AGENT_POOL true
azd provision

For supported Container App builds, local Docker on a connected host is an alternative. The jumpbox does not include Docker by default. Automatic hosted image preparation and isolated custom source builds require the supported ACR Tasks path. See isolated image builds.

Verify: Confirm the selected environment has the provisioned pool output and that a build runs in it. Then resume the topology's deployment sequence; azd deploy resumes automatic hosted image preparation.

docs.title: Package installation fails inside the build pool
docs.text:
Symptom: An ACR run starts, but package installation fails. npm can report Exit handler never called!, followed by tsc: not found.

Diagnose: Retrieve the failed ACR run log from a connected host. Correlate timestamps and the build-agent source address with firewall deny logs. Check the pinned lockfile's resolved URLs, including redirect CDN destinations. Base-image registries and package feeds can require separate firewall allowances.

Correct: Confirm the pool and extendFirewallForAcrTaskBuilds are enabled and the shipped firewall changes are provisioned. The platform includes the orchestrator's Microsoft npm feeds, *.vsblob.vsassets.io and the existing packages.microsoft.com OS-package allowance. For additional verified dependencies, use application-specific package feeds. Keep exceptions limited to build-subnet HTTPS traffic.

Verify: Retry the same pinned source and confirm package installation and compilation both complete. Once dependencies are installed, diagnose the first remaining compilation error.

docs.title: Tokenizer initialization fails with an empty cache
docs.text:
Symptom: Orchestrator or ingestion startup fails while downloading a tiktoken encoding from openaipublic.blob.core.windows.net.

Diagnose: Check the failing HTTPS/443 destination and the actual workload subnet against firewall logs. A warm tokenizer cache can conceal this dependency; successful image builds do not verify runtime egress.

Correct: Review the selected components' runtime egress declarations. Both bundled tokenizer consumers declare this exact host. For a managed firewall, follow the normal provisioning sequence to save the declaration plan and reconcile its owned rules. For an external firewall, send the read-only resolved report to its policy owner. Keep the exception on the required workload subnet; do not allow all Blob Storage or Internet traffic.

Verify: From the actual workload network, initialize the configured tokenizer with a newly empty cache and confirm its asset download and startup complete. A local cold-cache test establishes the dependency, not traversal through the deployed firewall.

docs.title: Component egress reconciliation stops
docs.text:
Symptom: A hook reports a missing or stale egress plan, ownership collision, invalid source subnet or concurrent policy change.

Correct: Keep the same application binding. Review python -m config.deployment.egress --plan --environment <environment-name> and rerun the normal provisioning sequence after approved input changes. For collisions or changed policies, have the network owner inspect the reported group and current rules before retrying; do not delete unrelated entries, broaden sources or bypass the ownership checks.

Verify: The read-only --review report has the intended destinations and actual workload prefixes. Managed reconciliation completes without changing unrelated rules; external policies remain report-only.

docs.title: Stale component checkout
docs.text:
Symptom: Remove or relocate the stale sibling checkout.

Diagnose: An Agent Application component's sibling folder exists at a different commit from manifest.json. Check HEAD and local modifications before replacing it.

Correct: Inspect the named checkout, preserve local modifications and move it aside. Retry deployment to obtain the expected source. Delete it only after confirming it contains nothing needed; keep component development elsewhere.

Verify: The deployed source matches the manifest's tag and commit, and the intended application revision is healthy.

docs.title: A component deployment fails
docs.text:
Symptom: One or more components failed. See logs above.

Diagnose: Find the first failing component and its newest .logs file. Distinguish source checkout, image build/push, role and application-update failures.

Correct: Repair the dependency identified by that log. Use the private connectivity or build-pool entries above when appropriate.

Verify: Retry the failed workflow and inspect the actual image, intended revision and startup logs.

docs.title: Deploy succeeds but the UI or administrative panel does not start
docs.text:
Symptom: Child commands succeed, but the latest revision is unhealthy. Logs name OAUTH_AZURE_AD_CLIENT_ID, OAUTH_AZURE_AD_CLIENT_SECRET, OAUTH_AZURE_AD_TENANT_ID or missing panel OAuth settings.

Diagnose: Inspect the intended revision and image. A previous healthy placeholder can still serve HTTP 200 while the new revision fails.

Correct: Configure delegated authentication. Store the credential in Key Vault and publish its reference, not its value, under label agent-lz. Reload configuration through the supported lifecycle workflow.

Verify: Check revision health, the Entra login redirect, real user login, OBO and rejection of unauthenticated panel data requests. Keep panel authentication required throughout recovery.

docs.title: Search shared private links are not ready
docs.text:
Symptom: Private native azureBlob source configuration reports pending approval, denied Search reads or a readiness timeout.

Diagnose: Inspect the exact reported Search service, link name, target and group. Search uses its own outbound private links to storage and models, separately from the runner's network access. Each required source link must report both Approved and Succeeded.

Correct:

  • Pending: Have an authorized administrator investigate and approve only the exact target request using Microsoft's procedure.
  • ARM 401/403: Review the runner's Microsoft.Search/searchServices/sharedPrivateLinkResources/read permission. The runner needs this read permission in addition to target approval.
  • Approved but provisioning: Allow propagation and inspect the failed link's state. Readiness polling has a 600-second budget, 10-second intervals and requests bounded by 30 seconds and the remaining budget.
  • Missing link manifest: Re-provision the reviewed template through an authorized deployment to publish SEARCH_SHARED_PRIVATE_LINKS under agent-lz. Use the published link names to identify the matching requests.

Verify: Rerun post-provision from a connected host, then verify source processing and authorized retrieval. The gate runs before dependent Search mutation and source creation. Retain private access and the readiness gate; approve only the requests for the intended source targets. See Private native Blob ingestion.

docs.title: Ingestion selection does not match the source configuration
docs.text:
Symptom: A fresh environment has no ingestion Container App, a source combination fails validation, or attachment behavior differs from expectations.

Diagnose: Fresh Agent Application deployments default to DEPLOY_INGESTION_CONTAINER_APP=false, independently of orchestrator hosting. Native source ingestion uses Search's service-managed pipeline. Conversation uploads and Agent App Ingestion features require separate selection. Existing environments and custom definitions retain their component selections.

Correct: Check the resolved component selection, retrieval backend, source kind and index bindings using Ingestion. To retain or restore Agent App Ingestion, select it explicitly and run the full workflow, not only azd deploy. An externally populated index must be named explicitly where required.

Verify: Confirm the effective agent-lz key and intended UI revision. With ingestion disabled, attachment controls must be hidden and direct/stale uploads rejected. Verify text chat and retrieval separately, including the delegated retrieval checks. Ingestion selection is not a source of delegated user or owner context.

If ingestion is selected, confirm the selection is true and test only eligible authenticated uploads. Processing success does not prove authorized conversation retrieval. Retire existing apps and permissions only as a separate authorized task, preserving documents and indexes.

docs.title: Shared-source permission options are rejected or unexpected
docs.text:
Symptom: Source configuration rejects FOUNDRY_IQ_INGESTION_PERMISSION_OPTIONS, or a source has unexpected permission metadata.

Diagnose: Omitted or null values retain ["rbacScope"]. For active native Blob ingestion, explicit [] selects shared access only for recognized non-ADLS azureBlob configuration. Unsupported or ambiguous active sources fail closed. In non-native ai_search or foundry_iq/searchIndex modes, accepted [] is unused metadata; the source's access policy remains unchanged.

Correct: Supply valid JSON for the intended source policy. For protected Blob ingestion, restore ["rbacScope"]. Nonempty non-ADLS Blob lists support only rbacScope and sensitivityLabels. Review the accepted permission values for source and pattern constraints.

Verify: Rerun source configuration, inspect permission metadata and test document allow/deny behavior. Select [] only for an intentionally shared corpus; resolve private-link, RBAC and authentication failures separately.

docs.title: Firewall DNS proxy is enabled but clients still resolve incorrectly
docs.text:
Symptom: Private names resolve incorrectly after enabling the DNS proxy.

Diagnose: ENABLE_FIREWALL_DNS_PROXY defaults to false; its opt-in applies only with firewall deployment and isolation enabled. VNet/VPN client DNS settings and build-feed egress are configured separately.

Correct: Inspect the affected client's DNS server, zone links and forwarding path. Make client DNS changes deliberately and separately from proxy enablement. See Firewall DNS proxy.

Verify: Resolve the required names and test private TLS from the actual client with public access still disabled.

docs.title: Hosted configuration TLS handshake stalls
docs.text:
Symptom: Hosted bootstrap stalls while loading App Configuration or Key Vault references.

Diagnose: Distinguish name resolution, routing, TLS and HTTP authorization errors at both endpoints. Confirm the actual runtime identity and identify which connection stage stalls before choosing a recovery action.

Correct: Only for the confirmed transport compatibility case, use the endpoint-scoped TLS profile. Supply the actual KEY_VAULT_URI, deliberately select APP_CONFIG_TLS_COMPATIBILITY=true and deploy a new agent version. To restore SDK defaults, use false and redeploy. Keep certificate verification, the minimum TLS version and scoped role assignments intact.

If bootstrap resolves a UI-only secret, inspect the actual label selectors: in the SDK, None selects all labels, while "\0" selects only unlabelled settings. Use the intended selector while retaining scoped vault permissions and labels.

Verify: The new version completes configuration using valid TLS and the intended identity. Test real application behavior separately.

docs.title: Search preflight region and quota
docs.text:
Symptom: Preflight checks AZURE_LOCATION despite AZURE_SEARCH_LOCATION, or counts only one service when two will be created.

Diagnose: An empty AZURE_SEARCH_LOCATION falls back to AZURE_LOCATION. Both workload and newly created Agent Service Search must be accounted for.

Correct: Check the effective region and selected resources using Search region and quota. Verify local hooks and repository-owned infrastructure match the intended coordinated source. Request quota or deliberately select a supported region; do not set PREFLIGHT_SKIP or AGENTLZ_REGIONAL_PREFLIGHT_SKIP.

Verify: Preflight checks the effective region and full creation count, then provisioning succeeds. Capacity remains subject to availability at provisioning time.

docs.title: Quota check rejects an unchanged existing deployment
docs.text:
Symptom: Re-provision reports insufficient remaining model quota for the same account, deployment and configured capacity.

Diagnose: Compare the requested capacity with the existing successful deployment and remaining regional quota. Reprovisioning must use the same reviewed account and model inputs. Hosted image preparation itself does not require reprovisioning.

Correct: Verify environment, account region, deployment, model/version and SKU. Preflight credits only verified successful matching capacity and aggregates quota pools. Fresh allocations and changed/unverified targets still need capacity. If a matching deployment is not credited, retain the gates and escalate with sanitized account, region, model and capacity evidence.

Verify: Both preflight gates evaluate the intended incremental request. Retain the existing deployment, intended capacity and preflight gates. Model availability checks still apply.

docs.title: Foundry rejects evaluation API-key creation
docs.text:
Symptom: Failed to list key. disableLocalAuth is set to be true.

Diagnose: The account requires Entra ID. Identify the caller still trying to obtain an API key.

Correct: Keep local authentication disabled and use Entra ID for evaluation. The supported configuration skips inapplicable key injection. Investigate unexpected key or Key Vault errors instead of enabling local authentication.

Verify: Post-provision reports the expected Entra-only path and evaluation works with the intended identity while local authentication remains disabled.

docs.title: Administrative panel cannot resolve its Cosmos database
docs.text:
Symptom: DEPLOY_ADMINISTRATIVE_PANEL is true but DATABASE_ACCOUNT_NAME is not set.

Diagnose: Identify the selected database account and name, then check process inputs and the settings published in App Configuration.

Correct: Confirm the two settings under agent-lz for the selected environment. Setup reads published settings when process inputs are absent. Resolve missing or conflicting values in their provisioning source.

Verify: Panel configuration resolves the actual account/database and preserves container-scoped grants. Compare the resolved names with the provisioned resources and keep permissions scoped to the required containers.

docs.title: Missing endpoint output
docs.text:
Symptom:

Missing <KEY>. Run provisioning and load the selected azd environment outputs before this stage.

Diagnose: The selected environment lacks a required output such as APP_CONFIG_ENDPOINT, AZURE_AI_PROJECT_ENDPOINT or AZURE_CONTAINER_REGISTRY_ENDPOINT.

Correct: Confirm the environment first. If it is already provisioned and you moved machines, use azd env refresh. If provision is incomplete, follow the Deploy infra only runbook to generate the required outputs.

Verify: Confirm the outputs identify this environment's resources before retrying the failed stage.

docs.title: Private post-provision prerequisites failed
docs.text:
Symptom:

Private post-provision prerequisites failed. Connect through VPN/VNet and rerun postProvision; configuration has not started.

Diagnose: Provisioning completed, but the runner cannot reach private App Configuration, so configuration has not started.

Correct: Connect through an approved jumpbox, VPN or peered VNet. Follow Complete a deferred post-provision.

Verify: Complete the configuration hook from the connected host before resuming application deployment.

docs.title: Post-provision was deferred
docs.text:
Symptom:

Post-provision configuration explicitly deferred; application setup is incomplete.

Diagnose: An explicit deferral can exit successfully without configuring the application. In isolated mode, RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX=false (also 0, no, skip) or a truthy AZURE_SKIP_NETWORK_ISOLATION_WARNING without a truthy RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX selects deferral.

Correct: Complete the deferred step from a connected host. A truthy RUN_FROM_JUMPBOX requests connectivity checking from the runner's existing network path.

Verify: Post-provision logs show completed configuration rather than another deferral before resuming application deployment.

docs.title: NETWORK_ISOLATION is not a boolean
docs.text:
Symptom: A hook rejects the isolation value.

Diagnose: The selected environment contains a value other than literal true or false.

Correct: Restore the value required by the intended network design, for example azd env set NETWORK_ISOLATION true for an isolated environment. Use false only when the intended network design is non-isolated.

Verify: The effective value matches the intended network design and validation passes before any provisioning changes.

docs.title: Provisioning fails in Azure
docs.text:
Symptom: Preflight passes but Azure resource deployment fails.

Diagnose: Open Resource group > Deployments in the Azure portal and inspect the first failed operation, including its policy, quota, region or resource-name error.

Correct: Resolve that specific cause. Region/name changes can replace stateful resources, so review their impact before retrying the foundation workflow. For a name conflict, identify the existing resource and its owner before deciding whether to reuse it or choose another name.

Verify: The failed deployment and post-provision configuration both complete. Then deploy the application and run its authenticated task and access checks.

docs.title: Protected retrieval fails after hosted sign-in
docs.text:
Symptom: UI login and a greeting work, but protected Foundry IQ retrieval lacks delegated user context, is denied or omits documents.

Diagnose: Distinguish UI-to-Foundry OBO from downstream source authorization. The hosted gateway does not forward the caller's Authorization header unchanged. The built-in native path instead uses a separately exchanged Search token in x-client-search-token, followed by x-ms-query-source-authorization at Search.

Correct:

  1. Check the implementation. Confirm the UI and hosted runtime are the matching implementation with RETRIEVAL_AUTH_MODE=native_search.
  2. Check the delegated retrieval path. Review delegated Search consent, the authenticated UI assertion/refresh, supported custom-header forwarding, source permission metadata and private connectivity.

  3. Match recovery to the failure. A transport-role denial and a user's source denial are different failures:

    Consent or Conditional Access: Use the UI's explicit authentication recovery action. Standalone sessions complete the configured OAuth callback; embedded sessions use portal MSAL and authenticated bootstrap.

    Source 403 without usable claims: Diagnose source access rather than repeating sign-in.

  4. Submit a new turn after authentication recovery. The failed turn is not automatically replayed.

Do not bypass user authorization

Do not log tokens or claims challenges. Do not invent identity headers, enable anonymous retrieval or replace the user with a service identity. Stop sensitive-data rollout until denial works.

Verify: Use two users with different source permissions and confirm permitted retrieval and denial through the actual UI or channel, including references and downloads. A unit test or successful greeting is not authorization evidence for a deployed source.

docs.title: A protected citation download is denied
docs.text:
Diagnose: Distinguish shared-source Storage authorization from upload authorization. Shared Blob/ADLS reads require the current user's Storage OBO, delegated user_impersonation consent and source RBAC/ACLs. Uploads require a fresh Search-authorized match for the exact document, conversation and uploader, plus the UI's Search transport role. Knowing the URL or possessing an old signed selector is not sufficient.

Correct: Sign in again after session expiry and resolve consent or source permissions at their own boundary. Confirm the configured storage locations, Search index and bundled UI retrieval-reader profile. The native route limits a download to 100 MiB and 120 seconds; upload authorization examines at most 1,000 Search rows within 4 MiB and 30 seconds. An unverified target beyond those bounds is denied, not read with elevated access. Do not re-enable the legacy reader, mint SAS or replace user Storage access with workload access to make the download succeed.

Verify: Repeat allowed/denied-user, expiry and permission-revocation checks through the authenticated UI route, including an uploaded document. See protected citation downloads.

docs.title: The orchestrator returns HTTP 422
docs.text:
Symptom: The agent rejects a request with validation details.

Diagnose: The stateless Responses 2.0.0 adapter rejects non-null previous_response_id, empty asks and message arrays not ending with a user message. The adapter ignores top-level conversation. The UI's /invocations?api-version=v1 uses another request shape.

Correct: Use the returned validation detail and the correct request format. For stateless Responses, remove state selectors and supply complete, ordered context.

Verify: A request in the intended endpoint's format succeeds through that endpoint.

docs.title: Hosted chat works but history is unavailable
docs.text:
Symptom: A greeting works, but history is unavailable or panel history returns 503.

Diagnose: Hosted runtime is stateless. Without separately activated continuity, context is limited to the active UI session. Agent Application Cosmos DB in hosted-panel stores owner/index and feedback metadata, not transcripts. UI history requires continuity and the separately documented panel gates.

Correct: Review continuity activation, panel gates, owner binding and agent-scoped permissions in Hosted agents. Apply configuration changes through the full workflow using hosted continuity and owner-scoped permissions. Keep the hosted container's conversation access restricted; do not enable the panel merely to obtain persistence.

Verify: Open a saved conversation in a new session as its owner and confirm the transcript is available. Repeat as another user and confirm access is denied.

docs.title: The application starts but does not answer
docs.text:
Symptom: The application loads but an authenticated task fails.

Diagnose:

  1. Confirm the intended image and revision or routed hosted version using health checks.
  2. Read startup and request logs using correlated diagnostics.
  3. Inspect the effective configuration using the actual component selectors.
  4. Follow the first failing model, retrieval, tool or identity dependency.

Correct: Repair the identified dependency, then use the appropriate runtime-setting lifecycle or redeployment. Use provisioning for infrastructure changes and a new process or hosted version for startup settings, as specified in those workflows.

Verify: Repeat the same authenticated task and test document authorization when retrieval is involved. Keep credentials and content out of diagnostics.

docs.title: Access denied between services
docs.text:
Symptom: A dependency returns HTTP 401/403 or names a denied action.

Diagnose: Identify the caller's actual principal, target, denied action and scope. Project, deployment and hosted runtime principals each have their own grants. Check service authentication separately from delegated-user authorization.

Correct: Compare the deployed grants with capability profiles and the hosted runtime access model. Allow new assignments to propagate before requesting additional access. Use hosted recovery where required, keeping role assignments scoped to the required resources.

For application-component configuration failures, use this checklist of base capability permissions:

Role Intended resource scope Purpose App Configuration Data Reader Selected App Configuration store Read runtime settings AcrPull Selected container registry Pull images Key Vault Secrets User Selected Key Vault Resolve secret references

Additional grants depend on declared profiles, selected resources and topology. Hosted bootstrap, continuity and panel permissions are reconciled separately. Use the relevant workflow to grant only the roles required by the actual caller.

Verify: The same intended identity can perform the required operation while unauthorized users/documents remain denied.

docs.title: Check application health
docs.text:
List the latest and latest-ready Container Apps revisions:

az containerapp list -g "<resource-group>" --query "[].{name:name,state:properties.runningStatus,latest:properties.latestRevisionName,ready:properties.latestReadyRevisionName}" -o table
az containerapp revision list -g "<resource-group>" -n "<container-app-name>" --query "[].{name:name,active:properties.active,health:properties.healthState,image:properties.template.containers[].image}" -o json

Compare the intended image/revision with the ready revision and traffic routing. An older placeholder can return HTTP 200 while the intended application fails. Inspect system and startup logs for that exact revision.

For a Foundry hosted orchestrator, inspect its routed version, immutable image and Foundry runtime logs separately. Container Apps commands cover the UI, optional ingestion and Container App orchestration, not hosted agent compute.

docs.title: Stream logs from a container app
docs.text:
Select the failing revision explicitly:

az containerapp logs show -g "<resource-group>" -n "<container-app-name>" --revision "<revision-name>" --follow

If the revision has multiple replicas or containers, select the relevant ones using the command's --replica and --container options. Confirm the logs belong to the failed revision and image.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
Use Application Insights > Transaction search to correlate a request with its dependencies and traces. Use Log Analytics for container output and platform events. Confirm diagnostic settings and the selected workspace if expected logs are absent.

Recent Container Apps errors:

ContainerAppConsoleLogs_CL
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where Log_s has_any ("ERROR", "Exception", "Traceback")
| project TimeGenerated, ContainerAppName_s, Log_s
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Revision, scaling and startup events:

ContainerAppSystemLogs_CL
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| project TimeGenerated, ContainerAppName_s, Reason_s, Log_s
| order by TimeGenerated desc

These queries depend on the configured Container Apps log destination and schema; they cover Container Apps rather than Foundry hosted runtime logs. If no rows match, check the time range, log destination and failing revision, then inspect application health directly.

UI records containing exception_type and failure_site intentionally omit dependency error payloads. Correlate the static operation, code location and request reference with dependency telemetry. Do not enable raw token, cookie, claim, signed-URL or document logging to fill that gap. A failed optional panel index write needs repair even when the chat continues. Confirm the expected owner-index record exists after retrying the write.

Telemetry content capture is off by default. Keep prompts and answers private; diagnose with request references and dependency status.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
1. Repeat the exact operation that failed, from the intended host and identity.
  2. Confirm the intended source commit, immutable image and routed hosted version or Container App revision. A placeholder response is not application health.
  3. Test user sign-in, the required tool or retrieval operation, and allowed and denied access to protected data. Treat an unexpected allow as a failure; preserve source permissions while correcting it.
  4. Record sanitized timestamps, request IDs, statuses and the scoped correction. Do not claim success from a green hook exit alone.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
1. Stop retries and promotion. Preserve the diagnostic record and known-good source, input and image records.
  2. Restore only the settings or grants changed during diagnosis, using the recorded values and exact assignment IDs. Preserve unrelated access.
  3. If an application or infrastructure redeployment is required, follow deployment rollback or infrastructure rollback.
  4. Repeat Validation. Keep access closed if safe reversal or protected-data enforcement is not established. Arrange service-specific data recovery with the owner when necessary.

docs.title: User feedback
docs.text:
The default hosted-no-panel application has no supported feedback collection or feedback administration surface. Optional hosted-panel provides Cosmos-backed APIs, but the supplied chat controls do not call those APIs. Hosted feedback requires a custom UI control and validated conversation ownership. Foundry hosted agents provide the container runtime, not this feedback integration.

This page describes those boundaries. The Deploy full stack runbook covers deployment and redeployment, not a ready-made feedback customization.

docs.title: Available surfaces
docs.text:
Surface Supplied behavior hosted-no-panel Chat without application feedback storage. hosted-panel Metadata storage and gated APIs; selection alone does not activate feedback. ENABLE_USER_FEEDBACK Default false. Existing Chainlit thumbs call the non-hosted orchestrator backend, not the panel API. USER_FEEDBACK_RATING Default false. Changes those same controls to a rating/comment form; it does not connect them to hosted feedback.

Anonymous embedded sessions cannot use feedback actions. Keeping both control flags off avoids presenting a hosted feedback integration that is not supplied.

docs.title: Hosted-panel integration contract
docs.text:
User-facing history, feedback and deletion share the same gates.

Dependency Contract Panel deployment DEPLOY_ADMINISTRATIVE_PANEL reflects actual hosted-panel provisioning. Continuity Active owner-bound hosted continuity, not just HOSTED_CONTINUITY_ENABLED=true. User surfaces PANEL_HISTORY_ENABLED defaults to false. Token validation PANEL_CONVERSATIONS_TOKEN_AUDIENCE identifies the delegated token audience; tenant comes from PANEL_CONVERSATIONS_TENANT_ID or the OAuth tenant. Metadata Provisioned DATABASE_ACCOUNT_NAME, DATABASE_NAME and UI identity access to Cosmos. Enumeration PANEL_CONVERSATION_ENUMERATION_MODE=owner_index is the default. Delegated mode requires its own evidence gate.

The default containers are panel-conversation-owner-index and panel-feedback. HOSTED_CONVERSATION_OWNER_BINDING_VALIDATED gates delegated continuity; PANEL_HISTORY_OWNER_BINDING_VALIDATED independently gates delegated panel enumeration. Neither grants permissions. Provisioning resets owner-validation and operator-surface gates to false; they remain false until deployment-specific authorization evidence exists. Agent hosting describes the continuity protocol and permission requirements.

The custom control calls the UI service, not the hosted container:

UI endpoint Purpose GET /panel/conversations Lists the caller's conversation IDs. POST /panel/conversations/{conversation_id}/feedback Creates or upserts that owner's feedback. GET /panel/conversations/{conversation_id}/feedback Reads feedback after the same ownership check.

Every request requires a delegated user bearer with user_impersonation, valid tenant/audience and active gates. Listing is scoped to the caller; per-conversation operations require a Cosmos owner-index match. A conversation ID alone grants no access.

The body contains feedback_id and message_ref (1–128 characters each), optional integer rating from -5 to 5, category up to 64 characters and comment up to 2,000. Unknown fields are rejected. The feedback ID is unique across that owner's conversations; retrying it upserts the owner's record. Tokens are not body fields or URL parameters.

Runtime settings normally use App Configuration label agent-lz and load at UI startup. Deployment settings describes overrides; changes require a UI process reload. Source changes require a compatible application build. Neither enabling flags nor deploying the panel implements the missing control.

docs.title: Expected isolation and failures
docs.text:
An owner can submit and read back saved fields and timestamp. Another user receives 404, indistinguishable from a missing conversation. Missing active gates return 503; invalid identity returns 401/403; invalid input returns 422. Metadata or managed-conversation failures can return 502, not an empty successful feedback list.

PANEL_HISTORY_ENABLED=false disables user history, feedback and deletion after reload without deleting stored metadata or changing hosted chat routing.

docs.title: Administrative views
docs.text:
When the ingestion service is selected, its separate hosted-panel API exposes GET /api/panel/feedback and counts in GET /api/panel/overview. It validates an Entra bearer with the Admin app role and rejects missing tenant configuration. Its schema uses conversationId, messageId, rating: "up" | "down", comment and tags.

The UI schema instead uses message_ref and numeric ratings. There is no shipped adapter joining these schemas into an administrative view.

Operator overview/curation is separately gated by PANEL_OPERATOR_SURFACES_ENABLED, actual deployment, an explicit PANEL_OPERATOR_APP_ROLE or PANEL_OPERATOR_GROUP_ID, and the backend cursor-signing secret. Provisioning leaves it disabled pending authorization validation. The Admin role and user-history gate do not substitute for this operator contract.

docs.title: Privacy and retention
docs.text: Panel Cosmos stores ownership and feedback metadata, not chat transcripts or citations. Comments are still user-authored data and can contain sensitive content. Operator authorization and feedback retention need explicit policy separate from Foundry conversation retention. Cosmos DB time to live can expire configured metadata; this integration sets no automatic retention period. Conversation deletion attempts feedback cleanup, which can fail and needs result verification. Backups have their own retention boundary.

docs.text: Major updates by month. See the release notes for all changes and fixes.

docs.text: Release Highlights v5.5.3 Lower-cost Basic firewall by default for isolated standalone deployments, with matching Bicep/Terraform management networking and topology-aware subnet reservations. v5.5.0 Integrated per-user knowledge security: native Search document permissions, protected citation downloads and interactive Conditional Access recovery. v5.4.0 Integrated Terraform with the native azd lifecycle for infrastructure-only and full-stack deployment, using Azure Storage remote state. Bicep remains the default. v5.3.0 Added 12 default subnets for isolated deployments, including Power Platform and AI Gateway. v5.2.0 Simplified hosted deployment: azd up now prepares the agent image automatically, with no separate preparation step. v5.1.0 Added reviewable outbound firewall rules based on each application's declared network requirements. v5.0.0 Separated Foundry, application and networking resources into three resource groups by default for new deployments. v4.3.0 Made native Foundry IQ ingestion the default, with standalone ingestion as an option. v4.0.0 Separate infrastructure and application deployment workflows.

docs.title: Work IQ
docs.text:
Work IQ provides the signed-in user's Microsoft 365 context, including documents, email and meetings. As a Foundry IQ workIQ knowledge source, it queries that context at retrieval time, without Agent App Ingestion or a landing-zone index copy of the Microsoft 365 corpus.

This page explains the integration contract. Deployment procedures remain in the Deploy full stack runbook.

docs.title: Product support and application readiness
docs.text:
Microsoft supports a Work IQ knowledge source in preview. The source can participate in a Foundry IQ knowledge base called by Foundry Agent Service. Preview status does not require a custom ingestion pipeline.

The supplied source template includes the app-authentication contract and the UI/hosted path keeps Work IQ's app-audience assertion separate from the Search token. No custom retrieval connector is required. Administrator registration, consent, federation and billing remain prerequisites.

Enable the named source with WORK_IQ_ENABLED and WORK_IQ_KNOWLEDGE_SOURCE_NAME, configure the identity values below, and select FOUNDRY_IQ_API_VERSION=2026-08-01-preview. Missing required settings or unverified consent stop provisioning instead of silently removing the source. Foundry IQ explains the integrated identity boundary.

docs.title: Tenant and governance requirements
docs.text:
The Work IQ tenant guide describes administrator enablement and billing. It requires a usage-based billing plan, its Azure subscription/resource group and assignment of querying users. Microsoft 365 Copilot licensing does not replace this billing setup.

Tenant enablement, delegated consent and retrieval-service access are separate requirements. The source administrator needs permission to manage knowledge objects; Microsoft recommends Search Service Contributor for keyless management. Network-isolated Azure resources still need the permitted paths to Microsoft 365 and Microsoft Entra services.

Preview scope

Microsoft warns that this source can invoke Work IQ capabilities that perform actions, not only retrieve information. A pilot needs trusted applications/users, reviewed permissions, billing and data-handling approval. Preview functionality has no SLA and is not recommended for production.

docs.title: Authentication contract
docs.text:
The accelerator defaults to Search API 2026-05-01-preview. Microsoft's current 2026-08-01-preview source contract requires workIQParameters.entraAppAuthentication, including the app's client ID and federated credential object ID. The tenant ID is required for a cross-tenant app registration. These are distinct Entra objects, not source names.

Runtime setting Required value WORK_IQ_APPLICATION_ID Work IQ app's application/client ID; the bundled UI requires the same value as OAUTH_AZURE_AD_CLIENT_ID. WORK_IQ_FEDERATED_CREDENTIAL_ID Object ID returned when creating the app's federated credential, not the Search principal ID or credential name. WORK_IQ_TENANT_ID App tenant ID when different from Search's tenant; otherwise optional. It must match the bundled UI's OAuth tenant.

These are nonsecret UUIDs, published with label agent-lz when explicitly supplied as deployment environment inputs. They do not create the Entra objects or grant tenant consent.

The customer-owned app exposes access_as_user and has the delegated WorkIQAgent.Ask permission with administrator consent. A federated credential allows the Search managed identity to authenticate as that app without storing a client secret in the source.

At query time, service authentication to Search is separate from the signed-in user's assertion:

  • The user assertion targets the customer-owned Work IQ app and includes access_as_user.
  • The current contract carries the raw assertion in x-ms-query-work-iq-source-authorization, not x-ms-query-source-authorization.
  • Search exchanges that assertion for delegated Work IQ access. A Search-audience user token or the agent's managed-identity token is not a substitute.

The official authentication procedure defines registration, federation and client consent. For the bundled UI, use its OAuth app as the Work IQ application: expose access_as_user, grant WorkIQAgent.Ask and configure Search federation on that registration. The built-in path validates and forwards the original app-audience assertion through x-client-work-iq-assertion; it never substitutes the Search token or invokes Work IQ as the workload. It does not exchange an assertion for a separate Work IQ app; mismatched application or UI-tenant settings fail closed. Bearer tokens must stay out of prompts, history and logs.

docs.title: Acceptance and recovery
docs.text:
A pilot needs a known Microsoft 365 document and two accounts with different permissions. Acceptance includes the allowed user's grounded answer and source reference, exclusion of that document for the denied user, and rejection of missing or expired assertions. Concurrent sessions must not share tokens or retrieved content.

Provisioning can overwrite manual knowledge-base edits. Recovery restores the previous application/settings and removes the pilot source reference without deleting shared tenant objects. Revocation of pilot-only grants is a separate, authorized action.

The separate Work IQ MCP product exposes callable tools. It is separate from the workIQ knowledge source and does not replace this source's consent or delegated assertion requirements.

docs.title: AI Gateway Landing Zone
docs.text:
AI Gateway Landing Zone is an enterprise-grade landing zone that provides a centralized, governable, and observable gateway plane for AI consumption across teams and environments. It is delivered by the Citadel Governance Hub solution accelerator, a comprehensive solution for governing, observing, and accelerating AI deployments at scale with unified security, compliance, and intelligent orchestration.

The accelerator helps you deploy and operate the gateway using:

  • Infrastructure-as-code (Bicep, Terraform)
  • A unified AI gateway pattern (Azure API Management)
  • Usage ingestion components (Logic Apps + Event Hub + Cosmos DB)
  • Validation notebooks and operational guides

Use it on its own, or together with Agent Landing Zone, which provides the Azure foundation for the agents and applications that consume the gateway.

Source code: Azure-Samples/ai-hub-gateway-solution-accelerator (Bicep) and Azure/terraform-ai-gateway-landing-zone (Terraform).

docs.title: Part of the AI Citadel Blueprint
docs.text:
Important

This accelerator is the reference implementation of Layer 1 – Governance Hub in the AI Citadel Blueprint layered security architecture.

The AI Citadel Blueprint is a unified, layered approach to AI security and compliance, designed to enable enterprises to scale AI innovation while maintaining trust, security, and regulatory alignment. The blueprint is composed of four interlocking layers:

Layer Name Responsibility Implementation 🔷 Layer 1 Governance Hub Runtime enforcement — unified AI gateway, policy-as-code, identity validation, token rate limiting, content filtering, cost attribution 👉 This Accelerator (aka.ms/ai-hub-gateway) 🔶 Layer 2 Agent Operations Agent runtime, observability & compliance — agent traces, AI evaluations, fleet operations, automated compliance checks Microsoft Foundry Agents & Control Plane 🟢 Layer 3 Agent Management Agent identity & lifecycle governance and security — unique agent identities, blueprints, shadow agent detection, sponsorship model, access packages Governing Agent Identities with Agent 365 🛡️ Layer 4 Security Foundation Unified protection — Microsoft Defender for AI threat intelligence, Purview for data governance, Entra for authentication and authorization Microsoft Defender, Purview & Entra

The layers are not isolated silos — they form an integrated architecture grounded in the principle of separation of concerns with unified oversight.

Layer 1: Governance Hub (this accelerator) acts as the runtime gateway through a hub-and-spoke deployment where a centrally managed AI gateway (Azure API Management) enforces runtime policies, while Layer 2: Agent Operations spoke environments give each business unit autonomous development within guardrails. Adding Layer 3: Agent Management ensures that every agent has a unique, governable identity, while Layer 4: Security Foundation provides unified threat protection and data governance across the entire architecture.

📎 For the full Citadel Blueprint approach and guidance, see the AI Citadel Blueprint section of this site.

docs.title: Benefits (Summary)
docs.text:
Citadel Governance Hub helps you standardize AI governance while maintaining developer velocity:

  • Governance & security: consistent access control, identity patterns, policy enforcement
  • Observability & compliance: central logging/metrics and near real-time usage analytics
  • Developer velocity: repeatable onboarding patterns and contract-driven configuration

For a detailed stakeholder- and capability-level breakdown, see Governance Hub Benefits.

docs.title: What's included
docs.text:
The Bicep implementation includes:

  • bicep/infra: main IaC entrypoint and modules for provisioning the hub in addition to submodules for operational processes.
  • src/usage-ingestion-logicapp: Logic App workflows for processing usage/log streams and other governance workflows.
  • Validation notebooks: Jupyter notebooks for post-deployment validation and onboarding.
  • Operational and architecture guides, published on this site.

The Terraform implementation has a parallel structure to the Bicep implementation.

docs.title: Architecture Overview
docs.text: AI Citadel Governance Hub follows a Central-Control-Plane with decentralized Agent-Execution-Plane architecture that integrates seamlessly with your existing Azure Enterprise Landing Zone network topology:

docs.title: Networking approach
docs.text:
Detailed networking approach guidance for Citadel Governance Hub can be found in the Network Approach Guide.

Initial deployments support optional private-only Logic App website and SCM/Kudu access. This is opt-in; defaults remain public access enabled with no Logic App private endpoint.

Below is a high-level overview of the two supported deployment approaches:

docs.title: Part of spoke network (peered to a hub VNet in the connectivity subscription)
docs.text:
In this approach, the Citadel Governance Hub is deployed within a dedicated spoke VNet that connects to the hub VNet via VNet peering.

Agentic workloads in other spokes are routed first to the hub network firewall through direct peering, then forwarded to the Citadel Governance Hub gateway network.

This provides an additional layer of isolation for AI workloads while still enabling secure communication with other enterprise resources in the hub.

This is the recommended approach for large enterprises with strict network segmentation requirements or those who want to isolate AI workloads from other enterprise resources.

docs.title: Part of the enterprise network hub (usually in Connectivity subscription)
docs.text:
In this approach, the Citadel Governance Hub is deployed within the existing enterprise hub virtual network (VNet) of your Azure Enterprise Landing Zone.

This allows for direct communication between the unified AI gateway and connected agentic spokes (as the hub already peered with all spoke networks), leveraging existing networking configurations.

This approach is suitable for enterprises that prefer to integrate the governance hub within their existing network architecture without additional segmentation.

docs.title: Citadel Governance Hub Components - Central Runtime Control Plane
docs.text: The central governance layer with unified AI Gateway that all AI workloads route through.

docs.title: Agents Onboarding - for existing and new agents
docs.text: To govern AI agents through Citadel Governance Hub, agents must communicate with AI backends (central LLMs, tools and agents) through the Citadel's unified AI gateway.

docs.title: Access Contracts
docs.text:
Leverage Citadel Access Contracts to declare the required access to LLMs, tools and agents through the gateway along with precise governance policies.

Access contracts are infrastructure-as-code declarations of the access requirements and governance policies for an agent, which are then automatically enforced at runtime by the gateway.

NOTE: Recommendation is to create one contract per business-unit/use-case/environment to allow for precise governance policies and better observability in the hub.

docs.title: Publish Contracts (Preview)
docs.text:
Leverage Citadel Publish Contracts to onboard and publish centrally protected AI assets — Tools (MCP) and Agents (A2A) — through the gateway with per-asset backends, resiliency, baseline policies, usage tracking, and optional API Center registration.

Publish contracts are infrastructure-as-code declarations of the AI assets published on the gateway. See the Publish Contract Guide for asset types, backend/auth options, and Foundry A2A publishing.

NOTE: Publish Contracts and Foundry-hosted A2A publishing are available in Preview (publish-contract-version: 1.0.0-preview). Publishing an asset does not grant access to it — governed access (products/subscriptions) is handled by Access Contracts.

docs.title: Existing agents
docs.text:
Guidance to bring existing agents is through updating endpoint and credentials to access central LLMs, tools and agents through the unified gateway endpoint and credentials that are produced by the access contract provisioning for each agent.

NOTE: Recommendation is to use Azure Key Vault to store these information due to its sensitivity when the agent is running on Azure.

docs.title: New agents (AI Landing Zone for Microsoft Foundry)
docs.text:
Building new agents is accelerated through the AI Landing Zone for Microsoft Foundry guidance, which helps enterprises adopt AI faster by offering a governed, secure, and repeatable foundation for deploying AI applications and agents on Azure at scale.

For detailed guidance and technical implementation, see Agent Landing Zone.

Deployment Approach:

  • One Agent Execution Plane per business unit or use case - Deploy dedicated Foundry landing zone environments for each business unit, such as insurance claims processing, customer support automation, or other agentic scenarios
  • Flexible runtime options - with Microsoft Foundry Agents (fully managed agent runtime) you get to choose between native Foundry agents or bring-your-own agent container frameworks like LangChain, Microsoft Agent Framework, or custom implementations while still benefiting from the unified governance and security of the hub
  • Pre-configured infrastructure - Automated deployment via Bicep or Terraform with all networking, security, and monitoring built-in
  • Hub integration - Seamless connection to Citadel Governance Hub through Citadel Access Contracts

Deployment Patterns:

  • Greenfield (Standalone with New Resources) - Creates all infrastructure from scratch with new VNet and Log Analytics workspace
  • Brownfield (Standalone with Existing Resources) - Integrates with existing enterprise landing zones, reusing VNets and centralized monitoring

NOTE: As per Citadel Blueprint principles for Layer 2: Agents Operations, this landing zone provides a standardized foundation for enterprise AI workloads, with implementation options in Terraform and Bicep deployment. By activating Access Contracts, agents deployed in this landing zone can seamlessly integrate with the Citadel Governance Hub for unified runtime governance and observability.

docs.title: Governance Hub Operations - Contract-Driven Governance
docs.text:
Day-to-day operation of the Citadel Governance Hub is contract-driven: every change to what the gateway serves and who can consume it is declared as version-controlled infrastructure-as-code (.bicepparam files) rather than manual portal configuration. Three complementary contract types govern the gateway lifecycle:

  • 🔌 Backend Contracts — govern the supply side: which LLM backends and models the gateway can route to.
  • 📤 Publish Contracts (Preview) — govern which Tools (MCP) and Agents (A2A) are published through the gateway.
  • 📝 Access Contracts — govern the demand side: which use cases and agents can consume those models, and under which policies.

Together they create a clean separation of concerns: platform teams curate AI capacity and published assets, while business units onboard use cases against those governed assets without touching gateway internals.

flowchart LR
    subgraph Supply["🔌 Backend Contracts (Supply)"]
        B1[LLM Backends & Models]
        B2[Load Balancing & Failover]
        B3[Model Aliases]
    end
    subgraph Publishing["📤 Publish Contracts (Preview)"]
        P1[Tools / MCP]
        P2[Agents / A2A]
    end
    subgraph Gateway["🚪 AI Gateway (APIM)"]
        G1[Routing & Policy Engine]
    end
    subgraph Demand["📝 Access Contracts (Demand)"]
        A1[Products & Subscriptions]
        A2[Per-use-case Policies]
        A3[Foundry / Key Vault Credentials]
    end
    Supply --> Gateway
    Publishing --> Gateway
    Gateway --> Demand

docs.title: Backend Contracts — Onboard LLM backends and models
docs.text:
Declares the governed AI capacity the gateway can route to, enabling dynamic backend routing without modifying APIM policies:

  • Multi-provider backends (Microsoft Foundry, Azure OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, external/OpenAI-compatible providers)
  • Automatic load balancing and failover across backends serving the same model
  • Model aliases that abstract a client-facing name over multiple underlying models (with priority/weighted routing)
  • Dynamic model discovery (GET /deployments) so clients and Microsoft Foundry can enumerate available models

🔗 Learn More: Governance Hub Backend Contract Guide

docs.title: Access Contracts — Onboard use cases and agents
docs.text:
Declares the governed dependencies an agent or use case needs—LLMs, AI services, tools, and reusable agents—along with precise access policies enforced at runtime by the gateway:

  • Model selection and capacity allocation (scoped to the curated backend capacity)
  • Per-use-case APIM product, subscription, and policy (one contract per business-unit / use-case / environment)
  • Safety and security guardrails (content safety, PII handling, layered API key + JWT authentication, OAuth scopes)
  • Usage quotas, cost limits, and flexible credential delivery (Key Vault, Microsoft Foundry connection, or direct output)

🔗 Learn More: AI Citadel Access Contracts Guide

docs.title: Publish Contracts (Preview)
docs.text:
Publishes Tools (MCP) and Agents (A2A) through the gateway with declarative endpoint and backend configuration, baseline policies, usage tracking, resiliency for supported backend types, and optional Azure API Center registration. Foundry-hosted agents can be exposed as A2A endpoints.

NOTE: This capability is available in Preview (publish-contract-version: 1.0.0-preview). Its contract surface may change before general availability. See the Publish Contract Guide.

docs.title: Why Contract-Driven Governance
docs.text:
• ✅ Separation of concerns — platform teams manage backends; business units manage their own access contracts
  • ✅ Audit-ready traceability — every backend and access change is captured as reviewable infrastructure-as-code
  • ✅ Faster release cycles — repeatable, declarative onboarding with automated approvals via DevOps pipelines
  • ✅ Reduced manual effort — no manual gateway configuration for onboarding models or use cases
  • ✅ Continuous policy compliance — guardrails are enforced consistently at runtime for every request

docs.title: Deployment Prerequisites (Basic/Fast)
docs.text:
For fast deployment, ensure you have the following prerequisites in place:

Azure Requirements:

  • Azure CLI and Azure Developer CLI installed and signed in
  • Owner or Contributor + User Access Administrator permissions on the subscription
  • All required subscription resource providers registered (providers are outlined in the Full Deployment Guide).

Tools: Although it is recommended to have the below tools installed on a local machine or through DevOps agents to conduct the provisioning, you still can leverage Azure Cloud Shell (mounted to storage account) as an alternative which has all the tools pre-installed.

  • Azure Developer CLI (azd)
  • Azure CLI
  • VS Code (optional)

NOTE: Azure Cloud Shell is a great option for quick deployment without local setup, but for ongoing development and operations, having the tools installed locally or in your DevOps environment along with a git-repo will provide a better experience especially when it comes to production deployments.

docs.title: Quick Deploy
docs.text:
Deploy your Citadel Governance Hub in minutes with Azure Developer CLI:

# Authenticate and setup environment
azd auth login

# in a new folder, initialize the template (i.e. folder name: ai-hub-citadel-dev)
azd init --template Azure-Samples/ai-hub-gateway-solution-accelerator -e ai-hub-citadel-dev --branch citadel-v1

# Deploy Citadel Governance Hub
azd up

💡 Tip: Use Azure Cloud Shell to avoid local setup. This accelerator is setup by default to deploy ready to use Governance Hub. Review main.bicepparam configuration in case your need adjustments before deployment.

To deploy with Terraform instead, follow the Terraform quick start.

docs.title: Transient deployment issues
docs.text:
During deployment, you might encounter transient errors related to resource provisioning, which are common in complex deployments. If you encounter errors, please try to rerun the azd up command. If the issue persists, please check the error message for specific details and ensure that all prerequisites are met.

TIP: For bicep deployments, a full list of deployed resources and status can be found in the Azure Portal under the resource group created -> Deployments.

docs.title: Validation Notebooks
docs.text:
After successful deployment, validate your Citadel Governance Hub setup using our interactive notebooks.

Detailed list and guidance of the available notebooks can be found in the Validation Notebooks Guide, which includes step-by-step instructions to test key functionalities.

docs.title: Release Version
docs.text:
The accelerator tracks its release state in a single source-of-truth manifest at the repository root — release.json. Instead of one monolithic version, it uses independent, component-scoped version tracks so a change in one subsystem does not force re-versioning of unrelated ones:

Track Meaning master-version Umbrella accelerator release version routing-version LLM request routing logic (backend pools, model resolution, failover) backend-contract-version Shape of the llmBackendConfig backend onboarding contract access-contract-version Shape of the Citadel Access Contract (products & access policies) gateway-upgrade-version In-place APIM Gateway Upgrade tooling (currently -preview) usage-ingestion-version Usage ingestion pipeline (Logic App + Function)

The deployed manifest is exposed at runtime through the Release Version API in API Management:

curl https://<your-apim-gateway-host>/version

This GET /version endpoint returns release.json. It is created automatically by the primary deployment and created/updated by the APIM Gateway Upgrade, so the endpoint always reflects the currently deployed release.

The same API also exposes GET /version/backend-contract, which returns the active LLM backend routing contract — a detailed projection of the effective onboarding configuration (APIM target, full llmBackendConfig with per-model metadata, circuit breaker and session affinity settings, model aliases, and derived pools), plus the backend-contract-version:

curl https://<your-apim-gateway-host>/version/backend-contract

Important

The primary deployment (main.bicep) is used for the initial implementation only. After the hub is live, the APIM Gateway Upgrade submodule is the standard way to move the accelerator to new releases — applying the new version in place without re-provisioning the APIM service or landing-zone infrastructure.

📎 For version-track semantics, SemVer rules, and per-track migration guidance, see the Release Version Management Guide.

docs.title: Full announcement: Citadel Governance Hub v1 is generally available
docs.text:
We are announcing the general availability of Citadel Governance Hub v1, the Layer 1 reference implementation of the AI Citadel Blueprint.

Citadel Governance Hub is an enterprise AI landing-zone accelerator that provides a centralized, governable, and observable gateway plane for AI consumption. Built on Azure API Management, it gives platform teams a repeatable way to onboard AI backends, enforce runtime policy, provide governed access to applications and agents, and attribute usage across teams and environments.

The accelerator is available from the Azure Samples repository and at aka.ms/ai-hub-gateway.

docs.title: One governed gateway for multi-provider AI
docs.text:
• Unified routing for Microsoft Foundry, Azure OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, Google Gemini, Anthropic Claude, and OpenAI-compatible providers.
  • Native and OpenAI-compatible API surfaces for chat, embeddings, responses, realtime, and supported image-generation scenarios.
  • Dynamic model discovery and model aliases that decouple client-facing model names from backend deployments.

docs.title: Contract-driven onboarding and governance
docs.text:
• Backend Contracts declare providers, models, authentication, pools, routing behavior, and resiliency settings as infrastructure-as-code.
  • Access Contracts create governed APIM products and subscriptions with model authorization, throttling, quotas, content safety, PII controls, and optional layered JWT authentication.
  • Version-controlled Bicep parameters support repeatable onboarding through pull requests and CI/CD workflows without requiring teams to edit shared gateway policies.

docs.title: Resilient routing for production workloads
docs.text:
• Load-balanced backend pools with priority and weighted routing.
  • Circuit breakers, automated failover, retry-aware behavior, and configurable error handling.
  • Session affinity for stateful model workloads that need follow-up requests routed to the same backend.
  • Multi-region and business-continuity guidance for globally deployed governance hubs.

docs.title: Security, observability, and cost attribution
docs.text:
• Managed identity for supported Azure service-to-service authentication.
  • Central policy enforcement for content safety, PII handling, API keys, JWT validation, rate limits, and quotas.
  • Application Insights, Log Analytics, Event Hubs, Logic Apps, and Cosmos DB integration for operational and usage telemetry.
  • Power BI reporting for usage analysis, cost allocation, and chargeback by product, application, model, and backend.

docs.title: Deployment, operations, and validation
docs.text:
• Bicep-based deployment through Azure Developer CLI, with a separate Terraform implementation.
  • Quick-start and full deployment paths for evaluation and enterprise landing-zone scenarios.
  • Post-deployment guides for backend onboarding, access contracts, authentication, reporting, resiliency, and business continuity.
  • Validation notebooks covering routing, model aliases, multi-provider access, image models, session affinity, security policies, and agent-framework integration.
  • Runtime release visibility through GET /version and active backend-contract visibility through GET /version/backend-contract.

docs.text:
The following capabilities ship with v1 as functional Preview features. Their configuration surfaces may change before general availability, so pin exact versions and validate changes in a non-production environment:

  • Citadel Publish Contracts 1.0.0-preview for publishing Tools (MCP) and Agents (A2A), including Foundry-hosted A2A agents, with baseline policies, usage tracking, supported backend resiliency, and optional Azure API Center registration.
  • Microsoft Foundry APIM connection and Foundry-hosted A2A integration, enabling governed agent access and agent publishing through the gateway.
  • APIM Gateway Upgrade 1.0.0-preview for applying gateway capabilities to an existing Citadel or classic AI Hub Gateway deployment without re-provisioning the surrounding landing-zone infrastructure.
