docs.title: Onboarding New API Types to the Unified AI API
Overview
docs.text:
The Unified AI API uses a modular, fragment-based architecture that supports adding new LLM provider API types without modifying the core routing logic. Each API type is defined by a set of configurations and policy rules that control:

  • Path detection: How the gateway recognizes which API type a request targets
  • Model extraction: How the requested model is identified from the request
  • Path construction: How the backend URI is built for the target provider
  • Authentication: How credentials are set for the backend provider

This guide walks through every step required to add a new API type, using Amazon Bedrock as a concrete example.

Another worked example: image models. The image api-type (Azure OpenAI gpt-image, Black Forest Labs FLUX, Microsoft MAI) was added following exactly these steps — a new image api-type with base-path: /v1/images, new azure-flux/azure-mai backend types with their own backend-path-templates, a {modelPath} slug placeholder resolved in path-builder, and an x-ai-model header fallback for multipart edits in request-processor. See LLM Access Guide — Image Models and LLM Backend Onboarding — Image Models.

docs.title: Architecture Context
docs.text:
The Unified AI API handles all request patterns through a single wildcard endpoint (/unified-ai/*). The routing flow is:

Client Request → Request Processor (detect API type + extract model)
              → Security Handler (authenticate client)
              → Backend Pool Selection (find target backend)
              → Backend Authorization (authenticate to backend)
              → Path Builder (construct backend URI)
              → Forward to Backend

Each step uses APIM policy fragments. Adding a new API type requires updates to specific fragments and configuration files.

docs.title: Two Access Modes per Provider
docs.text:
Most non-Azure providers can be onboarded under one or both of the following access modes. Pick the one(s) you need before editing fragments.

Mode Inbound API surface Path examples Backend poolType URL rewrite responsibility OpenAI-compatible Universal LLM (/models/*) and Unified AI inference (/unified-ai/v1/*) /models/chat/completions, /unified-ai/v1/chat/completions azure-openai, ai-foundry, aws-bedrock-mantle, gemini-openai frag-set-backend-authorization (Universal LLM) or frag-path-builder via config-backend-path-templates (Unified AI inference) Native (provider-specific) Unified AI prefixed paths only (/unified-ai/{provider}/*) /unified-ai/bedrock/model/{id}/converse, /unified-ai/gemini/v1beta/models/{id}:generateContent, /unified-ai/claude/v1/messages aws-bedrock, gemini, anthropic frag-path-builder (per api-type <when> block)

Two design rules that protect surface isolation:

  1. Universal LLM API restricts pool selection to OpenAI-compat pool types. Its policy sets compatiblePoolTypes="azure-openai,ai-foundry,aws-bedrock-mantle,gemini-openai" before set-target-backend-pool runs. If the same model id is registered against both a native pool (e.g. aws-bedrock) and an OpenAI-compat pool (e.g. aws-bedrock-mantle), the gateway will only consider the OpenAI-compat pool — the native one has no /chat/completions rewrite branch and would let an unrewritten path reach the provider, returning errors like com.amazon.coral.service#UnknownOperationException from AWS Bedrock.
  2. Each Unified AI api-type declares its own compatible-pool-types. Native api-types like bedrock declare compatible-pool-types: 'aws-bedrock'; the OpenAI-compat inference api-type declares compatible-pool-types: 'ai-foundry,azure-openai,aws-bedrock-mantle,gemini-openai'. This keeps surfaces from cross-routing without relying on suffix tricks.

When you add a new provider, decide whether you need:

  • Native only (e.g. provider has no OpenAI-compat surface): add a Unified AI api-type with its own prefix and compatible-pool-types matching its native pool type.
  • OpenAI-compat only (e.g. provider exposes only /v1/chat/completions): add the backend with a pool type already in Universal LLM's compatible list (aws-bedrock-mantle, gemini-openai, etc.). Add a <when> rewrite branch in frag-set-backend-authorization for Universal LLM, and a path template in config-backend-path-templates for the Unified AI inference api-type.
  • Both: define two backends (one per pool type) and update both the api-type entry and the OpenAI-compat artifacts.

docs.title: Updating set-llm-requested-model for new providers
docs.text:
The set-llm-requested-model fragment is invoked from all three LLM API policies (Universal LLM, Azure OpenAI, Unified AI request-processor falls back to it implicitly via shared logic) and from Citadel access-contract product policies (default-ai-product-policy.xml) so that validate-model-access can enforce allowedModels regardless of which surface the call lands on.

Existing patterns it recognizes (in order):

  1. deployment-id named path parameter (Azure OpenAI named operations)
  2. /deployments/{model}/... segment (Azure OpenAI wildcards, /openai/deployments/...)
  3. /model/{modelId}/... singular segment (AWS Bedrock Converse / Invoke; URL-decoded)
  4. /models/{modelId}:method plural segment with : terminator (Gemini native; URL-decoded)
  5. Request body model field (OpenAI-compat, Anthropic Messages, Bedrock OpenAI-compat)

If your new provider exposes the model in a different URL position (anything other than the patterns above) or in a body field other than model, you must extend frag-set-llm-requested-model.xml (both copies under bicep/infra/modules/apim/policies/ and bicep/infra/llm-backend-onboarding/modules/policies/). Otherwise the access contract will return 400 missing_model_parameter for every native call, even when the request is valid for the provider.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before starting, ensure you have:

  • A working deployment of AI Citadel Governance Hub with the Unified AI API
  • Understanding of the target provider's API format (endpoint URLs, auth mechanism, request/response format)
  • Access to deploy Bicep templates to your APIM instance

docs.title: Step 1: Define the API Type in Metadata Configuration
docs.text:
The metadata-config fragment is the central configuration that defines all supported API types. Each API type needs three properties:

Property Description base-path The URL path prefix that identifies this API type in incoming requests path-segment The path segment used for model extraction from the URL api-version Default API version sent to the backend

File: bicep/infra/llm-backend-onboarding/modules/policies/frag-metadata-config.xml (also mirrored in bicep/infra/modules/apim/policies/frag-metadata-config.xml)

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: The request-processor fragment iterates over all entries in api-types and matches the incoming request path against each base-path. The first match determines the API type.

docs.title: Adding Your API Type
docs.text:
Add a new entry to the api-types object in the metadata config. The key is your API type identifier (used throughout all fragments).

Example — Adding Amazon Bedrock (native Converse / InvokeModel):

'bedrock-native': {
    'base-path': '/bedrock',
    'path-segment': '/bedrock',
    'api-version': 'bedrock-2024-04-15',
    'compatible-pool-types': 'aws-bedrock'
}

The compatible-pool-types CSV restricts which backend pools the request can land on — here, only pools whose poolType == 'aws-bedrock'. This prevents the gateway from accidentally routing a /unified-ai/bedrock/... call to an aws-bedrock-mantle (OpenAI-compat) pool that happens to advertise the same model name. Native and OpenAI-compat surfaces stay isolated without requiring suffix tricks on model ids.

docs.title: Important Considerations
docs.text:
1. Prefix matching with longest-match wins: The request-processor uses case-insensitive StartsWith matching against the request path (after stripping the /unified-ai API prefix) and selects the longest matching base-path. This means declaration order in api-types does not affect routing — /openai/v1/responses will always win over /openai/v1 or /openai for a request like /openai/v1/responses/{id}. Unrecognized prefixes (e.g. /v2/openai/...) are rejected with 403 PathNotAllowed.

  2. The base-path must be unique: No two API types should declare the same base-path value.

  3. Optional backend property: If your API type should always route to a specific backend (bypassing model-based pool routing), add a backend property: 

    'my-api-type': {
    'base-path': '/my-path',
    'path-segment': '/my-path',
    'api-version': '2024-01-01',
    'backend': 'my-specific-backend-id'
}
    This sets apiTypeOverrideBackend in the request processor, which tells set-target-backend-pool to skip pool matching.

  4. Both copies must be updated: The metadata config exists in two locations:

    • bicep/infra/llm-backend-onboarding/modules/policies/frag-metadata-config.xml — Used when deploying via the LLM backend onboarding module
    • bicep/infra/modules/apim/policies/frag-metadata-config.xml — Used when deploying the full Citadel infrastructure

docs.title: Step 2: Add Path Construction Logic
docs.text:
The path-builder fragment reconstructs the backend URI based on the detected API type. You need to add a <when> condition for your new API type.

File: bicep/infra/modules/apim/policies/frag-path-builder.xml

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: The path builder uses a <choose> block to select path construction logic based on the api-type variable (set by request-processor). It sets the finalPath variable, which is then used to rewrite the request URI.

docs.title: Available Variables
docs.text: Variable Source Description api-type request-processor The detected API type identifier api-base-path request-processor The base path from metadata config requestedModel request-processor The extracted model name response-id request-processor Response ID (for responses API) selected-api-version request-processor API version for the request

docs.title: Adding Your Path Logic
docs.text:
Add a new <when> block inside the <choose> element, before the default <otherwise> block.

Example — Amazon Bedrock path (strip the /bedrock prefix and forward the rest):

<!-- Amazon Bedrock native: /bedrock/model/{model}/converse → /model/{model}/converse -->
<when condition="@(context.Variables.GetValueOrDefault<string>("api-type", "").Equals("bedrock-native", StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase))">
    <set-variable name="finalPath" value="@{
        var basePath = context.Variables.GetValueOrDefault<string>("api-base-path", "");
        var rawPath  = context.Request.OriginalUrl.Path;
        var idx      = rawPath.IndexOf(basePath, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase);
        return idx >= 0 ? rawPath.Substring(idx + basePath.Length) : rawPath;
    }" />
</when>

docs.title: Path Pattern Reference
docs.text:
Pattern When to Use Example {base-path}/chat/completions OpenAI-compatible APIs Gemini, Inference {base-path}/deployments/{model}/chat/completions Deployment-based APIs Azure OpenAI {base-path} or {base-path}/{id} Resource-based APIs Responses API /bedrock/model/{model}/converse (prefix-strip) Provider-specific native paths Amazon Bedrock, Gemini native Fixed path with body-model rewrite Provider-specific paths whose API has no model in URL Anthropic Claude (/claude/v1/messages)

Stateful APIs (Responses API) — When your new api-type exposes server-side stateful resources keyed by an id (similar to OpenAI's Responses API response_id), pair it with the cross-API responses-id-security / responses-id-cache-store fragments described in LLM access guide. Those fragments are wired in once per API policy and cover Universal LLM, Azure OpenAI, and Unified AI surfaces, returning 403 on cross-subscription or cross-product access and 404 on unknown ids. Ownership mappings last 30 days, matching the default OpenAI Responses API retention period.

docs.title: Additional Behaviors
docs.text:
Your path builder block can also:

  • Set query parameters: Use <set-query-parameter> to inject API version or other params
  • Modify the request body: Use <set-body> to add/transform fields (e.g., inject model field)
  • URL-encode model IDs: Use System.Uri.EscapeDataString() for models with special characters (e.g., Bedrock's us.anthropic.claude-3-5-haiku-20241022-v1:0)

docs.title: Step 3: Add Backend Authentication
docs.text:
The set-backend-authorization fragment configures how APIM authenticates to each backend type. If your new API type uses a different authentication mechanism than the existing ones, you need to add a new <when> block.

Files (both must be updated):

  • bicep/infra/llm-backend-onboarding/modules/policies/frag-set-backend-authorization.xml
  • bicep/infra/modules/apim/policies/frag-set-backend-authorization.xml

docs.title: Existing Auth Patterns
docs.text: Backend Type Auth Mechanism Implementation ai-foundry Azure Managed Identity <authentication-managed-identity> with Cognitive Services scope azure-openai Azure Managed Identity Same as ai-foundry + URL rewriting external Backend credentials No auth header (credentials configured on backend resource) aws-bedrock AWS SigV4 Custom policy computing HMAC-SHA256 signature

docs.title: Adding Your Auth Logic
docs.text:
Add a new <when> block that matches on targetPoolType (which comes from the backendType in your backend configuration).

Example — AWS SigV4 for Amazon Bedrock:

The AWS Signature Version 4 authentication requires:

  1. Computing a SHA-256 hash of the request body
  2. Constructing a canonical request string
  3. Deriving a signing key from the secret key + date + region + service
  4. Computing an HMAC-SHA256 signature
  5. Setting the Authorization, X-Amz-Date, X-Amz-Content-Sha256, and Host headers

The full implementation uses APIM named values for credentials:

  • aws-access-key: AWS IAM access key ID
  • aws-secret-key: AWS IAM secret access key
  • aws-region: AWS region (e.g., us-east-1)

See the Microsoft Learn guide on Amazon Bedrock APIM integration for the complete SigV4 policy implementation.

docs.title: Named Values for Credentials
docs.text:
If your auth mechanism requires secrets (API keys, tokens), store them as APIM named values:

  1. Add parameters to llm-policy-fragments.bicep for the credentials
  2. Create named value resources conditionally (only when backends of your type exist)
  3. Reference in policy using {{named-value-name}} syntax

Example — Adding AWS named values in Bicep:

// In llm-policy-fragments.bicep

// Parameters
@secure()
param awsAccessKey string = ''
@secure()
param awsSecretKey string = ''
param awsRegion string = ''

// Check if any backend uses this type
var hasBedrockBackend = length(filter(llmBackendConfig, config => config.backendType == 'aws-bedrock')) > 0

// Always create named values (with safe defaults) so the policy fragment compiles
// even when no backends of this type are configured.
resource awsAccessKeyNamedValue 'Microsoft.ApiManagement/service/namedValues@2024-06-01-preview' = {
  name: 'aws-access-key'
  parent: apimService
  properties: {
    displayName: 'aws-access-key'
    value: !empty(awsAccessKey) ? awsAccessKey : 'NOT_CONFIGURED'
    secret: true
  }
}

Important: APIM resolves {{named-value}} references at policy save/compile time, not at runtime. If a named value doesn't exist in APIM, the policy fragment deployment will fail. Always create the named values — even with placeholder defaults — and add a runtime guard in the policy to return a clear error when the placeholder is detected. For example: 

<choose>
    <when condition="@("{{aws-access-key}}" == "NOT_CONFIGURED")">
        <return-response>
            <set-status code="500" reason="Internal Server Error" />
            <set-body>{"error": {"code": "AWSCredentialsNotConfigured", ...}}</set-body>
        </return-response>
    </when>
</choose>

docs.title: Step 4: Configure the Backend in LLM Onboarding
docs.text:
Add your backend to the llmBackendConfig array in your .bicepparam file with a new backendType value.

File: Your deployment parameter file (e.g., llm-backends-dev-local.bicepparam)

docs.title: Backend Configuration Properties
docs.text:
Property Value for Your API Type backendId Unique identifier (e.g., bedrock-us-east-1) backendType Your new type identifier (e.g., aws-bedrock) — must match the targetPoolType in auth fragment endpoint Base URL of the provider (e.g., https://bedrock-runtime.us-east-1.amazonaws.com) authType Authentication type (e.g., aws-sigv4, managed-identity, api-key-bearer). The legacy authScheme is still tolerated but superseded by authType. supportedModels Array of model definitions with metadata

Stateful models: add sessionAwareModel: true to any model object that must keep a client pinned to one backend across a session (e.g., the OpenAI Responses / Assistants APIs). When that model is served by a multi-backend pool, the pool gets session affinity so requests replaying the affinity cookie stick to the same backend. A single backend can mix session-aware and stateless models. Tune the cookie with configureSessionAffinity / sessionAffinityDefaults (default cookie ai-gateway-affinity) or a per-backend sessionAffinity override. See LLM Backend Onboarding — Session Affinity Configuration.

Example — Amazon Bedrock backend:

param llmBackendConfig = [
  {
    backendId: 'bedrock-us-east-1'
    backendType: 'aws-bedrock'
    endpoint: 'https://bedrock-runtime.us-east-1.amazonaws.com'
    authType: 'aws-sigv4'
    supportedModels: [
      {
        "name": "us.anthropic.claude-3-5-haiku-20241022-v1:0"
        "sku": "OnDemand"
        "capacity": 1
        "modelFormat": "Anthropic"
        "modelVersion": "1"
        "retirementDate": "2099-12-30"
      }
      {
        "name": "us.anthropic.claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022-v2:0"
        "sku": "OnDemand"
        "capacity": 1
        "modelFormat": "Anthropic"
        "modelVersion": "2"
        "retirementDate": "2099-12-30"
      }
    ]
    priority: 1
    weight: 100
  }
]

// AWS credentials (required for aws-bedrock backends)
param awsAccessKey = '<your-aws-access-key-id>'
param awsSecretKey = '<your-aws-secret-access-key>'
param awsRegion = 'us-east-1'

docs.title: Pass-Through Parameters
docs.text:
Ensure the new parameters flow through the module chain:

  1. main.bicep — Add parameters and pass to llmPolicyFragments module
  2. modules/llm-policy-fragments.bicep — Accept parameters and create named values
  3. modules/llm-backends.bicep — No changes needed (backend creation is generic)
  4. modules/llm-backend-pools.bicep — No changes needed (pool creation is generic)

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
az deployment sub create \
  --name llm-backend-onboarding \
  --location <location> \
  --template-file main.bicep \
  --parameters llm-backends-dev-local.bicepparam

docs.title: Verify Configuration
docs.text:
1. Check APIM backends: Verify the new backend resource was created in the Azure Portal under API Management → Backends
  2. Check named values: Verify credential named values were created (e.g., aws-access-key, aws-secret-key, aws-region)
  3. Check policy fragments: Verify metadata-config fragment includes your new API type and model mappings

docs.title: Test the Endpoint
docs.text:
Send a request through the Unified AI API using your new API type's path pattern:

curl -X POST "https://<apim-gateway>/unified-ai/bedrock/model/us.anthropic.claude-3-5-haiku-20241022-v1:0/converse" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "api-key: <subscription-key>" \
  -d '{
    "messages": [
      {
        "role": "user",
        "content": [{"text": "Hello"}]
      }
    ],
    "inferenceConfig": {
      "maxTokens": 512,
      "temperature": 0.5
    }
  }'

docs.title: Frontier, made executable — one governed platform for any agent, any data, any tool, any model
docs.text:
Frontier Transformation is the destination. The AI Citadel Blueprint is how you get there.

Frontier Transformation is Microsoft's strategy for how organizations move from experimenting with AI to transforming at enterprise scale — the what and the why. The AI Citadel Blueprint is the how: the opinionated technical implementation that carries that strategy into production, securely and at scale.

The promise of that how is universality. Regardless of the agent you build, the data you hold, the tools you need, or the models you choose, you get intelligence delivered through one governed platform — where trust is everybody's responsibility, layered by design.

Note

AI Citadel Blueprint provides opinionated, pre-built patterns for AI governance that leverage Microsoft's unique capabilities and ecosystem while remaining model-diverse, open, and supportive of heterogeneous environments. It is not a one-size-fits-all solution — it is a proven architectural approach to adapt and extend based on your organizational structure, risk profile, and regulatory context.

Opinionated where it speeds you up — open everywhere it matters.

docs.title: The opportunity — and the wall
docs.text:
The ambition is proven. Execution is where it breaks.

🟣 THE OPPORTUNITY 🔴 THE WALL

88% of Frontier Firms report strength in top-line growth — compared to just 23% for laggards.

2.3x average ROI reported for agentic AI.

95% of AI pilots never reach production — as agents scale, risk, integration, and cost compound exponentially.

84% of companies haven't redesigned work around AI capabilities.

Sources: Deloitte, State of AI in the Enterprise (Jan 2026); IDC InfoBrief sponsored by Microsoft (US53838325, Nov 2025); Microsoft (95% pilot figure).

Strategy sets the destination — something must carry it into production, securely and at scale.

docs.title: Why scaling agents breaks current infrastructure
docs.text:
Early AI innovation feels fast — teams spin up agents quickly. But once organizations move beyond 50–100 agents, things break. Not because the technology failed, but because governance didn't scale. Two things happen at once:

  • Shadow AI emerges outside central control.
  • Operational friction explodes as security and risk teams fall back on manual reviews.

The result is higher cost, less visibility, and loss of trust. This is the production wall — a structural problem, not a tooling problem.

docs.title: Traditional security is blind to agentic intent
docs.text:
When AI moves from chatting to acting, the threat model changes completely. Traditional security inspects packets, headers, and endpoints — but it cannot understand intent. Agents reason, plan, and take actions at machine speed, which introduces semantic risk: prompt injection, jailbreaks, unintended actions, and cascading failures.

Identity changes too. Agents are not users and they are not applications. They require dynamic, policy-aware identities, not static service accounts. Governance must understand context, intent, and behavior in real time.

The real question: what must be true for an organization to scale from 10 agents to 10,000, while staying grounded in insight, control, and trust?

The answer: AI governance is the bridge to scale. This is where governance stops being a blocker and becomes an enabler.

Tip

The proof. In January 2026, Microsoft was named a Leader in the IDC MarketScape for Worldwide Unified AI Governance Platforms 2025–2026, recognized for end-to-end governance spanning traditional machine learning, generative AI, and agentic AI. But the real differentiator is not the analyst label — it is the ability to execute governance at enterprise scale.

docs.title: Frontier success framework: four pillars
docs.text:
Frontier Firms move beyond experimentation to enterprise-scale transformation — organized around four pillars of business value, not technology.

# Pillar What it means 01 Enrich employee experiences Automate the routine so people do their best, most human work — with AI in the flow of work. 02 Reinvent customer engagement Deliver personalized, responsive experiences at every touchpoint — grounded in your context. 03 Reshape business processes Reimagine workflows end-to-end — not incremental fixes — with agents acting on the business. 04 Bend the curve on innovation Put the power to build in every role, closest to the problem — and scale it enterprise-wide.

Every one of these pillars is delivered by the same platform — just pointed at a different experience.

docs.title: The Frontier transformation engine: Intelligence + Trust
docs.text:
Frontier Transformation rests on two forces working together:

  • Intelligence — deep business context: the agents that actually deliver the experience.
  • Trust — security, governance, and control: what lets you move faster with confidence.

Citadel Blueprint is the opinionated implementation of that engine — layered, yet integrated, so rich intelligence and uncompromised trust ship together at the speed of innovation.

Rich intelligence Uncompromised trust Undiminished speed Intelligence layer Trust, shared Speed of innovation Any model, any agent type — SaaS, managed, BYO, 3rd-party Agent-level: traces, evals, red-teaming, guardrails Opinionated defaults, not a blank canvas Grounded in heterogeneous context (IQ) Platform-level: Governance Hub, Agent Management Controls live in the platform, not in every build Extended by your tools (MCP), agent-to-agent Security Foundation protects & detects across the estate New agents inherit trust on day one

docs.title: The mapping that matters
docs.text:
Both forces map onto the blueprint — but not the way people expect:

  • Intelligence is surfaced through Agent Operations (Layer 2). The agents that deliver the experience: any type, grounded in your data, using your tools, on any model.
  • Trust is not the job of a couple of security controls off to the side. It starts inside Agent Operations — end-to-end traces, AI evaluations, red-teaming, and guardrails tuned to each agent's type and objective. That is agent-level trust, and the builder owns it.
  • Three platform controls then extend trust across the whole estate — Governance Hub governs every call, Agent Management makes every agent accountable, and Security Foundation protects and detects.

The layer that delivers intelligence is also the first line of trust — then the platform controls make it hold at scale.

docs.title: Citadel Blueprint: the four layers
docs.text:
These are not four disconnected point tools. They are four reinforcing layers that compound into one governed, defensible system for production AI.

Layer Name Role Built on The advantage 🔷 L1 Governance Hub Runtime enforcement plane — govern every call Azure API Management · Azure API Center Govern once, enforce everywhere. Policy set centrally applies to every model, tool, and agent — control scales with adoption instead of fighting it. 🔶 L2 Agent Operations The AI experience engine and its first line of trust Microsoft Foundry · Agent Service · Foundry IQ · Control Plane · Container Apps / AKS Ship agents faster, safely. Templated landing zones and built-in guardrails turn months of setup into repeatable, observable deployments. Foundry serves as runtime and as the observability plane for agents running anywhere. 🟢 L3 Agent Management The command center for every agent — every agent owned Microsoft Agent 365 · Entra Agent ID · Agent 365 SDK Every agent owned and accountable. One registry, one identity model, one audit trail — spanning SaaS, managed runtime, BYO, and third-party agents. Identity is the connective tissue that lights up Layer 4. 🛡️ L4 Security Foundation Unified protection across all layers — protect & detect Microsoft Defender · Microsoft Purview · Microsoft Entra Security & compliance, built in. Continuous threat protection, data governance, and access control beneath every layer.

Regardless of the agent, data, tools, or models — trust is shared: agent-level in Agent Operations, platform-level across the controls.

docs.title: Separation of concerns with unified oversight
docs.text:
Each layer owns a distinct governance responsibility, yet all layers interlock. This layered separation means teams can evolve any single capability — upgrade the gateway, add new compliance evaluators, onboard new agent types, adopt emerging detections — without destabilizing the rest of the stack. The result is an architecture that scales from 10 to 10,000 agents while keeping governance both comprehensive and composable.

The Governance Hub and the Agent Operations spokes are deployed hub-and-spoke: a centrally managed gateway enforces runtime policy while each business unit gets an autonomous environment to build in. Governance stays centralized; execution scales horizontally. In short — local freedom, global rules.

docs.title: Trust is everybody's responsibility
docs.text:
Trust isn't one team's job — it's layered across four interconnected controls that are complementary, not sequential. Note the ownership line under each; this is the heart of the model.

Control Scope What it delivers Owned by 🔶 Agent Operations Agent-level End-to-end traces, AI evals, red-teaming & guardrails — tuned to each agent's type and objective The agent builder 🔷 Governance Hub Platform · Govern Every model, tool & agent call flows through one governed gateway — routing, policy, content safety, capacity & observability The AI CoE & platform team 🟢 Agent Management Platform · Identify Every agent is an owned enterprise asset — a first-class identity, sponsor, lifecycle & audit trail, whoever built it and wherever it runs IAM & security 🛡️ Security Foundation Platform · Protect Defender, Purview & Entra deliver threat protection, data governance & access beneath every agent The security org

Trust starts inside the agent and extends across the platform — from 10 to 10,000 agents.

➡️ Full operating model and RACI: Organizational Alignment & Ownership

docs.title: Agent Management is the command center — and the connective tissue
docs.text:
One layer deserves a closer look, because it is the most under-scoped in practice and the highest-leverage in effect.

Microsoft Agent 365 is not the control plane for Microsoft agents. It is the control plane for every agent.

Agent type How it lands in Agent 365 SaaS — Microsoft 365 Copilot, Copilot Studio Native — automatic identity and registry entry Managed runtime — Microsoft Foundry Agent Service Native — identity per project and per published agent Platform / BYO — your framework on AKS, ACA, Agent Framework Register via workload identity + the Agent 365 SDK Third-party & on-prem — partner and non-Microsoft runtimes Federate via the Agent 365 SDK, which a broad partner ecosystem already integrates with

One registry. One identity model. One policy surface. One audit trail. Organised around three pillars — Observe (registry, agent map, analytics), Govern (onboarding, lifecycle, audit, data compliance), and Secure (access control, data security, threat protection).

It earns the "command center" name in two ways:

  1. It attributes traffic to an agent. Most AI calls reach models via proxies or gateways, losing the calling identity in the process. Without this layer you can see that something called a model — not which agent, on whose behalf, under what approval, or with what data.
  2. It aggregates signals from the whole stack. Agent 365 consolidates Entra, Defender, and Purview insights — alongside gateway audit logs and Foundry traces — into one agent-centric control plane with detailed logs for audit and triage.

The governing principle: the best way to manage agents is to extend the infrastructure you already use to manage users. Same Entra, same Purview, same Defender, same admin center — agents simply become another identity type.

➡️ Full detail: Layer 3 · Agent Management

docs.title: Defense in depth: no single point of failure
docs.text:
One control is never enough — enforce critical guardrails in more than one place.

Standard security practice: never depend on a single layer. If it's bypassed or simply can't apply, the system is exposed. Citadel's controls deliberately overlap, so coverage holds however an agent is built or hosted.

Worked example — content safety is enforceable at three controls:

Control Where it applies 🔷 Governance Hub At the AI gateway and at Foundry-hosted models 🔶 Agent Operations In Foundry — Agent Service runtime & control-plane guardrails 🛡️ Security Foundation Microsoft Defender (Defender for AI) monitoring across the estate

When one control can't apply, another holds the line:

Scenario What breaks What holds Agent runs outside Foundry — a self-hosted model on a GPU VM Agent Operations & Security Foundation can't apply out of the box ➡️ Governance Hub enforces it at the gateway, because that traffic still flows through the gateway as mediator between agent and model Microsoft Copilot agents — traffic doesn't traverse your gateway or Foundry Governance Hub & Agent Operations can't apply out of the box ➡️ Agent Management (Agent 365) and Security Foundation (Defender) enforce it — on top of Copilot's native protections

Same risk, multiple enforcement points — if one control can't apply or is bypassed, another does.

docs.title: Layered observability: one estate, many lenses
docs.text:
The same telemetry, surfaced for the people who act on it. Redundancy isn't waste — it's the right altitude for each audience, and each lens ends in an action.

🟣 CENTRAL IT, FinOps & SECURITYSee the whole estate 🔵 AGENT OWNERS & BUILDERSSee their own agents

Agent 365 dashboard — organization-wide view of every agent: security signals, access patterns, usage and activation.

Governance Hub performance, usage & chargeback — organization-wide, via the AI Gateway, surfaced through Power BI–powered dashboards.

Act on it

  • Assign capacity controls and quotas
  • Govern model access with RBAC — Governance Hub
  • Suspend rogue agents — block in Agent 365 or revoke the access contract
  • Alert on critical events — backend, authorization, content-safety, PII failures

Foundry Observability — end-to-end performance, traces, evals and quality signals per agent.

Foundry usage & cost — per-agent consumption for the team that owns it.

Act on it

  • Apply capacity controls to their own agents
  • Agent Optimizer — learns from agent behavior and recommends better configurations: sharper instructions, skills and tool descriptions, and model selection

Same signals, different altitude — everyone sees what they need to act on, nobody flies blind.

docs.title: Every Frontier pillar, delivered
docs.text:
One experience engine, four experiences. The trust controls are identical in every row — that's the point: they don't change with the agent type.

Pillar The experience Agent pattern Public proof point 01 · Enrich employee experiences Copilot — and pro-code agents in the flow of work. Low-code SaaS agents get every maker started; then publish pro-code Foundry agents straight into Microsoft 365, bringing specialist depth into the same employee experience. Copilot Studio (SaaS) + Foundry Agents published to Microsoft 365 Children International — cut solution development from 3 months to 2 days; on track to grow direct child interventions 25% in four years with no budget increase. 02 · Reinvent customer engagement Customer-facing agents that act — grounded in your product and customer IQ, using MCP tools to act in real systems, at scale, without running the infrastructure. Managed runtime — Microsoft Foundry Agent Service Alaska Airlines — embedded AI into service workflows: 75% less customer planning time, 90% guest satisfaction, 87% would use it again. 03 · Reshape business processes Autonomous, collaborating agents. Redesign the workflow, don't just speed it up — bring your own framework on Azure managed compute and let multiple agents collaborate on the state of the business, within clear boundaries. Managed compute (BYO) on AKS / ACA + multi-agent collaboration Levi's — work once estimated at up to a year completed in a single day; a 97% productivity gain. 04 · Bend the curve on innovation A maker in every role. Innovation stalls when only specialists can build — give every role the full range of agent types on one platform, with shared IQ, tools, and templates. The full mix — SaaS + Foundry + BYO + 3rd-party/on-prem, any model Accenture — centralized enterprise AI platform: build time down 50%, efficiency up 30%, costs down 20%; 17 use cases shipped in 4 months.

docs.title: Agent Operations: runtime and observability & control plane
docs.text:
A second layer worth calling out, because the distinction unlocks adoption for customers who cannot re-platform.

Microsoft Foundry plays two independent roles — adopt either, or both:

Role What it means ① Runtime Host agents in Foundry — prompt agents and hosted agents (your own container and framework). They automatically inherit every Foundry capability: tracing, evaluations, guardrails, identity, IQ grounding, MCP tools, and fleet operations. ② Observability plane for agents running elsewhere Agents on AKS, Azure Container Apps, other clouds, or on-premises forward OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic traces into Foundry-connected Application Insights — and light up in the same plane for centralized traces, AI evaluations, quality and safety signals, and fleet operations, without being hosted in Foundry at all.

This decouples the hosting decision from the governance decision. There is no forced choice between "adopt Foundry as a runtime" and "no Foundry at all" — estate-wide observability is adoptable on its own, and it is often the faster route to visibility across a heterogeneous estate.

The managed runtime is a convenience; the observability is the strategic value.

➡️ Full detail: Layer 2 · Agent Operations

docs.title: Measurable business impact
docs.text: Outcome What it looks like 🚀 Faster time-to-value Pre-built patterns and templated landing zones turn months of build-out into days 🛡️ Reduced risk Compliance is woven in from the start, not bolted on — agents operate within safe boundaries from day one 💰 Cost control Granular usage tracking, quotas, and per-consumer chargeback — no surprise invoices 📈 Scalable adoption When one team succeeds, others follow the same blueprint instead of reinventing the wheel 🤝 Cross-functional alignment Compliance officers and AI developers work from the same explicit, automated requirements 🔁 Unified AI ecosystem & reuse All shared models, tools, and agents reachable through one gateway and listed in one registry — more reuse, less duplication

docs.title: Future-proofing
docs.text:
• 🔌 Protocol-agnostic — REST, MCP, A2A, and emerging protocols
  • ☁️ Multi-cloud and hybrid capable — one control plane, data plane everywhere
  • 🧩 Extensible — partner integrations (Credo AI, Saidot, Palo Alto Networks, Zenity) enhance capabilities
  • 📜 Regulatory alignment — with layered controls in place, mapping new regulatory requirements to technical controls becomes straightforward

docs.title: The bottom line
docs.text:
Frontier is the destination. The AI Citadel Blueprint is how you get there — any agent, at scale.

It reduces to two ideas:

  1. One experience engine. Agent Operations delivers every experience — any agent, grounded in your data, using your tools, on any model.
  2. Shared trust. It starts inside the agent with traces, evals, red-teaming, and guardrails, and extends across the platform through Governance Hub, Agent Management, and Security Foundation — layered deliberately, so no single control is a single point of failure.

That is what lets you scale from ten agents to ten thousand without trading away cost control, identity, data protection, or compliance. And it isn't theoretical for Microsoft — we are Customer Zero.

💡 Those that can trust will scale. Those that scale AI effectively will win.

  • Backend contracts registered for every approved model source (Azure, on-prem, other clouds)
  • Access contracts defined per consuming use case, with auth, limits, and safety policy bundled
  • Universal AI catalog populated in Azure API Center — models, tools, agents, skills
  • Performance, usage, and chargeback dashboards live and attributed per consumer
  • Audit logs streaming to Defender / Sentinel

➡️ Layer 1 · Governance Hub in detail

docs.title: Track 2 · Agent Operations
docs.text:
Speed without sacrificing control.

Stage Activity Deep Dive Deep dive into Microsoft Foundry and the Foundry Control Plane for rapid agent development, observability, evaluations, and fleet-wide operations. Proof of Value Show how teams build, onboard, and iterate on agents quickly while maintaining guardrails, quality signals, and production readiness. Production Scale to fleet-wide operations with full observability and continuous evaluations across the estate.

Deploy: Foundry Landing Zone — Agent Landing Zone — one spoke per business unit or use case.

Tip

This track has two independent adoption paths — run either, or both.

Path A — Foundry as runtime. Start with prompt agents or hosted agents (your own container and framework). Controls are inherited automatically: tracing, evaluations, guardrails, identity, IQ grounding, MCP tools. You configure only the gateway connection.

Path B — Foundry as the observability plane. Keep agents where they run today — AKS, Azure Container Apps, other clouds, on-premises, Copilot Studio, third-party runtimes — and instrument them with OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions exporting to Foundry-connected Application Insights. They land in the same plane for centralized traces, AI evaluations, and fleet visibility without re-platforming a single agent.

Path B is often the faster route to estate-wide visibility, and it decouples the hosting decision from the governance decision. See Layer 2 · Agent Operations.

Accountable owners: AI CoE (runtime & tooling approval) · Platform Engineering (runtime infra) · AI Engineering (build & operate) · LOB (business value)

Exit criteria

  • At least one spoke landing zone deployed from template
  • Application Insights connected; end-to-end tracing live for the pilot agents
  • Agent-specific evaluators running pre-ship and continuously in production
  • AI Red Teaming Agent scan completed with a scorecard
  • Guardrails configured at the right lifecycle points — inputs, tool calls, tool responses, outputs
  • Non-Foundry agents emitting gen_ai.* OTel spans into the same observability plane (Path B)
  • Evaluation GitHub Action / Azure DevOps extension wired into CI with baseline variant comparison
  • Monitoring dashboard live; KQL-derived alert rules defined with agreed thresholds and routing
  • Fleet dashboard showing health, performance, cost, and compliance for registered agents

➡️ Layer 2 · Agent Operations in detail

docs.title: Track 3 · Agent Management
docs.text:
Treat agents as enterprise assets.

Stage Activity Deep Dive Using Microsoft Agent 365, establish agent management, ownership, and lifecycle — and design the agent identity blueprints. Proof of Value Register, activate, monitor, and retire real agents — proving visibility and control end to end. Production Scale agent identities safely and consistently across the organization.

Activate: Microsoft Agent 365 — no landing zone required.

Accountable owners: IAM (identity, lifecycle & inventory) · AI Engineering (register & own) · Security (behavioural insight)

Exit criteria

  • Agent 365 activated and the agent identity blueprint defined
  • Every published agent carries a unique Entra Agent ID with a named human or team owner
  • Shadow-agent detection running; discovered agents triaged
  • Lifecycle workflows in place — provision, change scope, decommission, access review and expiry
  • Authoritative agent inventory visible in the Agent 365 dashboard
  • Revocation tested — a rogue agent can be blocked in Agent 365 or have its access contract revoked

➡️ Layer 3 · Agent Management in detail

docs.title: Track 4 · Security Foundation
docs.text:
Embed security and compliance by default.

Stage Activity Deep Dive With Defender and Purview, map threat models, data governance, and regulatory requirements. Proof of Value Demonstrate real controls in action — threat detection, data classification, and compliance evidence — so security is operational and measurable, not theoretical. Production Arrive at a unified, measurable security posture across the estate.

Activate: Defender for AI / Cloud · Microsoft Purview · Microsoft Entra — across every layer.

Accountable owners: SecOps (posture & threat) · DPO (data security) · GRC (compliance & evidence) — all under the CISO.

Warning

For banking and government accounts, the DPO and GRC are gatekeepers, not stakeholders — no production AI reaches users without their sign-off. Engage them at deep-dive stage, not at the finish line.

Exit criteria

  • Defender for AI enabled; posture recommendations and attack-path analysis reviewed
  • Purview sensitivity labels applied to AI-reachable data; agent activity flowing into Purview audit
  • Entra conditional access and least-privilege policies applied to agent identities
  • Gateway audit logs and Foundry traces feeding SIEM/XDR
  • Compliance evidence pack assembled and mapped to the applicable regime (e.g. EU AI Act)
  • Regulated-account sign-off from DPO and GRC obtained

➡️ Layer 4 · Security Foundation in detail

docs.title: Convergence
docs.text:
The four tracks come together in a single production adoption workshop.

Converge on Detail Target operating model Who owns which layer in steady state — see Organizational Alignment & Ownership Rollout waves Which business units and use cases onboard in which order Success metrics Time-to-value, cost per use case, compliance coverage, fleet health, shadow-agent rate

Outcome: a clear, actionable path to scale agentic AI — securely, governably, and at enterprise velocity — run by your AI Center of Excellence.

docs.title: Deployment approach: hub-and-spoke for scale
docs.text: The architecture is intentionally designed around a hub-and-spoke model.

docs.title: AI Governance Hub — central deployment
docs.text:
AI Hub Gateway Landing Zone — AI Gateway Landing Zone

  • Deployed centrally
  • One deployment governing both production and non-production, or two (one production, one non-production) — more can be added per requirements
  • Hosts the unified AI Gateway, the model and tool registry, centralized logging and monitoring, and policy enforcement
  • Enforces runtime policies-as-code for all AI interactions across the organization
  • Platform-level observability and audit trail: centralized performance metrics, usage tracking, with optional request/response logging

docs.title: Agents Environment — spoke deployment
docs.text:
Foundry Landing Zone — Agent Landing Zone

  • Deployed at a spoke, with many deployments across the organization
  • One deployment per business unit or use case
  • Fully self-contained and secure, with dedicated compute, storage, data, and dependent services
  • Teams work autonomously without stepping on each other's toes
  • Accelerates development through templated deployment that is configurable
  • Each spoke connects back to the hub for centralized governance and observability

Every AI workload — whether an agent, a tool, or a model call — connects back to the hub to access centrally protected AI assets.

Governance stays centralized, while execution scales horizontally. That is how organizations grow from a handful of use cases to hundreds or thousands of agents with full visibility, consistent control, and no loss of trust.

In short: local freedom, global rules.

docs.title: Sizing guidance
docs.text:
Citadel positions four layers: two are infrastructure layers, two are activation layers. Suggested sizing approach:

Layer Type Sizing driver Guidance 🔷 L1 · Governance Hub (via APIM) Infrastructure Gateway throughput and tier T-shirt sizing guide: AI Citadel Governance Hub sizing guide 🔶 L2 · Agent Operations (via Foundry) Infrastructure Agent type, dependent services (AI Search, databases), and active consumption — an agent serving 20 internal users is very different from one serving 2M external users Cost Guide — Azure AI Landing Zones 🟢 L3 · Agent Management (via Agent 365) Activation License per user per month — no per-agent or per-agent-instance licensing. Strongly recommend alignment with the Security team for customer assessment and sizing. Microsoft Agent 365 field FAQ (Microsoft internal) 🛡️ L4 · Security Foundation (Defender for AI, Purview, Entra) Activation Defender for AI relies on estimated input/output tokens (usually a fixed price for each) AI threat protection in Microsoft Defender for Cloud

Note

Layer 2 sizing carries the widest variance of the four. Model it per-use-case rather than estate-wide, and revisit it after the Build & Iterate PoV when real consumption data exists.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
A strong place to begin the journey is Layer 1 (the runtime Governance Hub) together with Layer 2 (Agent Operations). These two layers establish the foundation required to scale AI safely and consistently.

That said, the sequencing advice from the operating model still applies:

  1. Start where you're strongest. Find the single layer where you're furthest ahead — that's your beachhead. The other three become your expansion path.
  2. Run the tracks in parallel, not in series. They are coordinated but independent; serializing them costs months for no risk reduction.
  3. Don't defer Layer 3. Identity is the hinge that lights up Layer 4 — it is the most under-scoped layer in most conversations, and the shadow-agent gap opens quietly.
  4. Engage Security early. In regulated industries they are gatekeepers, and late engagement means late rejection.
If the customer… Start with Has AI sprawl, no cost attribution, teams holding raw provider keys Track 1 — Governance Hub Has motivated builders but no sanctioned runtime or observability Track 2 — Agent Operations Already has agents in production but can't answer "who owns this one?" Track 3 — Agent Management Is in a regulated industry and blocked on security/compliance sign-off Track 4 — Security Foundation

docs.title: The runtime governance imperative
docs.text:
Moving from shadow AI to unified AI access.

In an AI system, three primary assets are critical and must be governed:

Asset Why it matters 🧠 LLMs Provide the brain for AI agents 🧰 Tools and knowledge Allow agents to be grounded, with the ability to act 🤖 External agents Enable collaboration as AI systems grow

All of these assets run on APIs with standard protocols — HTTP/REST, MCP, and A2A. Having those interactions governed is essential: AI APIs must be managed, secured, and governed to reduce both operational and security risk.

Without central AI access governance, organizations face:

Risk What it looks like 💸 Unpredictable costs Token misuse and lack of oversight lead to financial surprises and an inability to attribute cost to use cases or users ⚠️ Reliability issues Unchecked APIs suffer performance bottlenecks and downtime 🔓 Security threats Weak protection leaves APIs vulnerable to attacks and data breaches 😤 Developer friction Inefficient processes slow innovation and complicate workflows 😱 Governance nightmares Staying compliant becomes a struggle without clear oversight

The goal: transform AI governance from a bottleneck into an innovation accelerator.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
The Governance Hub is the runtime enforcement layer that mediates AI traffic between agents and LLMs, tools, and other agents. This is where governance becomes real — every AI call flows through this layer, and nothing bypasses it.

Core components

Component Platform Role 🌐 Unified AI Gateway Azure API Management Single control point for models, tools, and agents 📖 Universal AI Registry Azure API Center Centralized catalog for discovery and reuse

Enforcement capabilities

  • 🔑 Identity validation
  • 📜 Access contracts
  • 🚨 Per-request safety and guardrail enforcement
  • ⚙️ Smart operations — token rate limiting, capacity management, cost attribution

docs.title: The gateway as a mediator
docs.text:
Because every call is proxied through the gateway, governance is enforced centrally in policy — clients get resilient, observable, well-managed AI without changing app code. That single mediation point unlocks:

  • Content safety
  • Resilient AI routing
  • Scalable hub-and-spoke implementation
  • Pluggable traffic mediation for usage, access controls, and other critical policies
  • Global reports and dashboards across AI assets
  • Smooth developer and agentic-platform onboarding

docs.title: One governed front door: four dimensions
docs.text:
Every model, tool, and agent call flows through a single gateway — governed across four dimensions at the same time.

Dimension Capabilities Focus 01 · Governance 5 — Resiliency · Observability · Capacity Management · Universal AI Routing · Universal AI Catalog Run AI as a managed platform 02 · Security 4 — AuthN & AuthZ · Content Safety · PII Processing · Audit Logs Zero-trust access to every AI asset 03 · Operations 3 — Access Contracts · Publish Contracts · Backend Contracts Declarative, automated day-2 onboarding 04 · Cloud & Hybrid 3 — Hybrid Data Plane · Any Model, Tool or Agent · Centrally protected, anywhere One control plane, data plane everywhere

One control plane. Consistent routing, security, operations, and placement — applied to every AI asset the enterprise consumes.

Instead of each team wiring up its own routing, keys, and monitoring, one consistent control plane applies to every AI asset the business consumes.

docs.title: Dimension 01 · Governance
docs.text:
Run AI as a managed platform — not a pile of one-off integrations.

Centralized routing, cataloging, capacity, observability, and resiliency for every model, tool, and agent. This is the operational backbone that keeps AI reliable and well-behaved as usage scales.

# Capability What it does Scope 01 Resiliency Circuit breaking, failover, and session affinity keep traffic flowing See deep dive 02 Observability Performance monitoring and FinOps cost tracking with chargeback Perf · Cost 03 Capacity Management Flexible request- and token-based limits per use case Rate limits 04 Universal AI Routing Centrally route to models, tools, and agents across environments One endpoint 05 Universal AI Catalog Discover models, tools, agents, and skills via Azure API Center API Center

Five capabilities, one platform: route · catalog · scale · observe · recover — governed from a single hub.

docs.title: 01 · Resiliency — keep LLM traffic flowing when backends throttle, fail, or hold state
docs.text:
What Fail-fast + recover — circuit breakers park unhealthy backends, then probe them backAutomated failover — retries transient 429 / 5xx on a healthy backend, pool, or providerSession affinity — pins stateful conversations to the member that holds their state How Central policy — enforced in gateway policy and backend config, no app-side changePools & aliases — priority / weight routing with cross-model, cross-provider fallbackStructured errors — every branch returns a typed error clients can react to Value Higher availability — graceful degradation across models, pools, and cloudsTransparent — protection applies to every consumer automatically

Four layers, one request: Affinity → Load balance → Retry / failover → Circuit breaker

docs.title: 02 · Observability — see performance and cost for every use case, team, model, and backend
docs.text:
What Performance monitoring — latency, throughput, throttling, and errors per product, model, and backendFinOps — token and request cost tracked for showback and chargeback How Proxied telemetry — every call is captured centrally in Application Insights / Log AnalyticsDebug headers — per-call routing decisions exposed for diagnosticsCost mapping — usage attributed to the calling access contract Value Full visibility — capacity planning and SLO management with no per-app instrumentationAccountability — each team and use case sees its own performance and spend

Signal to insight: Every call → Metrics + usage → Dashboards → Chargeback

docs.title: 03 · Capacity Management — protect shared model capacity with flexible, per-use-case limits
docs.text:
What Flexible limits — rate limiting by requests and by tokens, per access contractQuotas & priorities — fair share of scarce model capacity across teams and use cases How Policy at the gateway — token / request policies applied per product and subscriptionPriority routing — critical workloads served first when capacity is tightSpillover — overflow routes to additional backends when limits are reached Value No noisy neighbors — one workload can't exhaust capacity for the restBudget control — consumption is bounded and predictable per use case

How limits apply: Request / token limit → Quota + priority → Spillover

docs.title: 04 · Universal AI Routing — one endpoint, many backends
docs.text:
What Centrally managed — route to models, tools, and agents on Azure, on-premises, and hybridStrategy-driven — select by performance, model, or priority How Pools & aliases — a logical name resolves to the best available backendPriority or weighted — failover across members, models, and providersOne protocol surface — works for LLMs, MCP tools, and A2A agents alike Value Stable endpoint — clients call one address; placement stays swappableGoverned by default — routing and fallback remain centrally controlled

Resolution path: Logical name → Pool / alias → Best backend

docs.title: 05 · Universal AI Catalog — a single registry of models, tools, agents, and skills
docs.text:
What One catalog — models, tools, agents, and skills registered via Azure API CenterRight visibility — internal discovery plus potential external visibility How API Center registry — assets carry metadata, ownership, and versioningSearchable — teams find approved assets for reuse in minutesGateway-governed — access and policy apply through the same front door Value No shadow AI — duplicated, ungoverned endpoints are designed outReuse first — discover and consume vetted assets across the org

Catalog scope: Models → Tools → Agents → Skills

Tip

The registry also enables MCP discovery and consumption across the enterprise — including exposing your MCP servers to GitHub Copilot in VS Code and to Copilot Studio.

docs.title: Dimension 02 · Security
docs.text:
Zero-trust access to every AI asset.

Nothing reaches a model until it's authenticated, authorized, screened for safety and PII, and logged for audit — all enforced right at the gateway.

No master keys, no direct endpoints. Every request proves identity, is scoped to its contract, is screened for safety and PII, and is logged for audit.

# Capability What it does Scope 01 Authentication & Authorization API keys, IdP JWT tokens, and per-contract access to assets Per contract 02 Content Safety Prompt and response screening, tuned per access contract Per contract 03 PII Processing Detect and anonymize sensitive data in-line at the gateway Inline 04 Audit Logs Request metadata and optional bodies feed Defender / Sentinel SIEM / XDR

Defense in depth: identity, least-privilege, safety, data protection, and audit — layered on one governed path.

docs.title: 01 · Authentication & Authorization
docs.text:
What Layered identity — API key, or API key plus IdP-issued JWT tokensScoped access — per-access-contract authorization to specific models, tools, and agents How Gateway-managed — keys and JWTs validated before any backend is reachedAllow-lists — a contract binds a use case to the exact assets it may callLeast privilege — default-deny; access is granted explicitly Value No master keys — consumers never hold raw provider credentialsBlast-radius control — a compromised client is limited to its contract

Access path: API key + JWT → Access contract → Allowed assets

docs.title: 02 · Content Safety
docs.text:
What Two-way screening — moderation and prompt-shield on requests and responsesPer contract — categories and thresholds tuned to each use case's risk How Inline policy — Azure AI Content Safety invoked in the gateway pipelineBlock or flag — unsafe content stopped before it reaches model or clientNo app work — guardrails apply without any client-side integration Value Consistent guardrails — the same protection across every use caseRight-sized — strict where it must be, permissive where it can be

Screening path: Prompt → Content safety → Model → Response check

docs.title: 03 · PII Processing
docs.text:
What Inline detection — PII detected in request (and response) bodies at the gatewayAnonymization — sensitive entities redacted before forwarding upstream How Gateway policy — detection and anonymization run before the model is calledFail-safe — failures surface as a structured 502 clients can handleConfigurable — entity types and handling set per use case; supports both natural detection and regular expressions Value Central minimization — sensitive data protected regardless of app or modelCompliance-ready — consistent data handling across the estate

Protection path: Request → PII detect → Anonymize → Model

docs.title: 04 · Audit Logs
docs.text:
What Metadata always — every call logs request metadata by defaultBodies optional — request / response bodies captured where policy allows How Structured per call — identity, contract, model, routing, and outcome recordedStreamed to SIEM — logs feed Microsoft Defender and Microsoft SentinelOne choke point — all AI traffic is auditable from a single path Value Investigation-ready — trace any request end to endCompliance + detection — threats and misuse surface centrally

Audit path: Every call → Audit log → Defender / Sentinel

docs.title: Dimension 03 · Operations
docs.text:
Declarative, automated day-2 onboarding.

Instead of ticket-driven, ad-hoc changes every time someone wants to add a use case or a backend, everything is onboarded through contracts. Onboarding becomes configuration — versioned, repeatable, and centrally governed.

Governance Hub philosophy: policy as code. Shift governance left by treating backend and access rules as binding contracts.

# Contract type Direction Purpose 01 Access Contracts Northbound Onboard a consuming use case with the assets, limits, and policies it is allowed to use. Governance travels with the contract and is injected into every call. 02 Backend Contracts Southbound Onboard a model backend from Azure, on-premises, or hybrid — with its endpoint, auth, resiliency, and capacity — once, then reuse across many contracts.

docs.title: 01 · Access Contracts — onboard a use case with the models, limits, and policies it's allowed
docs.text:
What Use-case onboarding — a declarative contract for each consuming application or agentGovernance bundled — allowed assets plus security, capacity, and safety policy in one place How Declarative definition — assets, auth method, rate limits, content-safety, and PII settingsRuntime injection — the contract's policies are injected into every API callVersioned — changes are tracked and repeatable Value Self-describing — governance lives with the use case, not buried in app configFast, consistent — new use cases go live through configuration

Onboarding flow: Define contract → Gateway enforces → Use case live

docs.title: 02 · Backend Contracts — onboard a model backend from Azure, on-premises, or hybrid — once
docs.text:
What Backend onboarding — registers a model backend and its native properties into the gatewayReusable — one backend serves many access contracts How Endpoint + auth — connection and credentials defined declarativelyPool placement — priority / weight, plus native circuit-breaker resiliency, attached at onboardingAny location — Azure, on-premises, or hybrid targets Value Swap centrally — add or replace backends without touching consumersConsistent behavior — resiliency and routing are standard from day one

Onboarding flow: Register backend → Pool + resiliency → Available to contracts

docs.title: Dimension 04 · Cloud & Hybrid
docs.text:
One control plane, data plane everywhere.

Deploy the gateway on Azure, on-premises, or another cloud — and govern assets anywhere with network line-of-sight. That gives central governance without forcing all the traffic through one location.

The gateway is a mediator. Deploy it where your AI runs so traffic stays local, while policy, routing, and audit remain centrally governed.

docs.title: 01 · Hybrid Data Plane
docs.text:
What Deploy anywhere — gateway runs on Azure, on-premises, and on other cloudsMediator — data-plane traffic stays close to the models and agents How Central control plane — policy and configuration managed in one placeDistributed enforcement — local gateway instances handle traffic where it livesLine-of-sight — assets reachable wherever networking connects Value Low latency — requests avoid unnecessary round-tripsData residency — sensitive traffic stays within its boundary

Topology: Central control plane → Local gateway → Nearby models / agents

docs.title: 02 · Any Model, Tool, or Agent
docs.text:
Category Coverage Any model Out of the box — Azure AI Foundry, Google Gemini, AWS Bedrock, Anthropic ClaudeOpenAI-compatible — Llama, Qwen, and other open-source models Any tool MCP protocol — convert an existing REST API into MCPBring your own — register an existing MCP server under gateway governance Any agent A2A protocol — register A2A agents into the gatewayGoverned access — consumers reach protected agents through gateway security

Under one gateway: Foundry · Gemini · Bedrock · Claude → MCP tools → A2A agents

Central control, local data. Governance and visibility stay in one place; the traffic goes where it belongs.

docs.title: Resiliency deep dive
docs.text:
Reliable AI access to LLMs and protected AI assets — keeping traffic flowing when backends throttle, fail, or hold state.

# Capability What it does 01 Circuit Breaker Fail fast on an unhealthy backend, then auto-recover by probing it back 02 Session Affinity Keep stateful conversations on the backend that holds their state 03 Automated Failover Keep a request alive when the first-choice target throttles or errors 04 Error Handling Structured errors so clients can diagnose — and know what's safe to retry

Putting it together: a resilient production onboarding combines all four dimensions — governance, security, operations, and placement — behind a single access contract.

Reliable AI routing

  • Priority & resilient routing — set priority groups with automatic fallback for a failing LLM instance
  • Load balancing — weighted distribution across pool members
  • Capacity flow control — support for both token-based limits (suitable for LLMs) and request-based limits (suitable for tools / MCP)

docs.title: AI Governance Hub — central deployment
docs.text:
AI Hub Gateway Landing Zone — AI Gateway Landing Zone

  • Deployed centrally to serve as the runtime command center
  • One deployment governing both production and non-production, or two deployments (one each) — more can be added per requirements
  • Unified AI gateway for all model, tool, and agent access
  • Universal AI registry for centralized catalog and discovery
  • Centralized logging, monitoring, and policy enforcement
  • Platform-level observability and audit trail — centralized performance metrics, usage tracking, with optional request/response logging
  • Shared infrastructure every project leverages

docs.title: Agent Environment Spokes
docs.text:
Foundry Landing Zone — Agent Landing Zone

  • Deployed multiple times — one per business unit or use case
  • Fully self-contained and secure, with dedicated compute, storage, data, and dependent services
  • Teams work autonomously without stepping on each other's toes
  • Each spoke connects back to the hub for centralized governance and observability

This architecture delivers "local freedom" in each project area under a common governance framework enforced by the hub.

docs.title: Integration with the other layers
docs.text: Layer Integration 🔶 Layer 2 (Agent Operations) Foundry relies on the runtime AI Gateway for policy enforcement, and the gateway's telemetry feeds observability and compliance. Foundry agents route to governed models via a Foundry connection ("Admin-Connected-Models"). 🟢 Layer 3 (Agent Management) Agent 365 / Entra Agent ID identities are validated at the gateway for access control and policy enforcement. A rogue agent can be stopped by revoking its access contract. 🛡️ Layer 4 (Security Foundation) Defender for API provides an added layer of security and threat intelligence; gateway audit logs stream into Defender and Sentinel; Purview enforces data governance policies at the gateway level.

docs.title: Defense in depth
docs.text: The Governance Hub is one of three places content safety can be enforced (alongside Agent Operations and the Security Foundation). Critically, it is the control that holds the line when an agent runs outside Foundry — for example a self-hosted model on a GPU VM — because that traffic still flows through the gateway as a mediator between agent and model.

docs.title: Ownership & outcomes
docs.text:
Accountable AI CoE (standards) · Platform Engineering (gateway infrastructure) · FinOps (capacity & cost attribution) The question it answers "How do I give every team access to AI without losing control of cost, capacity, and policy?" What you gain One managed front door for all AI traffic — policy enforced centrally and spend attributable per consumer, turning AI sprawl into a charge-backable service. The advantage Govern once, enforce everywhere. Control scales with adoption instead of fighting it — the more AI you deploy, the more leverage this layer gives you.

Key RACI rows (full matrix in Organizational Alignment & Ownership)

# Decision Accountable Responsible 1.1 Set AI-adoption standards & policy AI CoE — 1.2 Provide & operate gateway infrastructure Platform Eng — 1.3 Capacity & cost management / attribution (PTU/PAYG) FinOps Platform Eng

It is infrastructure, not just policy. Platform Engineering provides and operates the gateway and offers assisted deployment; the AI CoE sets the policy it enforces; FinOps owns capacity economics and cost attribution.
