docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Posture, threat protection, data security, and compliance for AI workloads — Microsoft Defender, Microsoft Purview, and Microsoft Entra, built hand-in-hand with the security organization.

This layer provides real-time defense against AI-specific threats and integrates across all governance layers. It is the layer that converts a pilot into something approved for production.

Component Contribution Its job in one line 🛡️ Microsoft Defender Threat intelligence and AI security posture management Defend against emerging AI threats and vulnerabilities 📚 Microsoft Purview Data governance, labeling, and compliance Prevent sensitive data oversharing and ensure data compliance 🔐 Microsoft Entra Agent and application identity, authentication and authorization Manage agent sprawl, govern permissions, protect resource access

Together these create a defense-in-depth security fabric. The key takeaway: governance, identity, and security are not bolt-ons — they are built in from day one.

Important

This layer is switched on by identity. Once an agent has an Entra Agent ID and is registered in Agent 365, these controls apply to it automatically. That is why Layer 3 is the hinge — and why the two layers are deliberately coupled rather than separate programmes.

docs.title: The customer concerns this layer answers
docs.text:
Concern The data Data leakage and inaccuracy 80%+ of leaders cite leakage of sensitive data as their main concern Emerging AI threats and vulnerabilities 50%+ of successful cybersecurity attacks against AI agents are expected to exploit access control issues, using direct or indirect prompt injection as an attack vector through 2029 Agent sprawl and risk 88% of organizations are exploring or piloting AI agents — contributing to growing agent sprawl and increasing exposure Non-compliance 55% of leaders lack understanding of how AI is and will be regulated, and are seeking guidance on how to adhere

Sources: ISMG First Annual Generative AI Study (Q3 2023, N=400); Gartner, "How to Secure Custom-Built AI Agents" (17 March 2025); KPMG AI Pulse Survey (Q4 2024).

Security concerns aren't hypothetical — they show up in nearly every boardroom conversation about AI.

docs.title: The expanding attack surface
docs.text:
What used to be about securing cloud infrastructure and data — virtual machines, containers, storage, databases — has moved up into AI models, apps, and agents.

Layer of surface What's exposed Cloud application attack surfaces Virtual machine · container · storage · database Generative AI attack surfaces Prompts · AI model · grounding data · training data — prompt injection, data leakage, model manipulation Agentic AI attack surface Agent-to-agent · agentic memory · tool use · MCP servers · human-in-the-loop — memory leaks, agent-to-agent data sharing

Attackers are no longer just breaching networks — they're exploiting how AI understands and responds. And with agentic AI, agents talk to other agents, use external tools, and operate through orchestration frameworks like MCP servers. This connectedness unlocks huge potential but also creates new exposures.

docs.title: Threats in scope
docs.text: Direct prompt injection (UPIA) · indirect prompt injection (XPIA) · unauthorized access · denial of service / wallet abuse · sensitive data exfiltration · training data poisoning · model theft · credential theft · lateral movement · malicious tool use · intent breaking and goal manipulation · privilege compromise

docs.title: Protection across every build platform
docs.text:
Customers build AI agents in different ways, and Defender delivers consistent protection across the entire ecosystem — whether that's low-code/no-code makers in Copilot Studio through natural language, or developers building code-first applications in Microsoft Foundry, Azure, VS Code, and GitHub.

From build to runtime: start secure, stay secure.

docs.title: Microsoft Defender — AI security posture management
docs.text: Start secure. Get visibility across all AI assets, identify vulnerabilities early, and reduce risk before a breach happens.

docs.title: 1 · Get comprehensive AI visibility
docs.text:
• A unified inventory of all AI models and agents across platforms — Microsoft Foundry, Copilot Studio, Azure ML, Amazon Bedrock, and Google Vertex AI
  • See metadata, agent instructions, identities, and connected agentic tools
  • Understand what AI assets exist, who owns them, and how they connect
  • Agentless — visibility across multi-cloud environments with a few clicks, no deployment per workload
  • Cloud security explorer lets you discover assets and their components, build custom queries, or use built-in query templates

For organizations building dozens or hundreds of AI apps, this is the first step: minimize agent sprawl and eliminate shadow agents.

docs.title: 2 · Identify and remediate vulnerabilities
docs.text:
• Discover AI misconfigurations, insecure instructions, and excessive permissions to tools and agents
  • The agent detail page shows linked MCP servers, models, and connected tools — with risk-based recommendations
  • Recommendations are grouped by severity for prioritization, with detailed remediation guidance you can assign to an owner — promoting traceability and progress visibility across the team
  • Follow recommendations to remediate posture issues among AI pipelines, deployments, and sensitive data stores

A concrete example: a recommendation warning that essential agent instructions are absent — because if system instructions are missing, agents can act unpredictably and breach risk goes up.

docs.title: 3 · Prioritize and reduce risk with attack path analysis
docs.text:
• Use risk context to know what to fix first
  • Find direct and indirect exploitable paths to your AI assets
  • Visualizes relationships between cloud resources, agents, models, and data sources, mapping toxic combinations of posture issues

Worked example: an internet-exposed container with severe vulnerabilities enables lateral movement to a Foundry agent grounded with sensitive data. Defender correlates risk signals from the GitHub repository, the container, Foundry, and the sensitive data source — flagging posture risk from code to cloud, and illustrating how code issues amplify into future attacks. Descriptions and attack stories attached to each path give the security admin contextual understanding.

docs.title: Microsoft Defender — threat protection
docs.text: Stay secure. Continuously monitor for malicious AI activity, detect and respond in real time, and correlate signals into incidents.

docs.title: Detect threats across diverse forms and patterns
docs.text:
Signal class What it looks for Suspicious content Jailbreak (malicious intent) · secrets and sensitive data · malicious URLs · encodings and manipulations Suspicious behaviors User/agent behavior · application behavior · tool behavior · access parameters — powered by Microsoft Threat Intelligence

By analyzing both prompts and responses, Defender finds things that shouldn't be there — using both threat intelligence and AI to comb through each conversation.

Important

Certain attacks can't be found by looking at content alone. Malicious tool invocation, intent manipulation, and wallet abuse do not differ in content — but can be detected by looking at the patterns of the user or the application. By examining the control plane alongside threat intelligence, Defender identifies familiar attack vehicles and captures attacks even at the reconnaissance stage.

docs.title: Monitor, detect, respond
docs.text: Capability What it delivers Monitor for malicious activities Detect suspicious AI model interactions, agentic tool calling, memory changes, and LLM invocations — powered by Microsoft Threat Intelligence Real-time detection and response AI model alerts for jailbreak, sensitive data exposure, and credential theft — blocked in real time Agent-specific threats Intent breaking, goal manipulation, tool misuse, and privilege compromise — with evidence and response details that trace back to the problematic agent Out-of-the-box + custom detections Ready-made detections plus the ability to build your own Correlate and contextualize Incidents correlated across multiple assets and agents, integrated with Defender XDR and Microsoft Sentinel Advanced hunting Query agent invocation and inference activity directly to build custom detections

docs.title: Investigate and respond with rich context
docs.text:
Detecting suspicious events isn't enough — security teams need to triage, contain, and respond swiftly and in an informed way. Defender supplies the evidence that most organizations simply don't log:

Evidence type Why it matters Prompt and response evidence Visibility most orgs lack entirely — enables swift classification of user intent Application context AI resources are shared between applications; this lets the SOC differentiate expected from unexpected content User context Most AI calls go via proxy or gateway, losing user identity in the process. Defender recovers it — giving the SOC a real way to identify internal vs. external users and trace an attack to its source Grounding / prompt-to-grounding mapping Detects where the data originated — a true understanding of whether organizational data was compromised, and from where CNAPP posture context Adds runtime traffic insight back into posture — grounding data stores, search engines Built-in education Defender explains what the attack is, how it works, and what else to check in the investigation

docs.title: Enhanced protection with Foundry guardrails integration
docs.text:
Defender's threat protection for GenAI apps and agents works with Foundry's built-in content filtering to raise security alerts:

1. User inputs a malicious prompt into an app via Foundry models or agents
         ▼
2. Foundry guardrails detect the jailbreak attack and block the response
         ▼
3. Defender ingests the Foundry detection + application context, and synthesizes
   it with Microsoft Threat Intelligence to generate contextual security alerts
         ▼
4. Alerts correlate into incidents for investigation and response in Defender XDR

Real-time signal exchange between Foundry and Defender means the builder's guardrail and the SOC's alert are the same event, seen from two altitudes.

docs.title: Microsoft Purview — data security and compliance
docs.text:
DSPM for AI is a centralized place where you discover, protect, and then govern the interactions with AI apps.

Pillar What it delivers 🔍 Discover Insights and analytics into Microsoft Copilot experiences, enterprise AI, and other AI activity in your organization 🛡️ Protect Ready-to-use policies to monitor and protect data in AI prompts 📋 Govern Compliance controls to apply optimal data handling and storage policies

docs.title: Discover — see the AI data risk
docs.text: Capability Detail DSPM for AI reporting Total interactions over time · sensitive interactions per AI app · top unethical AI interactions · top sensitivity labels referenced · insider risk severity per AI app · potential risky AI usage Activity explorer AI interactions including prompts and responses · sensitive info types detected · DLP rule matched events Data risk assessment Identify oversharing exposure before and during rollout Audit Auditing of prompts and responses across Copilot experiences and agents Cross-platform visibility Sensitive data detection across Microsoft Copilot, enterprise AI apps, and third-party AI tools

docs.title: Protect — stop oversharing and leaks
docs.text:
Capability Detail Sensitivity labels Agents honour labels; a Copilot conversation inherits the most restrictive sensitivity label from the references used to form a response Access control on labeled content Only content the user has appropriate permission for is included in responses. If the user lacks rights, the agent informs them and provides a link but does not use the content Encryption rights Honouring view and extract usage rights for content encrypted by Information Protection DLP for AI Policy conditions that prevent processing of labeled Office files and PDFs in SharePoint — sensitive content isn't used to generate responses DLP for agents Block file processing based on sensitivity labels for agents in Microsoft 365 Insider Risk Management Risky AI Usage indicator and policy template Communication compliance Detect business or code-of-conduct violations in prompts and responses; detect prompt injection attacks, jailbreak, and mentions of protected materials in GenAI prompts and responses Purview SDK / APIs Bring the same level of security and compliance controls that Microsoft 365 Copilot supports to your own custom AI apps and agents registered in Entra

The controls above were developed with financial-services customers deploying Copilot in highly regulated environments — establishing a minimum standard for AI controls that unblocked adoption. Top customers now expect that bar whether it's Microsoft 365 Copilot or their own custom chatbot.

docs.title: Govern — evidence and lifecycle
docs.text: Capability Detail Compliance Manager Guided assistance to AI regulations via assessment templates for the EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, and ISO 42001 Data Lifecycle Management Retention policies to retain and/or delete AI interactions; auto-apply retention to referenced files via cloud-attachment policy eDiscovery Preserve, collect, analyze, review, and export AI interactions by creating an eDiscovery case Audit A durable record of interactions for investigation and regulatory response

docs.title: Coverage across Copilot experiences and agents
docs.text: Interactions in DSPM for AI, audit of interactions, capturing/classifying prompts and responses, Insider Risk Management, communication compliance, eDiscovery, and Data Lifecycle Management span Microsoft 365 Copilot (including Copilot Chat and agents in Microsoft 365), Security Copilot, Copilot in Fabric, and Copilot Studio agents. Sensitivity-label adherence, encryption adherence, and DLP apply to Microsoft 365 Copilot and to Copilot Studio agents when using SharePoint as the data source.

docs.title: Common causes of oversharing — fix these first
docs.text:
Site privacy set to public · default sharing option set to everyone · broken permission inheritance · use of the "everyone except external users" domain group · sites and files without sensitivity labels

A staged approach works: discover oversharing risk with data risk assessment → restrict sensitive information from agent access with DLP → increase site privacy and labeling → operate with lifecycle policies and continuous assessment.

docs.title: Microsoft Entra — identity and access
docs.text:
Identity, lineage, and access control for agents and applications.

Capability What it delivers Durable identity Every agent receives a durable identity at build time Access governance Enforces policy-based access and conditional permissions Identity alignment Agent identity aligns with existing enterprise identity systems Lineage tracking Tracks ownership and access lineage across the lifecycle Permission control Teams manage agent permissions through familiar identity governance Identity Protection for agents Risk signals — unfamiliar resource access, high sign-in volume, anomalous patterns — detected and responded to in real time Conditional Access for agents Policies targeting agent identities, conditioned on risk level, location, and device compliance Global Secure Access Web content filtering and threat filtering for agent-initiated web access and outbound agent traffic Lifecycle Workflows Auto-revoke on owner departure, agent retirement, or risk threshold exceeded Shadow agent discovery Surfaces agents operating outside central control

➡️ Entra is also the engine behind Layer 3 · Agent Management — the full identity model, blueprints, and third-party SDK integration are documented there.

docs.title: How the three work as one fabric
docs.text:
• 🔄 Coordinated threat response across Defender, Entra, and Purview
  • 👁️ End-to-end visibility and audit trails — every AI call auditable from a single path
  • ⚡ Real-time protection and compliance by design
  • 📡 Signals feed SIEM / XDR — gateway audit logs and Foundry traces stream into Defender and Microsoft Sentinel

docs.title: Signals surface where each team already works
docs.text:
Tip

The same signal appears in the console each persona already uses. Defender surfaces security signals inside Foundry Control Plane (so developers see compliance conflicts and fix them where they build) and inside Agent 365 (so IT sees them agent by agent). Purview detections and alerts appear directly in the Defender portal — so a SOC analyst investigating an incident sees the DLP verdict without switching tools. Nobody is forced into a single console, and nobody has to correlate by hand.

docs.title: A single investigation, three products
docs.text: Step Product What it showed Jailbreak attempt on an agent Foundry guardrails → Defender Attack blocked; Defender confirms and explains the technique Malicious URL sent to the agent Defender Blocked by policy preventing agents from accessing user-supplied URLs Sensitive data processing attempt Purview → surfaced in Defender Blocked from processing sensitive data and from sending it externally — exactly as it would have been for a user Resolution Agent 365 Agent confirmed trustworthy and returned to work, with evidence

docs.title: Defense in depth
docs.text:
One control is never enough — enforce critical guardrails in more than one place.

Standard security practice: never depend on a single layer. If it's bypassed or simply can't apply, the system is exposed. Citadel's controls deliberately overlap, so coverage holds however an agent is built or hosted.

Worked example — content safety is enforceable at three controls:

Control Where it applies 🔷 Governance Hub At the AI gateway and at Foundry-hosted models 🔶 Agent Operations In Foundry — Agent Service runtime & control-plane guardrails 🛡️ Security Foundation Microsoft Defender (Defender for AI) monitoring across the estate

When one control can't apply, another holds the line:

Scenario What can't apply What holds Agent runs outside Foundry — a self-hosted model on a GPU VM Agent Operations & Security Foundation can't apply out of the box 🔷 Governance Hub enforces it at the gateway Microsoft Copilot agents — traffic doesn't traverse your gateway or Foundry Governance Hub & Agent Operations can't apply out of the box 🟢 Agent Management (Agent 365) and 🛡️ Security Foundation (Defender) enforce it — with Copilot's native protections

Same risk, multiple enforcement points — if one control can't apply or is bypassed, another does. That's the whole point of layering.

docs.title: Regulatory alignment: EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO 42001
docs.text:
Compliance cannot be a manual checkbox at the scale of 10,000+ agents.

Governance approaches that depend on periodic audits or one-time approvals collapse the moment adoption scales. As soon as many agents are acting across tools, data, and workflows, governance must become built into the platform — not bolted on.

Citadel is positioned as a blueprint to future-proof AI investments: layered governance places controls that scale as adoption grows, and keeps the platform aligned not just with current regulations but with future updates. It is designed to address both limited-risk and high-risk use cases — which matters because enterprises rarely run only one category of AI workload. The controls flex with risk level, without forcing a rewrite of your architecture.

docs.title: Three things working together
docs.text: What it provides 1. Runtime enforcement — Governance Hub A unified AI gateway for models, tools, and agents, backed by a universal registry — enforcing identity validation, access contracts, and per-request safety and guardrail enforcement. When controls are enforced at runtime, compliance scales with adoption: you are not hoping teams follow guidelines, the platform applies policy consistently. 2. Attribution and accountability — Agent Management The registry, the named sponsor, approval gates, versioned blueprints, and agent-level audit logs — the connective tissue that ties an action back to a specific, owned agent rather than a shared gateway credential. 3. A unified security fabric — Security Foundation Defender for threat intelligence and AI security posture; Purview for data governance, labeling, audit, retention, eDiscovery and compliance; Entra for enterprise-grade authentication and authorization.

docs.title: Turning obligations into evidence
docs.text:
Obligation theme Evidence the stack produces Risk management & assessment Compliance Manager assessment templates for EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO 42001 — guided control mapping with evidence collection Record-keeping & logging Gateway audit logs, Foundry traces, Purview audit of prompts and responses, Entra agent sign-in logs Transparency & traceability Prompt-to-grounding mapping, sensitivity-label citation, per-call routing and outcome records Human oversight Named sponsor per agent, publish/activate approval gates, HITL escalation routing at the gateway Data governance Classification, labeling, DLP, oversharing assessment, retention and eDiscovery Accuracy & robustness Foundry evaluations, groundedness and task-adherence evaluators, continuous red teaming Cybersecurity Defender posture management, attack-path analysis, real-time threat detection, SIEM/XDR correlation Incident response Correlated incidents with prompt/response evidence, application and user context, and a tested revocation path

The point: a regulator does not ask whether your platform is secure. They ask you to show a specific decision, made by a specific system, and prove who was accountable. These layers together are what makes that answerable.

docs.title: AI TRiSM alignment
docs.text:
Gartner's AI TRiSM (Trust, Risk, and Security Management) framework addresses the new trust, risk, and security challenges introduced by AI systems — especially generative and agentic AI — by providing a unified framework of technical and governance controls that enforce policies, manage risk, and secure AI behavior at runtime rather than relying on static design-time guardrails.

It requires runtime technical controls that continuously inspect AI inputs — not just outputs or model configs. In RAG and agentic pipelines, retrieved content is effectively untrusted input: malicious or poisoned documents can alter model behavior through indirect prompt injection (IPI), making pre-ingestion validation a first-class governance concern.

In TRiSM-aligned systems, retrieved content is treated as untrusted input. If validation happens only at output time, indirect prompt injection remains unmitigated.

docs.title: The seven IPI controls mapped to Citadel
docs.text: # IPI control TRiSM pillar Citadel layer(s) How Citadel addresses it 1 Instruction-separation & role enforcement — detect retrieved content that issues instructions, redefines roles, or introduces execution directives Risk, Security 🔷 L1 + 🛡️ L4 Gateway content-safety and prompt-shield policies block instruction-injection patterns at runtime; Defender provides real-time jailbreak and prompt-injection detection; Purview communication compliance detects prompt-injection attempts in prompts and responses 2 Policy-aware semantic classification — classify chunks by intent (instructional vs. informational) rather than keyword blocklists Risk, Trust 🔶 L2 Foundry Control Plane evaluators run semantic classification against retrieved context; the AI Red Teaming Agent validates that paraphrased attacks are caught 3 Source authenticity & provenance — verify trusted source identity, approved pipeline, and document lineage Trust, Compliance 🔷 L1 (Universal AI Catalog) + 🟢 L3 Azure API Center catalogs approved assets and data sources; Entra Agent ID validates agent and service identities accessing retrieval pipelines; Defender's prompt-to-grounding mapping identifies where retrieved data actually originated 4 Sensitive data & policy constraints — detect PII / regulated data and enforce masking or exclusion before prompt assembly Compliance, Trust 🛡️ L4 (Purview) + 🔷 L1 (Gateway) Purview enforces labels, sensitivity labels for RAG, and DLP on retrieved content; gateway PII processing redacts or excludes flagged content before it leaves the boundary 5 Contextual relevance & scope bounding — ensure chunks are relevant and within task scope to reduce attack surface Trust, Risk 🔶 L2 Foundry evaluators assess retrieval relevance, task adherence, and scope drift; fleet dashboards surface over-retrieval anomalies across agents 6 Risk scoring & enforcement decisioning — score each chunk (Low/Medium/High) and route to allow, sanitize, exclude, or human review Risk, Security 🔶 L2 + 🔷 L1 Control Plane risk-scores retrieved content via evaluators; the gateway enforces the routing decision (pass / sanitize / block / escalate to HITL) 7 Audit logging & explainability — log content ID, validation result, enforcement action, and reason codes Compliance, Trust 🔶 L2 + 🛡️ L4 + 🟢 L3 Foundry traces capture end-to-end retrieval decisions; gateway audit logs and Purview audit trails provide compliance-ready evidence; Agent 365 attributes all of it to a named, owned agent

docs.title: Maturity model for retrieved-content controls
docs.text:
Level Capability Citadel coverage L0 No validation (raw retrieval injected) — L1 Keyword filtering 🔷 Gateway basic policies L2 Pattern + source allowlists 🔷 Gateway + 🔷 API Center registry L3 Semantic intent classification 🔶 Control Plane evaluators L4 (TRiSM) Policy-mapped, risk-scored, auditable validation before ingestion All four Citadel layers operating together

Note

Reaching L4 maturity requires all four Citadel layers working in concert: the Governance Hub enforces runtime decisions, Agent Operations provides risk scoring and observability, Agent Management ensures provenance and accountability, and the Security Foundation delivers threat detection, data governance, and audit trails.

docs.title: Integration with the other layers
docs.text:
Layer Integration 🔷 Layer 1 (Governance Hub) Defender provides runtime protection for the AI Gateway and consumes its audit logs; Purview enforces data governance policies at the gateway level; Entra backs gateway authentication and authorization. Gateway audit logs stream to Defender and Sentinel, recovering the user identity that proxying would otherwise lose. 🔶 Layer 2 (Agent Operations) Defender and Purview surface security insights and compliance monitoring directly inside Foundry Control Plane — developers see compliance conflicts and fix them where they work. Foundry guardrail detections flow to Defender in real time and are synthesized with threat intelligence into contextual alerts. Entra ensures identity governance for every project and published agent. Partner integrations (Palo Alto Networks, Zenity) extend coverage. 🟢 Layer 3 (Agent Management) Entra provides identity governance for agents; Defender monitors for identity-based threats and contributes agent inventory and attack-path context; Purview enforces data governance based on agent access and behavior. Agent 365 consolidates all three into one unified dashboard — and registration in Agent 365 is what switches this layer on for BYO and third-party agents.

Once an agent has an identity and is registered in Agent 365, this layer's controls apply automatically — that is why identity is the connective tissue.

docs.title: Ownership & outcomes
docs.text:
Accountable SecOps (posture & threat) · DPO / Purview (data security) · GRC (compliance & evidence) — all under the CISO The question it answers "Can I prove this AI estate is protected, compliant, and auditable — to my board and my regulator?" What you gain AI-specific threat protection, data-loss controls, and compliance evidence unified across the estate — the layer that converts pilot into approved-for-production. The advantage Security & compliance, built in. Defender, Purview, and Entra deliver continuous threat protection, data governance, and access control beneath every layer — a constant, not an afterthought.

Key RACI rows (full matrix in Organizational Alignment & Ownership)

# Decision Accountable 4.1 AI security posture & threat protection Security — SecOps 4.2 Data security & classification for AI Security — DPO 4.3 Compliance, audit & regulatory evidence Security — GRC

Warning

Regulated-industry gatekeepers. For banking and government accounts, the DPO and GRC are not just consulted — they are gatekeepers. There is no production AI without their sign-off. Bring them into the conversation early, not at the finish line.

docs.title: Activation
docs.text:
Track 4 — Security Foundation

Stage Activity Deep Dive Defender & Purview — threat models, data governance & compliance mapping Proof of Value Controls in Action PoV — detection, classification & compliance evidence Production Unified Posture — measurable security & compliance

Activate across every layer — there is no separate landing zone for this layer; it is switched on and integrated wherever AI runs.

docs.title: Discovery questions to run first
docs.text:
Identity & access

  • Are Conditional Access policies currently applied to non-human / workload identities?
  • Is Microsoft Entra ID Protection enabled and generating risk signals today?
  • Are there existing Privileged Identity Management policies in the tenant?
  • Do agents currently operate with broader permissions than strictly needed?

Data security

  • What sensitivity labels are in use — are they applied to SharePoint and OneDrive?
  • Have any data oversharing incidents involving Copilot or AI tools been identified?
  • Is Purview DLP actively enforced for Microsoft 365 workloads?
  • How is sensitive data (PII, IP, financial) currently protected from agent access?

Threat detection

  • Is Microsoft Defender XDR deployed and the Microsoft 365 connector configured?
  • Are audit logs enabled in the Purview portal?
  • Does the SOC have playbooks for responding to AI-related security incidents?
  • Are there existing advanced hunting queries or custom detections for AI workloads?
  • Has the security team assessed the risk of adversarial agent attacks or jailbreaks?

Lead with the Defender integration and Conditional Access story — these map directly to controls security stakeholders already understand.

Exit criteria

  • Defender for AI enabled; agent inventory populated across Foundry, Copilot Studio, and multi-cloud
  • Posture recommendations triaged and assigned; attack-path analysis reviewed
  • Foundry guardrail → Defender signal exchange verified end to end
  • Purview audit enabled; sensitivity labels published to SharePoint and OneDrive
  • DSPM for AI data risk assessment completed; oversharing remediation underway
  • DLP for AI policies enforced; Insider Risk Risky AI Usage policy live
  • Communication compliance detecting prompt injection and protected materials
  • Entra conditional access and least-privilege policies applied to agent identities
  • Gateway audit logs and Foundry traces feeding SIEM / XDR
  • Compliance Manager assessment started for the applicable regime (EU AI Act / NIST AI RMF / ISO 42001)
  • Retention and eDiscovery configured for AI interactions
  • Regulated-account sign-off from DPO and GRC obtained

Sizing: Defender for AI pricing relies on estimated input/output tokens (usually a fixed price for each). Engage the Security specialist team for a comprehensive estimation across Defender, Purview, and Entra.

docs.title: Why alignment decides the outcome
docs.text:
A blueprint only works if your organization is aligned behind it. The technology in Citadel is well understood — the failure mode is almost never the architecture. It is three roles people habitually blur together:

  1. Who sets the standards
  2. Who runs the platform
  3. Who builds the agents

The single biggest predictor of a smooth rollout is keeping those three functions distinct and giving every decision one clear accountable owner.

Important

No single team owns all four Citadel layers — and that's the point. Each layer has a different accountable owner. The job of the operating model is not to centralize ownership; it is to make the handoffs explicit.

docs.title: The operating model: three build-and-run functions
docs.text:
Three build-and-run functions, one governed estate.

Function What it owns Responsibility 🎓 AI CoE (AI Center of Excellence) OWNS THE POLICY Sets the standards: approved models, capacity rules, allowed runtimes, and the trustworthy-agent bar. It sets the bar without building the agents. 🏗️ Platform Engineering (CCoE) OWNS THE PLATFORM Provides the landing zone and infrastructure for Layers 1–2, plus assisted deployment to onboard teams. 👨‍💻 AI Engineering & App Dev OWNS THE PRODUCT Designs, builds, owns, and operates the agents — to the CoE's standards, on the platform provided.

The AI CoE owns the policy · Platform Engineering owns the platform · AI Engineering owns the product.

docs.text: Function Contribution 💰 FinOps Cost & capacity economics, chargeback 🔑 IAM Agent identity, lifecycle, inventory 🛡️ Security & Compliance Posture, threat, data protection, audit evidence (SecOps · DPO · GRC) 🏢 Line of Business Sponsors the use case and owns its business value 👔 Exec Sponsor (CAIO) Cross-layer convener; owns the overall outcome

docs.title: RACI legend
docs.text: Meaning R Responsible — does the work A Accountable — one owner, the buck stops here C Consulted — input before the decision (two-way) I Informed — kept up to date (one-way) – Not involved

docs.title: Trust is everybody's responsibility
docs.text:
Trust isn't one team's job and it isn't a couple of security controls bolted on the side. It's layered across four interconnected controls — complementary, not sequential — each with a named owner.

Control Scope What it delivers Owned by 🔶 Agent Operations Agent-level End-to-end traces, AI evals, red-teaming & guardrails — tuned to each agent's type and objective The agent builder 🔷 Governance Hub Platform · Govern Every model, tool & agent call flows through one governed gateway — routing, policy, content safety, capacity & observability The AI CoE & platform team 🟢 Agent Management Platform · Identify Every agent is an owned enterprise asset — first-class identity, owner, lifecycle & audit trail IAM & security 🛡️ Security Foundation Platform · Protect Defender, Purview & Entra deliver threat protection, data governance & access beneath every agent The security org

Trust starts inside the agent and extends across the platform — from 10 to 10,000 agents.

docs.title: Master RACI matrix
docs.text: Org units × Citadel Blueprint layers — one Accountable owner per decision.

docs.title: Layer 1 — Governance Hub · AI Hub Gateway: APIM + API Center
docs.text: # Activity / Decision AI CoE Plat Eng AI Eng FinOps IAM Sec & Comp Exec 1.1 Set AI-adoption standards & policy A C C C I C I 1.2 Provide & operate gateway infrastructure C A I I C C I 1.3 Capacity & cost management / attribution (PTU/PAYG) C R I A – I I

docs.title: Layer 2 — Agent Operations / Runtime · Microsoft Foundry, Agent Service, Container Apps
docs.text: # Activity / Decision AI CoE Plat Eng AI Eng FinOps IAM Sec & Comp Exec 2.1 Approve & standardize runtimes & dev tooling A C C I I C I 2.2 Provide runtime infrastructure C A C I I C I 2.3 Build, own & operate agents & use cases C C A I C C I

docs.title: Layer 3 — Agent Management & Lifecycle · Entra Agent ID, Workload Identity, Agent 365
docs.text: # Activity / Decision AI CoE Plat Eng AI Eng FinOps IAM Sec & Comp Exec 3.1 Issue & govern agent identities C C R – A C I 3.2 Agent lifecycle & ownership C I R – A C I 3.3 Agent inventory & behavioural insight I I C – A R I

docs.title: Layer 4 — Security Foundation · Defender for AI / Cloud, Microsoft Purview, Entra
docs.text:
# Activity / Decision AI CoE Plat Eng AI Eng FinOps IAM Sec & Comp Exec 4.1 AI security posture & threat protection C C C – C A (SecOps) I 4.2 Data security & classification for AI C I C – I A (DPO) I 4.3 Compliance, audit & regulatory evidence C I I – C A (GRC) I

Note

The Line-of-Business sponsor is Accountable for each use case's business value (row 2.3) and Informed elsewhere. It is kept in this footnote so the grid stays readable.

docs.title: How to read the matrix
docs.text:
• Read down a column → one team's total load across the whole estate.
  • Read across a row → exactly who needs to be in the room for that one decision.
  • Trace accountability diagonally → the philosophy in one glance:
    • The AI CoE is Accountable only on the standards rows (1.1 and 2.1). It owns the policy — the rules of the road. It does not own the infrastructure and it does not build the agents.
    • Platform Engineering is Accountable for the infrastructure rows (1.2, 2.2).
    • AI Engineering is Accountable for building and operating the agents (2.3).
    • IAM owns identity and inventory across all of Layer 3.
    • Security & Compliance owns posture, data, and audit across all of Layer 4.

docs.title: Layer-by-layer ownership and outcomes
docs.text: Each layer answers a question your teams are already asking — and delivers a concrete outcome. Frame every layer around the value it delivers, not the technology.

docs.title: Layer 1 · Governance Hub
docs.text:
AI Hub Gateway · Azure API Management + Azure API Center

What it is: the central control plane for all AI model and agent traffic — routing, capacity (PTU / PAYG) management, observability, policy enforcement, and cost attribution.

It is infrastructure, not just policy. That distinction tells you who does what: Platform Engineering provides and operates the gateway and offers assisted deployment; the AI CoE sets the policy it enforces; FinOps owns capacity economics and cost attribution.

Accountable AI CoE (standards) · Platform Eng (gateway infra) · FinOps (cost & chargeback) The question it answers "How do I give every team access to AI without losing control of cost, capacity, and policy?" What you gain One managed front door for all AI traffic — policy enforced centrally and spend attributable per consumer, turning AI sprawl into a charge-backable service.

docs.title: Layer 2 · Agent Operations
docs.text:
Microsoft Foundry · Foundry Agent Service · Azure Container Apps

What it is: where agents are built, hosted, orchestrated, and connected to enterprise data and tools.

Infrastructure plus standards. Platform Engineering provisions and operates the runtime; AI Engineering builds on top; the AI CoE approves which runtimes and dev tools are allowed — so builders innovate fast inside guardrails instead of dragging in an unvetted framework.

Accountable AI CoE (runtime & tooling approval) · Platform Eng (runtime infra) · AI Eng (build & operate) · LOB (business value) The question it answers "Can my teams build and ship agents fast, connected to our data, without re-platforming or breaking the rules?" What you gain A sanctioned runtime where builders move fast and automatically inherit the Layer 1, 3 & 4 controls — governance as an enabler, not a tax.

docs.title: Layer 3 · Agent Management & Lifecycle
docs.text:
Entra Agent ID · Workload Identity · Microsoft Agent 365

What it is: identity, authentication, and authorization for agents and the humans or systems they act on behalf of.

Identity is the asset-management control point. This is not "give the agent a login." An enterprise identity turns an agent into a managed asset — lifecycle (provision, change scope, decommission), named ownership so there are no orphaned agents, an authoritative inventory of every agent in the estate, and — through Agent 365 linking Entra, Defender, and Purview — genuine behavioural insight into how that agent actually acts.

Accountable IAM (identity, lifecycle & inventory) · AI Eng (register & own) · Security (behavioural insight) The question it answers "When an agent acts, whose identity is it using, who owns it, what can it touch, and can I see it and revoke it?" What you gain Every agent becomes a first-class, owned, least-privilege enterprise identity with full inventory and behavioural visibility — closing the shadow-agent gap before it appears.

Warning

This is the most under-scoped layer in almost every customer conversation. Slow down here.

docs.title: Layer 4 · Security Foundation
docs.text:
Defender for AI / Cloud · Microsoft Purview · Microsoft Entra

What it is: posture, threat protection, data security, and compliance for AI workloads — built hand-in-hand with the security organization.

Regulated-industry gatekeepers. For banking and government accounts, the DPO and GRC are not just consulted — they are gatekeepers. No production AI reaches users without their sign-off. Bring them in early, not at the finish line.

Accountable SecOps (posture & threat) · DPO / Purview (data security) · GRC (compliance & evidence) — all under the CISO The question it answers "Can I prove this AI estate is protected, compliant, and auditable — to my board and my regulator?" What you gain AI-specific threat protection, data-loss controls, and compliance evidence unified across the estate — the layer that converts pilot into approved-for-production.

docs.title: The cross-layer convener
docs.text:
No single team owns all four layers — and that's by design.

Role Scope Chief AI Officer / AI Governance Board Cross-layer convener — owns the outcome: deploy AI at scale without losing control of cost, identity, data, security & compliance. CIO / CTO Layers 1–2 CISO Layers 3–4 CRO Layer 4 compliance

Citadel gives you one coherent way to align four normally-siloed teams behind a single goal.

docs.title: Putting this into practice
docs.text:
# Step What to do 1 Map your teams to these roles Confirm you have a distinct AI CoE. If you don't, that's gap number one — flag it before anything else. 2 Start where you're strongest Find the single layer where you're furthest ahead — that's your beachhead. The other three become your expansion path. 3 Use the RACI to assign clear owners Each layer has a different accountable owner. Walk the matrix row by row and name a real person or team for every A. 4 Engage each owner on their outcomes Frame every layer around the value it delivers, not the technology — use the four questions above verbatim.

Important

Keep flexibility in mind. The blueprint is a guide, not a mandate — adapt it to your organization's unique structure and culture. The principle to preserve is separating standards, infrastructure, and builders across the layers, even if the exact team names and org-chart boxes differ.

docs.title: Common anti-patterns
docs.text: Anti-pattern Why it breaks The fix One team tries to do all three — sets the standards, runs the platform, and builds the agents Standards get bent to fit delivery deadlines; the platform becomes a bottleneck Split into AI CoE / Platform Engineering / AI Engineering, even if they are small No distinct AI CoE There is nobody accountable for approved models, capacity rules, or the trustworthy-agent bar — so each team invents its own Stand up the CoE first; it is gap number one Security engaged at the finish line In regulated industries, DPO and GRC are gatekeepers — late engagement means late rejection Bring SecOps, DPO, and GRC in at deep-dive stage, not at production Identity (Layer 3) treated as "just a login" The shadow-agent gap opens quietly and becomes the biggest risk at scale Reframe identity as the asset-management control point — it is what lights up Layer 4 Two Accountable owners on one decision The buck stops nowhere One A per row. Everyone else is R, C, or I Business value with no named sponsor Agents ship that nobody can justify LOB sponsor is Accountable for each use case's business value (row 2.3)

docs.title: Foundry Citadel Platform
docs.text:
Original platform guide

This guide describes the Foundry Citadel Platform as first published, organized around three pillars and a hub-and-spoke architecture. For the current layered guidance, see the AI Citadel Blueprint overview and its layer guides.

Scalable AI Landing Zone with Governance, Observability & Rapid Development

Foundry Citadel Platform is a solution accelerator designed as a supplemental AI landing zone that integrates seamlessly with your Azure environment. It provides a secure, scalable foundation for running AI applications and agents in production – with unified governance, end-to-end observability, and tools to accelerate development. Citadel delivers a pre-configured reference architecture (aligned to Azure’s Cloud Adoption and Well-Architected Frameworks) that can be deployed with one click and includes ready-made code, templates, and documentation following Microsoft’s best practices. This comprehensive approach helps organisations adopt AI responsibly and efficiently, ensuring that advanced AI agents can be developed quickly while remaining well-managed and compliant with enterprise requirements.

🛡️ Security 📊 Consumption 🧭 Guardrails 🗂️ Registry 62 % of practitioners cite security concerns as the top blocker to wider AI or agent adoption. 71 % of enterprises struggle to track AI usage, enforce quotas, and report costs per team. 47 % of organisations require explicit guardrails before deploying autonomous AI agents safely. 70 % of customers need an AI registry for both agents and tools to adopt AI at scale.

🧩 Citadel turns these pain points into platform strengths—governed access, transparent consumption, defensible guardrails, and a shared catalog of reusable AI capabilities.

These challenges highlight why Citadel’s capabilities are crucial. Foundry Citadel Platform focuses on three key pillars – Governance & Security, Observability & Compliance, and AI Development Velocity – to address these concerns end-to-end. Below, we outline each pillar and the core capabilities provided, with architecture components and features that ensure enterprise-grade AI deployments:

docs.title: Citadel Adoption Signals
docs.text: Enterprise teams highlight these blockers and enablers for scaling AI responsibly.

docs.title: 1. Governance & Security Pillar – Trustworthy AI Operations at Scale
docs.text:
Foundry Citadel Platform implements strong governance and security controls so that enterprises can adopt generative AI safely and in compliance. Key capabilities of this pillar include a unified AI gateway for all model access, granular policy enforcement, and robust safety mechanisms:

  • 🔐 Unified AI Gateway: At the core of Citadel’s security is the “AI Gateway” – a central entry point (built on Azure API Management) through which all AI model requests are routed. This gateway enforces organisation-wide policies consistently. For example, it implements universal LLM policies like rate limiting and token quotas to prevent misuse or cost overrun. No application calls the model directly; instead, apps call the gateway, which authenticates and forwards requests to the appropriate model (Azure OpenAI, open-source, or even third-party services like Amazon Bedrock) while applying the required controls. This design centralises oversight of all AI consumption.
  • 🗝️ Granular Access Control & Key Management: Citadel’s gateway introduces a gateway-keys model access pattern for developers. Rather than embedding master API keys for various AI services, teams use managed credentials issued by the gateway. The gateway can map these to backend keys or identity tokens, ensuring that no master keys are directly exposed in code. Access can be segmented by team or use-case, with role-based authorisation (e.g. only approved apps or users can invoke certain AI endpoints) for greater security. This prevents uncontrolled use of AI services and allows rapid revocation or rotation of credentials from a single place.
  • 🔑 Credential Management: Citadel secures API keys and service credentials by leveraging Azure Key Vault. Secrets are stored securely and accessed at runtime, ensuring that no raw keys are exposed in code or logs.
  • 🛡️ Policy Enforcement and Compliance: The governance layer allows administrators to define and enforce a range of custom policies. These include traffic mediation rules (e.g. routing requests to different model endpoints based on content or load) and usage policies (per-user or per-app call rate limits and monthly token budgets). It also supports complex expressions for policies – for example, automatically choosing an Azure OpenAI instance in a specific region for compliance, or requiring certain request headers/tags for auditing. All usage is captured centrally, enabling compliance auditing and simplifying answer to the question “Who is using which model, and how?”.
  • 🌐 Multi-Cloud and Hybrid Support: Citadel’s governance is flexible – it can govern not only Azure OpenAI, but also open-source model servers or third-party AI APIs. The AI Gateway speaks OpenAI-compatible APIs natively, meaning it can front-end virtually any generative model service. For instance, it can direct certain requests to Azure OpenAI or to an on-premises GPU-VM model, or even to Amazon Bedrock, all under the same policy umbrella. This multi-cloud ability gives organisations a single control plane for heterogeneous AI systems. Citadel’s gateway and related services can themselves run on-premises if needed (via APIM self-hosted gateways), supporting scenarios with strict data residency or partially air-gapped networks.
  • 🛡️ AI Content Safety & Guardrails: Citadel includes built-in AI safety mechanisms to enforce responsible AI usage. Every request and response can be scanned by Azure AI Content Safety – which detects hate speech, violent or sexual content, self-harm indications, and other harmful outputs. If an application user tries to prompt an agent to produce disallowed content or if a model’s answer contains such content, the system can block or filter that response automatically. Citadel’s safety system also includes “prompt shields” that detect attempts to jailbreak the agent with malicious instructions hidden in user input or documents. This protects the AI agents from executing unintended commands. Additionally, “protected content” checks can recognise if a model’s answer includes large verbatim excerpts of known copyrighted text (lyrics, articles, etc.) and prevent accidental leakage of such content. These guardrails give organisations confidence that AI systems won’t go off-policy or create liability.
  • 📊 Central Monitoring & Cost Governance: All AI usage through the gateway is logged centrally (calls, tokens used, timings, outcome). FCP provides built-in reports and dashboards to track this usage by application or department. This solves the cost attribution problem – e.g. you can see how many tokens the Finance team’s chatbot consumed this week and enforce per-team quotas. It also enables cost optimisation – detecting anomalous spikes or inefficient prompt usage. Combined with Azure Monitor, admins can set alerts (e.g. if a project exceeds its monthly AI budget, or if a spike in requests suggests a rogue script). By providing this transparency and control, Citadel helps prevent the “blank cheque” scenario of uncontrolled AI API spend. It effectively addresses the “shadow AI” governance nightmare by keeping all AI calls within the managed guardrails.
  • 📘 Central AI Registry for Agents and Tools: FCP provides a unified AI Registry powered by the Model Context Protocol (MCP), enabling organisations to manage and discover both first-party and third-party AI agents and tools. This registry acts as a central catalog where teams can securely share, document, and govern AI capabilities across the enterprise. By standardising metadata and access policies, the registry ensures that all agents and tools – whether developed in-house or sourced externally – are easily discoverable and can be integrated seamlessly into workflows. This capability fosters collaboration, reduces duplication of effort, and ensures consistent governance for all AI assets.
  • 🔒 Data Security: Citadel ensures the protection of sensitive data in AI workflows by integrating with Microsoft Purview. This enables governance through data sensitivity labels and policies, ensuring that sensitive information remains within approved boundaries. For example, an AI agent accessing a database will operate under Purview’s oversight, with all usage logged and any policy violations (such as accessing restricted customer data) flagged for review.

Governance & Security Features and Components: The table below summarises some of the key governance components of Citadel and their roles:

Governance Feature Description Unified AI Gateway Central gateway that mediates every AI call. It applies global policies (rate limits, authentication, routing) and provides a single secure endpoint for clients. This ensures all AI usage is centrally visible and controlled. Policy Engine Rich rule framework to enforce business rules – e.g. restrict certain models to specific regions, apply token quotas per user, or inject safety prompts. Administrators can write custom policies or use built-in templates for common requirements. Managed Credentials Uses gateway-keys with/without Identity Platform issued tokens (like Microsoft Entra ID) to abstract backend secrets. Developers no longer handle raw AI services master keys – the gateway issues tokens/keys with scoped access. This prevents key leakage and allows instant revocation if needed. Content Safety Filters Automated checks on prompts and responses using Azure AI Content Safety. Flags or removes profanity, hate, sexual or violent content, and can block outputs that violate compliance policies (e.g. privacy or confidential data). AI Registry & Catalog A registry (via Azure API Center) for discovering and managing AI endpoints and tools (known as MCP servers). This catalogue lets teams securely share AI “skills” (Agents, APIs, functions) across the enterprise with proper metadata and governance. Multi-cloud Connectors Built-in support to govern AI services beyond Azure. The gateway can proxy requests to open-source model APIs or other cloud’s AI endpoints (e.g. Bedrock) securely. This ensures consistent security and monitoring even for third-party AI services. Azure Key Vault Secure store for secrets and credentials by AI Apps/Agents. All API keys, connection strings, etc., used by agents or the gateway are kept in spoke Key Vault, and accessed via managed identities. This eliminates hard-coded secrets and protects sensitive data at rest.

In practice, these governance features mean AI applications can be deployed with confidence. For example, if you build a GPT-based internal assistant, it will run through Citadel’s gateway – ensuring it only answers within approved data sources, filters any policy-breaking content, and logs its activity. Administrators remain in control: they can update a policy to block a newly discovered prompt attack pattern, or quickly see which prompts are costing the most. FCP thus fosters strong customer and stakeholder trust in AI by providing the oversight needed beyond just “having a model”. Governance is no longer a roadblock – it’s baked into the platform so that compliance officers and developers can collaborate effectively without endless manual reviews. The result is faster deployment of AI solutions “with the guardrails on”, avoiding the common pitfalls of unchecked AI experimentation (data leaks, runaway costs, or reputational damage).

docs.title: Why Governance Matters
docs.text: Without centralized AI governance, organisations face unpredictable costs, reliability issues, security risks, developer friction, and compliance nightmares. Citadel fixes this by building guardrails into every AI call.

docs.title: 2. Observability & Compliance Pillar – End-to-End Monitoring, Evaluation & Trust
docs.text: The Observability & Compliance pillar of Foundry Citadel Platform equips organisations with the tools to monitor, trace, and evaluate AI agents and LLMs behaviour continuously through a structured layered observability approach. This ensures that AI applications are not a "black box" – instead, they are transparent and auditable at both platform and agent levels, which is essential for maintaining reliability and trust in their outputs.

docs.title: Full Visibility = Trust & Confidence
docs.text: Citadel provides holistic observability for AI systems through a dual-layer approach: centralised monitoring at the platform level and detailed tracing at the agent level. This ensures teams can debug issues, assure quality, and govern compliance in real time. "You need a dashboard, not a crystal ball" to manage AI.

docs.title: Platform-Level Observability
docs.text:
Platform observability provides centralised monitoring and governance across all AI workflows, offering enterprise-grade visibility without requiring any agent code changes:

  • 📊 Central Application Performance Monitoring (APM): Citadel integrates seamlessly with Azure Monitor Application Insights to provide comprehensive platform-wide APM capabilities. This centralised monitoring captures infrastructure-level metrics, performance data, and system health indicators across all AI workloads. Teams gain visibility into resource utilisation, system bottlenecks, and overall platform performance without needing to instrument individual agents.

  • 📈 Detailed Usage Tracking per Team/Use Case/Agent: The platform provides granular usage analytics that can be segmented by team, use case, or individual agent. This includes tracking metrics such as:

    • Token consumption trends broken down by team, project, or agent
    • Request volumes and patterns across different use cases
    • Cost allocation and budgeting with detailed spend visibility per organisational unit
    • User adoption patterns and engagement metrics across different AI applications

    For example, operations teams can see that "the Sales team's Q&A Bot consumed 1.2M tokens (cost ~£60) today across 5,000 requests, while the Legal team's document analysis agent used 800K tokens across 200 complex queries." This granular tracking enables accurate cost management, capacity planning, and resource allocation across the organisation.

  • 🔍 Centralised AI Evaluation (No Code Changes Required): One of FCP's key strengths is its ability to run comprehensive AI evaluations without requiring any modifications to agent code. The platform can:

    • Automatically intercept and evaluate AI outputs using predefined and custom metrics
    • Run periodic batch evaluations on historical data (e.g., evaluate 10% of conversations overnight)
    • Provide comparative analysis between different time periods, agent versions, or teams
    • Support custom business-specific evaluators that can be deployed centrally and applied across multiple agents

    The evaluation framework includes a comprehensive suite of pre-defined metrics:

    • Response Quality Metrics: groundedness (did the answer stick to the provided data sources?), relevance (did it address the user's query?), coherence and fluency of the language, and completeness (did it follow all instructions and provide all parts of the answer?)
    • Retrieval Accuracy: for agents using knowledge bases, Citadel checks whether facts in answers occur in retrieved documents (measuring truthfulness to sources)
    • Safety Metrics: evaluation for potential harms – offensive language, biased content, and "jailbreak" susceptibility (was the agent tricked into breaking rules?)

    This centralised approach means quality assurance and safety evaluations are consistent across all AI applications and can be managed by a central AI governance team without requiring development resources from individual agent teams.

  • 🚨 Enterprise Alerts and Automated Remediation: For sensitive AI use cases, the platform provides sophisticated alerting and automated response capabilities:

    • Configurable alert rules on critical metrics (e.g., groundedness scores below thresholds, token usage spikes, error rate increases)
    • Automated remediation actions such as temporarily disabling agents, switching to backup models, or escalating to human oversight
    • Integration with enterprise notification systems (Teams, email, ITSM platforms) for immediate response
    • Compliance monitoring with automated reporting for regulatory requirements

    For high-stakes scenarios, teams can configure cascading responses – for instance, if safety scores drop below acceptable levels, the system can automatically route queries to human reviewers while alerting the responsible teams. Early warning of anomalies (maybe a new version of the model started "hallucinating" more, or an API that agents rely on is down) is critical for maintaining high uptime and trust.

docs.title: Agent-Level Observability
docs.text:
Agent observability provides detailed, granular insights into individual AI agent behaviour, enabling deep debugging and optimisation:

  • 📋 Detailed Execution Traces: Citadel guidance for agent deployments allows records comprehensive execution traces for each AI query or conversation. These traces capture every step an agent takes – from the initial user prompt, to system and tool prompts, all intermediate reasoning or chain-of-thought messages, calls to external tools or knowledge bases, and the final response. Along with the content, traces log parameters, model identities, and timing (latency and token counts) for each step. These traces are visualised in a structured timeline for developers and engineers.

    For example, if an AI agent uses a calculator API as part of its reasoning, you will see the exact API call and result in the trace. This level of insight makes it far easier to debug issues – such as figuring out why an agent gave a wrong answer (maybe it chose a flawed chain of actions), or why latency spiked (perhaps one tool took too long). Traces are stored durably (via Azure Application Insights/Log Analytics), allowing comparative analysis between runs and even between different versions of an agent. In short, every conversation or action path is observable; nothing is truly "hidden" behind an AI magic curtain.

  • ⚡ Performance Monitoring: Agent-level monitoring captures detailed performance metrics including:

    • Response latency broken down by reasoning steps, tool calls, and model inference
    • Token usage patterns for each component of the agent's workflow
    • Tool utilisation efficiency and success rates
    • Memory and resource consumption during agent execution

    This granular performance data enables developers to identify bottlenecks, optimise agent workflows, and ensure consistent performance across different scenarios.

  • 🎯 Agent-Specific Quality Evaluations: Beyond platform-wide evaluations, agent-level observability includes metrics tailored to specific agent behaviours:

    • Intent fulfilment (did the agent actually achieve what the user asked?)
    • Tool use correctness (did it call the right tool with correct parameters?)
    • Reasoning efficiency (were there unnecessary steps or redundant operations?)
    • Multi-step coordination (for complex agents with multiple reasoning phases)

    These agent-specific metrics provide developers with actionable insights for improving agent design and prompt engineering.

  • 🔧 Advanced Debugging & Diagnostics: FCP's guidance provides rich tools to search and inspect logs and traces for any session or conversation. It has powerful filtering capabilities. This helps in root cause analysis. Moreover, developers can replay traces: taking a stored conversation and running it step-by-step (either on the same or updated version of the agent) to reproduce issues or test fixes.

  • 🔄 Continuous Improvement Integration: Agent observability feeds directly into the development and deployment lifecycle:

    • CI/CD integration with automated testing using historical prompt datasets
    • A/B testing capabilities for comparing different agent versions
    • Performance regression detection when deploying new agent versions
    • Feedback loop integration allowing insights from production to inform development

    For example, AI Evaluation tests can be integrated with your CI/CD pipeline: whenever a new version of an agent is deployed, a battery of automated tests and evaluations can run (using stored prompt datasets) to compare its performance versus the previous version. If any metric regresses or new safety issues appear, the deployment can be halted or flagged. This DevOps-style approach – sometimes called "AIOps" – ensures that quality is maintained even as the AI system evolves.

docs.title: Unified Platform & Agent Observability
docs.text:
The true power of FCP's observability recommendations lies in the seamless integration with platform layer and clear guidance for agent layers:

  • 🎛️ Unified Dashboards: Ready-to-use dashboards provide both platform-wide overviews and agent-specific drill-downs. Operations teams can monitor overall system health while developers can dive deep into individual agent performance. These dashboards give a bird's-eye view of the system including:

    • Platform metrics: Overall usage, cost trends, system performance, and compliance status
    • Agent metrics: Individual performance, quality scores, and usage patterns
    • Comparative analytics: Performance trends across teams, use cases, and time periods

    For example, an operations engineer can see that "today, across all teams, we served 15,000 AI requests, consumed 4.2M tokens (cost ~£180), with average platform latency 1.5s and 99.2% uptime, while the Sales Q&A Bot specifically had 1.8s average response time with 2 minor safety flags." Having this in one place allows both technical and business stakeholders to stay informed. The dashboard is dynamic – teams can drill down into specific time windows or filter by scenario/agent.

  • 🚨 Coordinated Alerting: Alerts can be configured at both platform and agent levels, with intelligent escalation paths that consider both individual agent issues and platform-wide concerns. For instance, if multiple agents start showing performance degradation simultaneously, this might indicate a platform-level issue rather than individual agent problems.
  • 📊 Cross-Layer Analytics: The platform provides correlation analysis between platform metrics and agent performance (when Azure Monitor used end-to-end), helping teams understand how infrastructure changes, model updates, or usage patterns affect individual agent behaviour and overall system performance.

Key Observability Tools in Citadel:

Observability Feature Purpose Layer Central APM Monitoring Infrastructure-level monitoring, resource utilisation, and system health indicators across all AI workloads without requiring agent code changes. Platform Usage Analytics & Cost Tracking Granular tracking of token consumption, request patterns, and cost allocation segmented by team, use case, or agent for enterprise resource management. Platform Centralised AI Evaluations Automated quality, safety, and compliance evaluations applied consistently across all agents without requiring code modifications from development teams. Platform Enterprise Alerting & Remediation Sophisticated alerting with automated responses for sensitive use cases, including agent disabling, human escalation, and compliance notifications. Platform End-to-End Tracing Captures every step of an AI agent's reasoning and interactions (prompts, tool calls, responses), enabling transparent debugging and post-mortem analysis. Agent Agent Performance Monitoring Detailed real-time metrics including response latency breakdown, token usage patterns, tool efficiency, and resource consumption per agent. Agent Agent-Specific Evaluations Tailored quality metrics for individual agent behaviours including intent fulfilment, tool use correctness, and reasoning efficiency. Agent Advanced Debugging Tools Powerful querying, filtering, and trace replay capabilities for root-cause analysis and issue reproduction at the agent level. Agent Unified Dashboards Integrated visual dashboards providing both platform-wide overviews and agent-specific drill-downs for comprehensive operational visibility. Both Continuous Improvement Loop Connects operational data back to development with CI/CD integration, A/B testing, and regression detection for ongoing AI system enhancement. Both

All these observability measures ensure AI systems are reliable and accountable. Teams using Citadel principals can confidently answer "What is my AI doing and why?" at any time – a question that's otherwise hard to address. This pillar thus mitigates one of the biggest barriers to enterprise AI adoption: the fear of not knowing what the AI might do. With Citadel, governance and observability go hand-in-hand: if the Governance pillar is about setting the rules and guardrails, the Observability pillar is about watching and verifying adherence to those rules, and catching anything that falls outside. Together, they create a closed-loop system for responsible AI management, where issues are not only prevented but also detected and learned from in an ongoing cycle.

docs.title: 3. AI Development Velocity Pillar – Accelerating Innovation with Templates & Tools
docs.text:
While governance and oversight are crucial, Foundry Citadel Platform is not a single tool but an AI Landing Zone—a pre-configured set of Azure resources designed to help organizations move quickly and capitalize on AI opportunities. The AI Development Velocity pillar ensures that the platform empowers AI developers and data scientists with a spectrum of agentic platform choices, frameworks, and reusable assets. FCP strikes a critical balance: it enables rapid development within established guardrails through a template-based approach, so speed doesn’t come at the cost of security or oversight. Key aspects of this pillar include:

  • 🚀 Pre-built Deployment Templates: FCP accelerates the provisioning of cloud environments with predefined deployment templates that can target single or multiple types of agents. These templates are integrated with the platform's central governance and security, allowing teams to quickly establish a production-ready environment for building and operating agents without manual configuration.

  • 🤖 Flexible Agent Development Models: FCP supports a variety of agent types, allowing teams to choose the right approach for their needs. Customers may use one or a mix of these agent types, even within a single multi-agent system. The built-in types include:

    • Copilot Studio Agents: For a low-code approach, FCP integrates with Copilot Studio, a fully managed graphical interface for building and deploying AI agents. This drag-and-drop environment allows developers and power-users to design AI workflows visually. Within FCP, Copilot Studio agents are enhanced by integrating with the Citadel AI Registry, enabling them to securely discover and reuse existing agents and tools (like Model Context Protocol servers), ensuring governance even in a low-code context.
    • Managed Runtime Agents: For developers who want more control without managing the underlying infrastructure, FCP offers managed runtimes. Options include the AI Foundry Agent Service, which provides a scalable environment for hosting agent logic, and Logic Apps Agent Loop, which allows for the creation of serverless agent workflows. These runtimes provide a balance of flexibility and operational simplicity.
    • Bring-Your-Own (BYO) Agents: For maximum flexibility, FCP allows teams to bring their own agent architectures. Developers can leverage Microsoft's first-party AI orchestrators like Semantic Kernel, Agent Framework, and AutoGen, or third-party orchestrators such as LangChain. These agents can be containerized and deployed into Citadel’s environment, inheriting the platform's governance, security, and observability benefits.
  • 📚 The Citadel AI Registry: At the heart of the platform's governance is the Unified AI Gateway (CGH) and its native capability to expose an AI Registry, which serves as a central catalog for all AI assets. Integration with the Citadel Governance Hub AI Gateway happens in two primary ways:
    • Getting Managed AI Access: Agents get secure access to LLMs, AI services, and published AI tools from the registry. This ensures that only approved models and tools are used within predefined capacity and security context.
    • Publishing: Service and team owners can publish their own tools and agents into the central AI Registry, making them discoverable and reusable by other teams across the organization. This fosters a secure collaborative environment and prevents duplication of effort.
  • 📦 One-Click Deployment & Reusable Blueprints: To truly accelerate time-to-value, FCP provides automation for environment setup and deployment. The entire FCP reference architecture can be deployed via an automated script or template (e.g., Bicep), essentially a “one-click deploy” of the agent AI landing zone. This drastically reduces the initial setup time. On top of this, Microsoft offers Gold Standard assets—ready-made AI solution blueprints for common patterns like "Chat with your data" or "Conversation summarization." These blueprints come with code, configuration, and deployment scripts, serving as accelerators that allow teams to adapt proven solutions rather than starting from scratch.
  • 🔄 DevOps Integration & Lifecycle Management: FCP treats AI solutions with the same rigor as any software project, embedding them into the DevOps toolchain. It provides seamless integration with GitHub and Azure DevOps, allowing developers to use pre-configured environments like GitHub Codespaces. Automated CI/CD pipelines can run evaluation suites on pull requests to ensure quality and deploy updated agents to staging or production environments. With APIs and CLI tools, teams can programmatically manage AI Gateway policies and safety settings as part of a release. FCP also supports A/B testing and shadow deployments, enabling teams to run multiple versions of an agent in parallel, compare their performance using observability data, and bring Agile principles to AI development.

Key Development Tools & Components:

Development Accelerator Role in Citadel Deployment Templates Pre-built, one-click templates (i.e. Bicep) to provision a secure, governed cloud environment for single or multiple agent types, accelerating time-to-production. Flexible Agent Runtimes (Copilot Studio, Managed Runtime, BYO) Supports a spectrum of development models, from low-code (Copilot Studio) to managed services (AI Foundry Agent Service) and fully custom "Bring-Your-Own" orchestrators (Semantic Kernel, LangChain), allowing teams to choose the best fit for their use case. Citadel AI Registry A central, governed catalog for discovering, managing, and reusing AI assets. It provides managed access to LLMs and tools and allows teams to publish their own, fostering collaboration and preventing redundant work. Reusable Blueprints (Gold Standard Solutions) End-to-end solution examples that demonstrate common AI patterns. They serve as accelerators for new projects, embodying proven architectures and best practices. DevOps Integration Integrates with GitHub and Azure DevOps for CI/CD, automated testing, and lifecycle management of AI solutions. Supports A/B testing and canary releases to bring modern software engineering speed to AI development.

All these capabilities mean that teams can innovate rapidly with AI. They can start with an idea, quickly assemble an MVP agent using existing building blocks, test it with real data (with governance in place), and iterate to improve it – all in a matter of days or weeks rather than months. Citadel’s approach of providing both low-code and pro-code options also ensures that different personas can collaborate: a business analyst could craft an initial agent behavior in Copilot Studio, then a software engineer could refine it using the code SDK for more complex logic – all deploying to the same managed environment.

Crucially, development speed does not mean throwing caution to the wind. Every agent built on Citadel pillars and guidance, no matter how fast it was created, runs within the secure, monitored framework described in the previous sections. This means organisations can encourage experimentation and pilot projects without fear: if something grows in importance, the governance and reliability scaffolding is already there for it. Citadel effectively frees teams from the heavy lifting of creating a safe AI infrastructure from scratch, so they can focus on applying AI in ways that differentiate their business (be it new customer experiences, process automation, or decision support).

Finally, this pillar embodies the idea of scaling AI responsibly. Once you’ve built one successful solution, Citadel makes it easier to rollout others (since the platform is already in place) and to templatise your approach. Over time, the catalogue of internal tools and connectors will grow – a “network effect” where each new AI project potentially adds reusable pieces for future projects. This accelerates AI adoption across the organisation in a governed way, helping build an “AI factory” capability. In summary, Citadel turns the typically slow, risky journey of AI solution development into a fast, repeatable, and governed process, accelerating innovation while maintaining enterprise-grade standards.
