The final response send back the client after deanonymization will be:

{
    "choices": [
        {
            "finish_reason": "stop",
            "index": 0,
            "logprobs": null,
            "message": {
                "content": "Hello Sarah Jones! I'm glad to help your question. To calculate the distance between the Earth and the Moon, you can use the average distance which is approximately 384,400 kilometers. This value can be found in astronomy references and is useful for many calculations and comparisons related to the Earth-Moon system. If you need further assistance or have any other questions, feel free to ask!",
                "role": "assistant"
            }
        }
    ],
    "usage": {
        "completion_tokens": 84,
        "prompt_tokens": 97,
        "total_tokens": 181
    }
}

docs.title: PII Blocking Product Policy Example
docs.text:
In some scenarios, you may want to completely block requests that contain PII data rather than anonymizing them. This is useful for strict compliance requirements where no PII should reach the backend services under any circumstances.

The following example shows how to implement PII blocking at the Product level:

<policies>
    <inbound>
        <base />

        ... other policies ...

        <!-- PII Detection and Blocking -->
        <set-variable name="piiBlockingEnabled" value="true" />
        <!-- Variables required by pii-detection fragment -->
        <choose>
            <when condition="@(context.Variables.GetValueOrDefault<string>("piiBlockingEnabled") == "true")">

                <!-- Configure PII detection settings -->
                <set-variable name="piiConfidenceThreshold" value="0.75" />
                <set-variable name="piiEntityCategoryExclusions" value="PersonType,CADriversLicenseNumber" />
                <set-variable name="piiDetectionLanguage" value="en" /> <!-- Use 'auto' if context have multiple languages -->

                <!-- Configure regex patterns for custom PII detection -->
                <set-variable name="piiRegexPatterns" value="@{
                    var patterns = new JArray {
                        new JObject {
                            ["pattern"] = @"\b\d{4}[- ]?\d{4}[- ]?\d{4}[- ]?\d{4}\b",
                            ["category"] = "CREDIT_CARD"
                        },
                        new JObject {
                            ["pattern"] = @"\b[A-Z]{2}\d{6}[A-Z]\b",
                            ["category"] = "PASSPORT_NUMBER"
                        },
                        new JObject {
                            ["pattern"] = @"\b\d{3}[-]?\d{4}[-]?\d{7}[-]?\d{1}\b",
                            ["category"] = "NATIONAL_ID"
                        }
                    };
                    return patterns.ToString();
                }" />
                <set-variable name="piiInputContent" value="@(context.Request.Body.As<string>(preserveContent: true))" />
                <!-- Include the PII detection fragment -->
                <include-fragment fragment-id="pii-detection" />
                <!-- Block request if PII is detected -->
                <choose>
                    <when condition="@(context.Variables.GetValueOrDefault<bool>("piiDetected", false))">
                        <return-response>
                            <set-status code="400" reason="Bad Request" />
                            <set-header name="Content-Type" exists-action="override">
                                <value>application/json</value>
                            </set-header>
                            <set-body>@{
                                var detectedEntities = context.Variables.GetValueOrDefault<string>("piiDetectedEntities", "");
                                return new JObject(
                                    new JProperty("error", new JObject(
                                        new JProperty("code", "PII_DETECTED"),
                                        new JProperty("message", "Request blocked: Personal Identifiable Information (PII) detected in the request."),
                                        new JProperty("detectedCategories", detectedEntities)
                                    ))
                                ).ToString();
                            }</set-body>
                        </return-response>
                    </when>
                </choose>
            </when>
        </choose>
        <!-- End of PII Detection and Blocking -->

    </inbound>
    <backend>
        <base />
    </backend>
    <outbound>
        <base />
    </outbound>
    <on-error>
        <base />
    </on-error>
</policies>

When PII is detected in a request, the API will return a 400 Bad Request response with details about the detected PII categories:

{
    "error": {
        "code": "PII_DETECTED",
        "message": "Request blocked: Personal Identifiable Information (PII) detected in the request.",
        "detectedCategories": "Email, Person, PhoneNumber, InternationalBankingAccountNumber"
    }
}

NOTE: The PII blocking approach is more restrictive than anonymization. Use this when your compliance requirements prohibit any PII from being processed by backend services, even in anonymized form.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: Using APIM to handle PII anonymization and deanonymization requests transparently for API requests that may contain PII data is a powerful way to ensure that sensitive data is protected while still allowing for the processing of requests. By using the above approach, you can ensure that PII data is handled securely and efficiently in your APIs.

docs.title: Validation Notebook Setup Guide
docs.text:
This guide sets up an isolated Python environment for the notebooks in this directory. It assumes you have not created a Python virtual environment before.

Start with Validation Environment Setup. It installs and verifies the shared dependency set for all 15 active scenario notebooks directly in validation, including the Foundry HR Web Search Chat and Self-hosted Gateway validation. The terminal instructions below are an alternative installation route, followed by the same notebook verification. Archived notebooks and other validation directories are outside this environment's scope.

Use the dedicated .venv-validation-local environment. Keep an existing repository .venv for other labs unchanged. Installing a requirements file does not uninstall packages omitted from it, so reusing a broader environment can leave incompatible, unrelated frameworks installed. The setup notebook deliberately rejects the old .venv kernel.

The finished setup has four parts that must agree:

  1. The repository has a .venv-validation-local virtual environment.
  2. Python packages are installed through that environment's Python executable.
  3. VS Code uses that Python executable as the notebook kernel.
  4. Notebooks run with validation as their working directory.

After setup, use Run All from a fresh kernel. The selected azd environment supplies deployment settings and models; required deployments default to allowed. Edit the configuration only for optional overrides or genuinely external inputs that are absent from azd. Every step shows a blue INFO section before execution and a green/amber/red RESULT section afterwards. Required parameters left blank or containing REPLACE stop initialization before deployment/testing, with all missing parameter names listed. Secrets must already be available through the documented environment/secret-store inputs; scenario execution does not prompt. Access Contracts requires explicit Key Vault and Foundry targets by default, unless their scenarios are explicitly disabled. See the execution guide. Use skipped_models = ["mini", "legacy"] to exclude case-insensitive model-name substrings from validation without removing models from backend deployment.

docs.title: Why Use a Virtual Environment?
docs.text:
A virtual environment is a private Python installation for one repository. Packages installed in .venv-validation-local do not modify your system Python or another project's packages.

pip installs packages for a particular Python interpreter. A bare command such as pip install requests can target the wrong interpreter. This guide therefore uses the .venv-validation-local Python executable explicitly:

.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip <command>

That form is the most reliable way to guarantee that packages are installed in this repository's .venv-validation-local.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Install the following before continuing:

  • Python 3.11 (latest available patch release). This is the supported setup target for the pinned dependency set; other Python minor versions are not validated by this workflow. Native packages can fail to build on newer interpreters.
  • Visual Studio Code.
  • The Microsoft Python and Jupyter VS Code extensions.
  • Azure CLI for Azure access used by the notebooks.
  • Azure Developer CLI when using notebook settings loaded from an azd environment.

Open PowerShell and verify the command-line tools:

py -0p
py -3.11 --version
az --version
azd version

py -0p lists the installed Python runtimes. Continue only when py -3.11 --version succeeds. If it fails, install the current Python 3.11 release from python.org and open a new terminal. Do not use the launcher's default Python 3.14 for this environment.

azd is optional when you set from_azd = False and provide notebook configuration manually.

docs.title: 1. Open the repository in VS Code
docs.text:
Open the repository root, not only the validation directory:

ai-hub-gateway-solution-accelerator

In VS Code, open Terminal > New Terminal. Confirm that PowerShell is at the repository root:

Get-Location

The final directory name should be ai-hub-gateway-solution-accelerator.

docs.title: 2. Create .venv-validation-local
docs.text:
From the repository root, run:

py -3.11 -m venv .venv-validation-local

Using py -3.11 is intentional. A generic py -m venv .venv-validation-local selects the launcher's default version, which may be too new for the complete dependency set.

The repository's .gitignore already excludes .venv-validation-local, so the environment will not be committed.

docs.title: 3. Verify the environment before installing
docs.text:
You do not need to activate the environment when you use its Python executable explicitly:

.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"
.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe --version
.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip --version
az --version
azd version

The Python executable and pip paths must contain the repository path followed by .venv-validation-local, and the Python version must be 3.11. Stop and recreate the environment if any check differs. az and azd are separate command-line tools, so their paths are not expected to be inside .venv-validation-local.

docs.title: 4. Upgrade Python packaging tools
docs.text: .\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel

docs.title: 5. Install all active notebook dependencies
docs.text:
From the repository root, first ask pip to resolve the complete dependency set without installing it:

.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --dry-run --ignore-installed -r .\validation\requirements.txt

Only continue if the dry run exits successfully. It checks the entire dependency graph independently of installed packages, but does not compile native packages or prove runtime API compatibility:

.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r .\validation\requirements.txt

The first installation can take several minutes. Install the complete requirements in one pip invocation so its resolver checks the frameworks together. ipykernel is included; no separate unpinned install is needed for the terminal-only route. Azure CLI is intentionally installed separately as a system tool; the notebooks invoke the external az command rather than importing it as a Python package.

For the notebook-first route, bootstrap ipykernel==7.3.0 into .venv-validation-local, select that kernel, then run the setup notebook's resolution and installation cells instead. After either route, restart the kernel, rerun setup step 1, then run step 4 to verify all direct versions and required SDK APIs.

Do not replace these commands with bare pip install commands. Using .venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip makes the installation target unambiguous even when another Python environment is activated.

docs.title: Optional: activate .venv-validation-local
docs.text:
Activation makes python resolve to .venv-validation-local for the current terminal session:

.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\Activate.ps1

The prompt normally begins with (.venv-validation-local). Verify it instead of relying only on the prompt:

python -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"
python -m pip --version

Both paths must contain .venv-validation-local. Even after activation, prefer python -m pip over bare pip.

If PowerShell blocks Activate.ps1, either continue using the explicit .venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe commands or permit local scripts for your Windows user:

Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser -ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned

Open a new PowerShell terminal after changing the policy. Do not change the machine-wide policy for this setup.

docs.title: First-Time Setup on macOS or Linux
docs.text:
From the repository root:

python3.11 -m venv .venv-validation-local
.venv-validation-local/bin/python -m pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel
.venv-validation-local/bin/python -m pip install --dry-run --ignore-installed -r validation/requirements.txt
.venv-validation-local/bin/python -m pip install -r validation/requirements.txt

If python3.11 is unavailable, install Python 3.11 first. Use python3 only if the following reports 3.11.x, not simply any newer Python:

python3 --version

Optional activation and verification:

source .venv-validation-local/bin/activate
python -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)'
python -m pip --version

docs.title: Verify the Installation
docs.text:
Run these commands from the repository root.

Windows PowerShell:

.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -c "import sys; print('Python:', sys.executable)"
.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -c "import requests; print('requests:', requests.__file__)"
.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -c "import azure.identity; import azure.mgmt.apimanagement; import openai; print('Baseline imports: OK')"
.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip check

macOS or Linux:

.venv-validation-local/bin/python -c "import sys; print('Python:', sys.executable)"
.venv-validation-local/bin/python -c "import requests; print('requests:', requests.__file__)"
.venv-validation-local/bin/python -c "import azure.identity; import azure.mgmt.apimanagement; import openai; print('Baseline imports: OK')"
.venv-validation-local/bin/python -m pip check

Expected results:

  • The Python executable path contains .venv-validation-local.
  • The Python version is 3.11.
  • The requests path is under .venv-validation-local.
  • The baseline import command prints Baseline imports: OK.
  • pip check prints No broken requirements found.

These terminal commands are quick baseline checks, not the final acceptance check. Open Validation Environment Setup, select .venv-validation-local, restart, and run step 1 followed by step 4. Its verification reports every pinned direct version and checks Agent Framework, Foundry PromptAgentDefinition, Key Vault, Cosmos DB, A2A, LangChain, charts, and shared helper imports without making Azure calls.

pip check only evaluates packages that are already installed. It can report success after a failed requirements installation if the failing packages were never installed, so always run the import checks too.

Get-Command python and where.exe python are useful diagnostics after activation, but the printed sys.executable path is the authoritative check.

docs.title: Select .venv-validation-local as the VS Code Notebook Kernel
docs.text:
Installing packages in .venv-validation-local does not automatically switch an already-open notebook to that environment.

If the new environment is not listed, run Python: Select Interpreter from the Command Palette, choose Enter interpreter path, and select .venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe on Windows or .venv-validation-local/bin/python on macOS/Linux. Then reopen the notebook's kernel picker.

  1. Open Validation Environment Setup under validation.
  2. Select the kernel name in the upper-right corner of the notebook editor.
  3. Choose Select Another Kernel if necessary.
  4. Choose Python Environments.
  5. Select the interpreter whose path ends with .venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe on Windows or .venv-validation-local/bin/python on macOS/Linux.
  6. Restart the notebook kernel after changing environments or installing packages.

Run this preflight cell before the notebook's first real cell:

import os
import sys
import requests

print("Python:", sys.executable)
print("Working directory:", os.getcwd())
print("requests:", requests.__file__)

Confirm that:

  • Python contains .venv-validation-local.
  • requests is loaded from .venv-validation-local.
  • Working directory ends with validation.

docs.title: Notebook Working Directory
docs.text:
The validation notebooks use paths such as:

sys.path.insert(1, "../shared")

They also read and generate files under ../bicep. These paths assume the current working directory is the repository's validation directory.

The recommended workflow is:

  1. Open the repository root as the VS Code workspace.
  2. Open the notebook from the validation directory.
  3. Select the repository's .venv-validation-local kernel.
  4. Check os.getcwd() with the preflight cell.

If the working directory is the repository root, change it once at the start of the notebook session:

import os
from pathlib import Path

current_dir = Path.cwd().resolve()
validation_dir = current_dir if current_dir.name == "validation" else current_dir / "validation"
if not (validation_dir / "requirements.txt").is_file() or not (validation_dir.parent / "shared" / "utils.py").is_file():
    raise RuntimeError("Run from the repository root or validation.")
os.chdir(validation_dir)
print(Path.cwd())

This cell is safe to repeat from either the repository root or validation; other locations fail explicitly. Working-directory state is per kernel session, so confirm it in every scenario notebook.

docs.title: Azure Authentication and Environment Selection
docs.text:
Most notebooks call Azure CLI from Python. Authenticate before running them:

az login
az account show --output table

If the wrong subscription is active:

az account set --subscription "<subscription-name-or-id>"
az account show --output table

For notebooks with from_azd = True, select the deployment environment first:

azd env list
azd env select <environment-name>
azd env get-values

Never place access tokens, API keys, client secrets, or provider credentials in terminal history. Follow each notebook's secret-storage instructions, particularly its Azure Key Vault guidance.

docs.title: Shared Dependencies and Version Policy
docs.text:
requirements.txt is the single source of truth for all direct dependencies of the 15 active scenario notebooks. Validation Environment Setup owns installation, version reporting, and SDK import/API checks. Agent Frameworks no longer installs packages, and PII analysis no longer upgrades Cosmos DB at runtime. MSAL, Key Vault, Cosmos DB, async support, and A2A are installed up front, including packages used only by optional scenarios.

  • Python: use Python 3.11. A virtual environment cannot change its base interpreter in place.
  • Direct versions: every direct dependency uses an exact == pin. Rerunning setup does not silently opt into newer SDK releases.
  • Framework components: the core, OpenAI, and A2A distributions replace the broad agent-framework metapackage. Component release numbers differ; their declared constraints, resolved together by pip, determine compatibility.
  • Preview versions: agent-framework-a2a==1.0.0b261002 is explicitly pinned. Do not use a global --pre, which can admit previews for unrelated dependencies.
  • Transitive versions: this is not a complete lockfile. Pip resolves transitive packages, so those versions can change between installations. pip check verifies installed dependency constraints; the setup notebook additionally verifies direct pins and imported SDK APIs.
  • Platform handling: pip resolves platform-specific dependencies from package metadata. There is no unconditional Windows-only pywin32 requirement for macOS/Linux users.
  • Updates: edit central pins as a compatible set, test a fresh Python 3.11 installation, run setup verification and affected scenario notebooks, and commit the requirements and guidance together. Do not fix conflicts with --no-deps, individual in-notebook upgrades, or silent fallback downgrades.

For a same-platform record after successful verification, from the repository root:

.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip freeze > .\.venv-validation-local\validation.freeze.txt

On macOS/Linux, use .venv-validation-local/bin/python -m pip freeze > .venv-validation-local/validation.freeze.txt. The snapshot stays in the ignored .venv-validation-local directory. It captures the resolved environment, not a portable, hash-verified lockfile. Inspect it before sharing; private package URLs can contain sensitive data.

The old all-labs dependency list included unused frameworks. Those and archived notebooks are deliberately outside this active-notebook environment. Do not combine requirements from validation, shared, or archived labs into this environment without separately validating their constraints.

docs.title: Normal Workflow After Initial Setup
docs.text:
You only create .venv-validation-local and install the shared requirements once, then reinstall when central pins change. For later sessions:

  1. Open the repository root in VS Code.
  2. Optionally activate .venv-validation-local in the terminal.
  3. Run az login if your Azure session has expired.
  4. Select the appropriate azd environment when the notebook uses it.
  5. Open a notebook under validation.
  6. Confirm its kernel is .venv-validation-local.
  7. Run the preflight cell and confirm the working directory.
  8. Run notebook cells in order.

docs.title: pip check reports dependency conflicts in step 4
docs.text:
Step 4 now captures pip's output explicitly and includes the conflict details in the raised error. A nonzero exit means installed packages have incompatible dependency constraints, not that the notebook's import-check loop is broken.

For example, an older all-labs environment can contain agent-framework-foundry requiring azure-ai-projects<2.8.0, openai-agents requiring openai<3, or semantic-kernel requiring pydantic<2.12. These are not required by the active validation suite. Installing this suite's requirements into that environment does not remove them.

Do not downgrade the central pins or disable pip check. Instead:

  1. Leave the existing .venv and its packages unchanged.
  2. Create .venv-validation-local from Python 3.11 using the setup commands above.
  3. Install the complete shared requirements into that environment.
  4. In every validation notebook, use Select Another Kernel > Python Environments, then choose .venv-validation-local.
  5. Restart and run setup step 1 followed by step 4. The printed interpreter must point to .venv-validation-local, and pip must report No broken requirements found.

If the dedicated environment has itself accumulated unrelated packages, use Recreate a damaged environment below, targeting only .venv-validation-local.

docs.title: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'requests'
docs.text:
First inspect the active notebook kernel:

import sys
print(sys.executable)

If the path does not contain .venv-validation-local, select the .venv-validation-local kernel. If it does contain .venv-validation-local, install and verify through that exact interpreter from the repository root:

.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r .\validation\requirements.txt
.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -c "import requests; print(requests.__file__)"

Restart the notebook kernel afterward.

docs.title: pip install -r requirements.txt fails
docs.text:
Avoid bare pip and first confirm the environment:

.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip --version
.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel
.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r .\validation\requirements.txt

Read the first ERROR: line in the pip output. Common causes include an unsupported Python version, a corporate proxy or package-index restriction, unavailable build tools, or a package-version conflict. Capture the complete command output when asking for help; an exit code alone does not identify the failed package.

Check the environment's Python version directly:

.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe --version

If it reports anything other than Python 3.11, install Python 3.11 and recreate .venv-validation-local using the commands in Recreate a damaged environment. A virtual environment cannot be changed to another Python version in place.

docs.title: Failed to build 'pymsalruntime'
docs.text:
pymsalruntime is a native dependency used by the pip-distributed Azure CLI. Its older source uses Python APIs removed in Python 3.12 and later, producing errors such as Py_UNICODE* has been removed or an incompatible MSALRUNTIME_LOG_CALLBACK_ROUTINE.

The validation notebooks do not need Azure CLI installed as a Python package. They execute the separately installed az command. The repository requirements therefore exclude azure-cli and treat it as a system prerequisite.

If this error occurred before that change, verify that the requirements file no longer contains an active azure-cli line:

Select-String -Path .\validation\requirements.txt -Pattern '^azure-cli$'
.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe --version

The first command should return no match. Then rerun the requirements installation; pip can continue using the existing environment because the failed pymsalruntime build did not install that package:

.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --dry-run --ignore-installed -r .\validation\requirements.txt
.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r .\validation\requirements.txt

If the dry run fails on another package, follow Recreate a damaged environment with Python 3.11. Confirm the external CLI independently:

az --version
az account show --output table

docs.title: Failed building wheel for pydantic-core or Python 3.14 is newer than PyO3's maximum supported version
docs.text:
This can indicate that the environment uses a Python version unsupported by the selected native dependency. Check the actual .venv-validation-local version rather than assuming the error identifies it. Installing Rust or setting PYO3_USE_ABI3_FORWARD_COMPATIBILITY is not the supported fix for this notebook suite.

Install Python 3.11, close any notebook kernel using .venv-validation-local, and recreate the environment with the commands in Recreate a damaged environment. Verify the new interpreter before installing packages:

.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe --version

It must report Python 3.11.x.

docs.title: A package installed successfully but the notebook cannot import it
docs.text:
The terminal and notebook are using different Python interpreters. Compare:

.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -c "import sys; print(sys.executable)"

with:

import sys
print(sys.executable)

Both paths must identify the same .venv-validation-local Python executable. Then restart the kernel.

docs.title: No module named 'utils' or No module named 'apimtools'
docs.text:
Check the notebook working directory:

import os
print(os.getcwd())

It must end with validation because the notebooks add ../shared to sys.path.

docs.title: PowerShell cannot run Activate.ps1
docs.text: Activation is optional. Use .\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip directly, or apply the current-user execution policy described earlier in this guide.

docs.title: az or azd is not recognized
docs.text: Install the missing CLI, close all terminals, open a new terminal, and rerun az --version or azd version. azd is unnecessary when from_azd = False.

docs.title: Recreate a damaged environment
docs.text:
Virtual environments are disposable. Close notebooks and terminals using .venv-validation-local. Confirm you are at the repository root and that .venv-validation-local is the environment you intend to remove before recreating it.

PowerShell from the repository root:

Remove-Item -LiteralPath .\.venv-validation-local -Recurse -Force
py -3.11 -m venv .venv-validation-local
.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel
.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install --dry-run --ignore-installed -r .\validation\requirements.txt
.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r .\validation\requirements.txt

Select the new .venv-validation-local kernel, restart, then run setup steps 1 and 4. Do not copy a .venv-validation-local from another computer or repository; recreate it from requirements.

docs.title: Checking Setup Changes
docs.text:
The setup regression tests use the standard library only. From the repository root:

.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m unittest discover -s .\validation\tests -v

They check notebook syntax, dependency coverage, kernel/working-directory guards, pip invocation, and failure propagation. They do not install packages, authenticate, or deploy resources. Maintainers must also verify a fresh requirements installation and the setup notebook's version/API checks when updating pins.

docs.title: Maintaining the Environment
docs.text:
Use the environment's interpreter for all package operations:

.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip list
.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip check
.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r .\validation\requirements.txt

Avoid these patterns:

  • pip install ... without verifying which Python owns pip.
  • py -m pip install ... after .venv-validation-local exists; the Python launcher can target global Python.
  • pip install --user ... for notebook dependencies.
  • Upgrading packages individually or enabling global --pre instead of updating central pins.
  • Running setup installation cells before selecting the .venv-validation-local kernel.
  • Committing .venv-validation-local, generated credentials, or notebook secrets.

docs.title: Snippets
docs.text: We use snippets to reduce redundancy and improve maintainability. Snippets are references from the many Jupyter notebook files throughout our labs. They work by using Python's %load magic command.

docs.title: Loaded Snippets
docs.text:
Jupyter notebooks will have Python code blocks similar to this one:

# %load ../../shared/snippets/openai-api-requests.py

import time
from openai import AzureOpenAI

...

What you see here is an executed load as the command is now commented out after the code has been loaded immediately below it.

While this is generally very maintable, the loading is static, unlike a function reference, for example. That means that code may be stale. When you are editing Jupyter notebook files, it is advisable that you execute the load commands fresh and check for git changes.

docs.title: Updating a Loaded Snippet
docs.text:
1. In a Jupyter Notebook's Python code cell, remove everything below the %load command in line 1.

  2. Uncomment the %load command. The cell should then look similar to this:

    %load ../../shared/snippets/openai-api-requests.py

  3. Press the Play button in the code cell to execute the %load command.

  4. Repeate these steps for all code blocks with %load commands in the current file.
  5. Save the file.
  6. Check git for any changes to the file.
  7. Test the changes.
  8. Check in the changes.

docs.title: Citadel validation notebooks
docs.text:
For private developer access before running these application scenarios, use the optional Developer VPN deployment and validation notebook and its Bicep deployment notes. It creates a separate connectivity resource group and does not require private APIM data-plane access to bootstrap. Provisioning is explicitly gated because VPN Gateway and DNS Private Resolver incur ongoing charges.

These notebooks have two purposes: prove the deployed feature works, and show how it is configured, deployed, and consumed. Feature definitions, policy previews, requests, SDK integration, and expected outcomes stay visible. Shared utilities handle repetitive mechanics; they are not a replacement for the feature demonstrations.

docs.title: Setup and execution
docs.text:
Start with Environment Setup and the setup guide. Use the repository-root .venv-validation-local Python 3.11 kernel and the dependencies in requirements.txt. The environment name is retained for compatibility; the active notebook directory is validation, not validation-local. Do not install or upgrade packages inside scenario notebooks.

Open the repository in VS Code and use Run All from a fresh kernel. Restart the kernel after updating repository helpers or installed packages: Python otherwise keeps previously imported modules cached. Alerting's configuration cell explicitly refreshes its consumer helpers before importing their functions, so rerunning that cell also picks up newly added helpers. Configuration defaults use the selected azd environment; no edits are needed for settings or models that azd already supplies. Only genuinely external inputs (such as separate target resources, provider credentials, or token/evidence fixtures) need to be supplied when absent. Scenario execution does not prompt for missing inputs. Both the repository root and this directory are supported working directories. Authenticate Azure CLI and select the intended azd environment before starting. The notebooks must not change your active subscription automatically.

Deploy the gateway first using the full deployment guide. These scenarios require an existing hub; the environment-setup notebook alone does not deploy or configure Azure resources.

docs.title: Step output and fail-fast initialization
docs.text:
Every executable cell has a short purpose, input, and expected-output guide. It emits two clearly separated sections:

Section What it shows INFO (blue) What will run: command or task, endpoint, selected models, coordinates, and expected outcome. RESULT (green) Task or check completed successfully, with actual response/output and elapsed time. Definition-only cells still confirm execution. RESULT (amber) A warning, optional skip, or an HTTP response whose expected outcome still needs validation. RESULT (red) Failed or blocked required checks, exceptions, and actionable details.

Shared output formatters render HTML cards and colored result tables in notebooks, with an ANSI terminal fallback. Output is compact by default: key inputs, models, actual API requests, deployment commands, and one step result. Routine successful azd/account queries, Bicep compilation, and individual passing assertions are not printed. Passing checks are counted in the step result; failures and skips keep their actionable details.

Large payloads are collapsed under Details, and API replies are summarized (chat content, response IDs, embedding dimensions, or image count) rather than dumping vectors, headers, or image data. Credentials remain redacted and actual response objects are unchanged. Set utils.set_output_verbose(True) after importing utils to temporarily restore diagnostic commands and detailed payloads; use False to return to compact output. Expected negative responses such as a policy's HTTP 403 still count as a green PASS when the assertion matches.

Initialization validates mandatory inputs before provisioning or feature tests. Missing, blank, or nested REPLACE values produce one error listing the missing parameter names, without showing secret values. Fill those values and rerun from the beginning. An empty model plan after exclusions is not a successful initialization, but operation annotations are not required by default.

Backend Onboarding loads coordinates and LLM_BACKEND_CONFIG from azd during initialization. Run All uses those values to generate and deploy contracts, without manual approval flags or a required capability map. It shows the Azure subscription ID/name, tenant, APIM, resource group, region, backend IDs and model operation mapping before deployment. Running this notebook refreshes shared routing from the selected environment's configuration. model_aliases=None loads optional MODEL_ALIASES/LLM_MODEL_ALIASES from azd; an explicit list wins. Its functionality tests use Universal LLM (/models) only, including discovery, chat, embeddings, Responses creation (POST only), SDK streaming and aliases. The SDK uses an OpenAI-compatible base URL, not Azure deployment-path routes; its temporary access contract grants only universal-llm-api. Other API deployments are unchanged. Responses GET and input-items are not tested by onboarding; All Models retains its separate Responses lifecycle coverage.

The same azd-first behavior applies throughout this suite. Deployments required by a scenario are enabled by default; review/source approval flags are not mandatory user inputs. Optional explicit routing parameter files and coordinate overrides still take precedence. Model skip keywords apply before selection and request planning, including when a scenario rebuilds its catalog. Unrelated image or embedding entries in a mixed deployment are not missing parameters for a chat scenario: inapplicable cases are reported as SKIP.

Access Contracts enables Key Vault and Foundry scenarios by default. Provide explicit target subscription/resource-group/vault and account/project coordinates in its configuration cell. The hub's azd resources are not silently substituted for these external targets. Setting an integration flag to False explicitly opts out and removes only that scenario's input requirement. No manually supplied Foundry project identity token is required. Access Contracts keeps ProjectManagedIdentity connection authentication and its JWT-enforcing policy, validates the deployed configuration/publication, and explicitly defers identity-protected API and load requests to Agent Frameworks. Direct API-key contracts are still exercised here; deferred identity checks are SKIP, not PASS.

Required secrets and token fixtures come from documented environment variables or an explicit secret-store lookup, never input()/getpass() midway through Run All. Interactive authentication examples are disabled by default and must be run deliberately. Environment Setup remains a prerequisite: package installation can require a kernel restart before running scenarios.

docs.title: Supplying genuinely external inputs once
docs.text:
These optional values can be resolved from the selected azd environment when provided; missing external values are reported by name rather than replaced with invented resources. Explicit notebook overrides still win.

Scenario input Supported configuration External Key Vault target VALIDATION_EXTERNAL_KEYVAULT JSON: {"subscriptionId":"<subscription>","resourceGroupName":"rg-consumers","name":"kv-consumers"} External Foundry target VALIDATION_EXTERNAL_FOUNDRY JSON: {"subscriptionId":"<subscription>","resourceGroupName":"rg-agents","accountName":"aif-agents","projectName":"project-agents"} Entra client secret / role-control tokens Automatically loaded/acquired after Entra setup. VALIDATION_ENTRA_CLIENT_SECRET, VALIDATION_JWT_NO_ROLE_TOKEN, and VALIDATION_JWT_DEVICE_TOKEN are optional overrides Existing published agent VALIDATION_FOUNDRY_AGENT_NAME or FOUNDRY_AGENT_NAME; project coordinates use FOUNDRY_ACCOUNT_NAME, FOUNDRY_PROJECT_NAME, FOUNDRY_PROJECT_ENDPOINT, or an unambiguous AI_FOUNDRY_SERVICES entry Agent predecessor contracts Automatically uses the latest complete local Access Contracts handoff for the selected gateway. Optional VALIDATION_ACCESS_CONTRACTS_MANIFEST or keyed JSON VALIDATION_AGENT_CONTRACTS pins an explicit source. Optional alert notification recipient VALIDATION_ALERT_EMAIL or ALERT_EMAIL_ADDRESS; no value runs rules without email. alert_email_address="" explicitly disables a saved recipient. Application Insights APIM_APP_INSIGHTS_NAME, otherwise exact unambiguous APIM logger resource discovery using the supported ARM REST API (az rest) Self-hosted gateway target VALIDATION_SELF_HOSTED_GATEWAY_URL (HTTPS origin, no /models) and VALIDATION_SELF_HOSTED_GATEWAY_ID (APIM gateway resource name); notebook overrides win Optional Cosmos key authentication VALIDATION_COSMOS_KEY; prefer the default identity-based access

The target JSON examples are illustrative, not valid deployed resources. Keep secrets in an approved secret store or private runtime environment, never saved notebook source or source control. Access Contracts intentionally does not substitute the hub's vault/project for these external target inputs.

docs.title: Recommended execution order
docs.text:
The 15 scenarios are:

Order Notebook What it proves / prerequisites 1 Backend Onboarding Backend/pool/fragment deployment, discovery, HTTP/SDK consumption and aliases through Universal LLM only. Review complete routing configuration before replacing shared fragments. 2 All Models Unrestricted discovery, chat, embeddings, stored Responses create/get/input-items. Operations are inferred by default. 3 Access Contracts Business-unit model grants and capacity; explicit Key Vault/Foundry targets are required by default, with deliberate opt-outs. Retain its manifest for the next notebook. 4 Agent Frameworks Microsoft Agent Framework, Foundry SDK, and LangChain consumption of the preceding contracts. 5 Model Aliases Discovery, direct controls, priority/weighted selection, and RBAC across APIs. Needs compatible alias members. 6 PII Processing Masking/restoration evidence, blocking, chunked large payloads, optional Cosmos analytics. Needs Language Service and appropriate telemetry access. 7 Unified AI API Native/compatible routing, Responses, streaming, authentication, denied paths, RBAC, and headers. 8 JWT Authentication Universal /models/chat/completions and Unified OpenAI v1 /unified-ai/v1/chat/completions only. Run after Entra setup without manual inputs. Automatically acquires/decodes application, current-user and negative-client tokens; tests both positive identities and missing-Model.Invoke rejection. 9 Extended Providers Bedrock, Gemini, Anthropic native versus OpenAI-compatible protocols, credential formats, and compatible aliases. Provider credentials are separate prerequisites. 10 Session Affinity Independent cookie jars and successful stateful response chaining. Requires a Responses-capable model served by multiple backends. 11 Gateway Alerting Restrictive capacity, HTTP 429/403, configured rules, and observed telemetry. Runs from azd without email; only chat-capable names containing gpt but not image are eligible, including explicit overrides and skip filters. Requires Application Insights/Monitor permissions. 12 Publish Contract MCP initialization/list/call, A2A card/invocation, mixed-asset grants, metrics, and resiliency configuration. Requires the selected source assets. 13 Image Models Real generation/edit images, body/path/header model selection, multipart requests, and negative policy cases. Uses inferred/overridden image operations and configured native provider paths. 14 Foundry HR Web Search Chat A real Foundry Prompt Agent reusing the HR contract, 10 visualized turns, web-search/citation evidence, and bounded visible token-limit recovery. Run Access Contracts first. 15 Self-hosted Gateway Existing gateway in another cloud/on premises; provisions an access contract with default-on token limits, model RBAC, Content Safety and request PII anonymization. Authenticated /models/deployments discovery and a filtered GPT text-only chat loop run exclusively against the self-hosted origin.

The environment-setup notebook is a separate prerequisite, not an additional scenario. Archived notebooks and validation-local are outside this workflow.

docs.title: Self-hosted gateways in other clouds or on premises
docs.text:
The Self-hosted Gateway notebook requires an existing gateway, a reachable trusted HTTPS origin, and the models API already associated with that gateway. It does not install containers, change shared routing, or fall back to the Azure managed gateway. Azure management access is still required to create or update the scenario's product/subscription.

Set the external target variables above or the corresponding notebook settings. Keep all four feature switches on, or explicitly turn individual features off before initialization. Optional model_allowlist and skipped_models narrow the configured GPT text/chat plan; empty or invalid selections fail before deployment. With model RBAC on, deployment discovery must match the grant exactly. With RBAC off, other deployments may be visible but are never added to the text test loop.

Use a gateway image supporting the selected AI policies. Configure off-cloud authentication and connectivity for shared inference routing, the Content Safety backend, and Azure AI Language. The contract reuses the PII implementation locally with Microsoft Entra Workload ID, not the managed identity of the Azure APIM resource; grant the workload identity the required Language-service permissions. No shared fragment is overwritten. PII is request-only anonymization with synthetic data and fail-closed service errors. Set REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE for private CAs; certificate verification stays enabled.

Highlighted feature tables appear at initialization, deployment and summary. Per-model checks require the actual edge gateway ID/current contract marker, token-accounting headers, completed safety-policy traversal and a masking transformation when enabled. RBAC denial is verified with its specific error code. An optional existing benign text blocklist fixture verifies Content Safety denial; without it negative enforcement is SKIP. Deliberate quota exhaustion is also SKIP, not claimed as proven by accounting headers. Token counters are gateway-local, not a global cross-cloud quota. Disabling a contract feature does not remove inherited global/API controls. Cleanup is opt-in and deletes only this run's newly created product/subscription, retaining the gateway and association.

docs.title: HR career-coaching chat with Foundry web search
docs.text:
Foundry HR Web Search Chat automatically loads the HR contract's project connection and granted model. It creates or reuses the stable HR-Career-Coach agent with Foundry's native WebSearchTool, then runs one persistent 10-turn conversation about career development, learning, privacy-conscious AI use and productivity. Every user message, assistant reply, actual source citation, usage and retry is visualized in the notebook. No separate Bing key is needed for the general web-search tool; see the official Foundry web-search guide. The tenth prompt asks the agent to recall the earlier name, role, time horizon and weekly learning budget before rehearsing the manager conversation, matching the final context-validation check.

The existing gateway-connected model and Foundry project must support that tool. The notebook does not silently substitute a direct model endpoint if tool use fails. Its summary requires observed web_search_call activity and URL citations, not just a successfully created agent.

SDK automatic retries are disabled. A rate/token-limit response is highlighted, then the notebook honors Retry-After/reset hints for at most one retry per turn. max_wait_seconds=300 bounds that wait; absent usable hints, a visible fallback_wait_seconds=90 pause is used. It does not claim to know token availability without a server hint. Quota exhaustion, repeated limits and waits beyond the ceiling stop clearly rather than producing invented replies or retrying forever. User messages are appended once; earlier transcript entries remain available after a failed turn. Retry idempotency headers are stable per turn.

This exercise creates billable Foundry resources and public-web searches. Use only the supplied synthetic employee context or equally non-sensitive prompts. Cleanup is off by default and limited to this run's agent version/conversation; it never deletes the HR contract or its published connection.

docs.title: Configuration and model selection
docs.text:
Explicit notebook configuration takes precedence over the selected azd environment. Manual mode requires complete resource coordinates and skips azd. Missing required values, placeholders, malformed JSON, ambiguous resources, or a subscription mismatch must be corrected before deployment. Enabling an integration is an explicit decision; discovering a vault does not itself enable Key Vault.

The context reads environment values once. Important existing outputs include LLM_BACKEND_CONFIG, APIM_NAME, AZURE_RESOURCE_GROUP, AZURE_LOCATION, AZURE_SUBSCRIPTION_ID, AI_FOUNDRY_SERVICES, and KEY_VAULT_NAME. Restart initialization after changing environment or provisioning outside the notebook. azd outputs describe configuration, not current provider availability.

docs.title: Automatic operations, overrides, and excluded models
docs.text:
Without operation overrides, models use explicitly supplied operation metadata when present, otherwise these case-insensitive substring rules, in order:

Model name contains Assumed operations image or flux image-generation, image-edit Otherwise embedding or text embeddings Otherwise gpt chat, responses Anything else chat

Image rules take priority over gpt (so GPT image models are not sent chat requests). Streaming is assumed for inferred chat models. These are test-planning assumptions, not evidence that every provider supports the operation; actual requests still determine the result. Image coverage belongs to Image Models, and text-only runners record it as explicitly out of scope rather than sending image models to chat.

Every scenario configuration includes these optional controls:

operation_overrides = None  # Use optional azd mapping, otherwise metadata/inference.
skipped_models = None       # Use optional VALIDATION_SKIPPED_MODELS, otherwise [].

# Examples: use exact names from the displayed model inventory.
operation_overrides = {
    "my-chat-model": ["chat", "responses"],
    "my-image-model": ["image-generation"],
    "my-disabled-model": [],
}
skipped_models = ["mini", "legacy"]  # Case-insensitive substring matching.

A supplied operation_overrides dictionary replaces the saved azd operation map. Each entry fully replaces that model's inferred operations; omitted models use their metadata/inference. An empty list disables a model's tests. operation_overrides={} clears azd operation overrides and restores automatic fallback. Optional VALIDATION_MODEL_CAPABILITIES is a JSON object with the same shape; it is no longer a required deployment output.

Skip keywords exclude requests, selections, and alias-member tests containing those names. They do not filter the deployed backend configuration or its discovery results; temporary validation contracts use the selected eligible test models. An explicit skipped_models=[] clears saved exclusions. If every eligible model is excluded, initialization explains why no tests can run.

For strict manually mapped operation support, set overrides["infer_operations"] = False and provide the required mappings. Operation labels are case-sensitive: chat, responses, embeddings, image-generation, image-edit, and explicit streaming for overridden chat models. Native provider scenarios retain their protocol-specific requests.

Responses GET and input-items GET returning HTTP 404 are warnings for every model, including explicitly overridden models. They are recorded as SKIP, not FAIL or PASS: retrieval was not validated, and the run may continue. This also applies to Unified AI's Responses GET; its DELETE checks retain their existing failure behavior.

Other unsupported retrieval results (405/501, or a specific unsupported-operation 400) remain optional only for inferred GPT-mini models. Explicit operation overrides make those non-404 checks required. Responses POST/create failures, authentication errors, throttling and general server failures still fail.

Each configuration guide includes input explanations and samples. Some scenarios need external credentials, existing agents, predecessor manifests, or observed telemetry that azd does not provide; those remain real prerequisites, not invented defaults. Access Contracts intentionally keeps explicit external targets mandatory.

Defaults are selected deterministically from compatible deployed entries. Explicit model overrides must also exist and meet operation/contract constraints. Declared retirement dates produce warnings, not automatic exclusion. Selecting a newer model requires deploying it; default operation inference then applies. Override only exceptions rather than changing thirteen notebooks. Infrastructure model defaults are not modified by this refactor.

docs.title: Contracts and artifacts
docs.text:
Access, backend, and publish deployments use .bicepparam as their primary editable parameter files and actual deployment inputs. Shared contract helpers render nested configuration, preserve escaping, and validate the current file before deployment.

  1. Define the feature configuration visibly.
  2. Generate and inspect the parameter/policy artifacts.
  3. Make any intentional edits to the generated .bicepparam.
  4. Run the deployment cell, which validates that actual file.
  5. Validate deployed state and make real feature requests.

New run artifacts belong under ignored .runs/<scenario>/<run-id>/.

docs.title: Stable asset identities and reruns
docs.text:
Cloud assets use stable, scenario-specific names, not a run ID or timestamp. Rerunning a notebook updates the same access-contract products (IDs and display names), subscriptions, connections, secret names, model aliases, alerts and action groups. Separate feature cases, such as PII masking, blocking and analytics, retain separate identities. Validation aliases replace only their own named entries while preserving unrelated aliases and the full backend inventory. ARM deployment names are stable too, with a deterministic gateway-scope suffix and a maximum length of 64 characters so different gateways do not collide.

Foundry uses the stable HR-ChatAgent and HR-Career-Coach agent names. An unchanged definition reuses its latest version; a changed definition creates a new immutable version under the same name, as required by the Foundry API. Only versions actually created by the current run are cleanup-eligible.

Run IDs still isolate local evidence, request correlation, conversations and the alerting probe's token counters. Reusing a product must not inherit the previous probe's exhausted quota. Run a given scenario serially against a gateway: its policy and configuration are shared, not concurrent per-run resources. Existing assets with old run-suffixed names are not automatically renamed or deleted.

Keep secrets out of saved notebooks, previews, manifests, and parameter files. Prefer Key Vault references for provider credentials. Do not print deployment outputs containing API keys. Retrieve the exact contract subscription rather than choosing the first available APIM key. Deployment output filtering preserves allowlisted product/subscription identifiers and Key Vault reference names, plus Foundry connection names, targets and authentication metadata, even when the compiled contract refers to secret plans. Credential values remain excluded; the matching subscription key is read separately through APIM. An omitted or empty Foundry connectionNamePrefix uses the existing Hub-<businessUnit>-<useCaseName>-<environment> naming convention, including when only selected foundryConfig fields are overridden.

The Access Contracts pilot writes a sanitized access-contracts.json manifest. Run Agent Frameworks afterwards: with its unchanged defaults, it automatically loads the latest complete manifest matching the selected subscription, resource group, APIM service and recorded azd environment. It maps the three contracts to:

Agent Framework Predecessor contract / consumption Sales Assistant Microsoft Agent Framework Sales Assistant contract; endpoint/key read from Key Vault HR Chat Agent Foundry Prompt Agent SDK HR ChatAgent contract; published project connection with ProjectManagedIdentity Support Bot LangChain ChatOpenAI Support Bot contract; exact APIM subscription credential

The actual product/subscription IDs, selected models and connection methods are displayed during initialization. Credentials are fetched afresh; the manifest does not contain keys. Explicit manifest_path/contract records or azd source overrides remain available, and ambiguous equally recent handoffs require an explicit selection. Keep these products until the successor notebook has finished. Disabled Foundry publication can return null-valued placeholder metadata; it is ignored for Sales/Support. Only the HR Foundry contract requires project coordinates.

Backend onboarding refreshes shared routing policies. Confirm that the supplied configuration includes all intended backends and aliases; a partial azd snapshot is not a safe source for a lossless shared update.

docs.title: Results and feature evidence
docs.text:
The shared result collector distinguishes:

  • PASS: the expected feature outcome was observed, including expected denial.
  • FAIL: unexpected response, transport error, or invalid response body.
  • SKIP: an explicitly disabled/unavailable optional feature, with a reason.
  • BLOCKED: missing prerequisites or evidence for required coverage.

Required failures/blocks and empty required runs cannot produce a successful final verdict. A green HTTP 200 does not by itself prove PII masking, correct model routing, streaming completion, or a working image edit.

JWT role tests need a real valid token lacking the required role; an invalid token's 401 is not evidence of role enforcement. Setup supplies a separate MCP.Invoke-only client, and the notebook obtains its token automatically. Decoded claims are checked locally; only live APIM requests prove signature acceptance. The current user's CLI session must be valid; required MFA/sign-in is surfaced as an explicit error, not an automatic interactive prompt. Telemetry checks distinguish configured rules, observed HTTP limits, metric ingestion, alert firing, and notification delivery. Never infer email delivery from a successful deployment. Circuit-breaker configuration is distinct from a disruptive trip/recovery test.

Feature-essential load tests are bounded and visible. Additional stress tests are opt-in. Retries must not hide throttling, weighted selection, or stateful routing behavior. Cloud requests, generated images, deployment, telemetry polling, and quota probes incur cost and can alter shared state.

docs.title: Cleanup and testing
docs.text:
Cleanup is off by default. Preview owned resources first. Delete only new products/assets created by that run, never a predecessor contract, reused resource, or shared backend configuration. Retained artifacts may be needed to investigate failures; a failed summary does not prevent manually running cleanup.

Run local helper/structure tests without cloud credentials from the repository:

.\.venv-validation-local\Scripts\python.exe -m unittest discover -s .\validation\tests -v

Tests mock external boundaries. Bicep compilation checks generated parameter syntax, not successful deployment. A fresh-kernel live run in the intended environment remains necessary to establish actual gateway/provider behavior.

docs.title: Citadel Governance Hub - Testing & Validation Guide
Executive Summary
docs.text:
This testing suite provides a comprehensive, end-to-end validation framework for the Citadel Governance Hub — an enterprise-grade AI gateway built on Azure API Management (APIM). The notebooks in this directory enable platform teams to onboard LLM backends, validate the full model surface area through the Universal LLM API, provision access contracts for different business units, and validate model-alias routing — all through guided, reproducible Jupyter workflows.

The recommended execution order is:

Strongly recommended baseline (steps 1–3): these three notebooks together exercise the core gateway plumbing — backend onboarding, full model surface area, and access-contract provisioning. Run them in order on every new Governance Hub deployment before moving on to the optional model-aliases notebook.

  1. Backend Contracts (LLM Onboarding) — Register AI backends and deploy routing logic into APIM ⭐ strongly recommended
  2. Universal LLM API — All-Models Tests — Validate every gateway-configured model (chat / embeddings / Responses API) through /models ⭐ strongly recommended
  3. Access Contracts — Create per-team access contracts with Key Vault and Foundry integrations ⭐ strongly recommended
  4. Model Aliases — Validate the shared resolve-model-alias policy fragment across the LLM APIs (priority + weighted strategies, RBAC, discovery)

Each notebook is self-contained with initialization, deployment, testing, visualization, and cleanup stages, enabling both interactive exploration and repeatable CI/CD validation.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before running any notebook, ensure the following are in place:

  • Citadel Governance Hub deployed (see the repository README — deploy with ./scripts/bootstrap-state.sh then ./scripts/deploy.sh dev)
  • Azure CLI installed and authenticated (az login)
  • Python 3.10+ with a virtual environment activated
  • Dependencies installed: 
    pip install -r requirements.txt
    (or the equivalent comprehensive list in ../shared/requirements.txt)
  • VS Code with the Jupyter extension (recommended for running notebooks)

docs.title: Optional (per notebook)
docs.text: Capability Required By Details Universal LLM API (models) imported in APIM Universal LLM All-Models Tests, Model Aliases Required for /models discovery and per-model operation tests Azure Key Vault Access Contracts A Key Vault with secrets for LLM endpoint and API key Azure AI Foundry Access Contracts A Foundry account and project for connection integration resolve-model-alias policy fragment + alias-aware backend onboarding Model Aliases Re-deployed by the notebook itself via the LLM backend onboarding Terraform/Bicep with modelAliases populated Unified AI API (unified-ai) imported in APIM Model Aliases (full cross-API coverage) Required for the wildcard /unified-ai/** routing patterns

docs.title: Configuring Notebook Variables
docs.text: Open the init cell, replace the "REPLACE" sentinel values (and any inline config blocks such as llm_backends_config / model_aliases) with values that match your deployment, then run the cell.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Each notebook's init cell follows the same pattern:

# Fill these in to match your Citadel Governance Hub deployment.
governance_hub_resource_group = "REPLACE"   # e.g. "rg-citadel-dev"
location                      = "REPLACE"   # e.g. "eastus", "swedencentral"
# ... other notebook-specific values (backends, aliases, Key Vault, Foundry) ...

Any value left as "REPLACE" (or empty) is flagged by a warning when the cell runs, so you can tell at a glance what still needs filling in. Notebooks that deploy via Terraform (backend onboarding, access contracts, model aliases) read their results back with terraform output -json from the relevant module after the scripts/deploy.sh run completes.

Tip: If you deployed the hub with this repo's Terraform flow, you can pull the values you need straight from the state with terraform output -raw resource_group_name, terraform output -raw location, terraform output -json llm_backend_config, etc. Run these from the repo root (or the llm-backend-onboarding/ module) and paste the results into the init cell.

docs.title: Per-Notebook Variable Map
docs.text:
The table below summarizes the variables you set in each notebook's init cell. Variables in italics are optional / only used when the notebook actually exercises the corresponding integration.

Notebook Variables to set manually llm-backend-onboarding-runner governance_hub_resource_grouplocationllm_backends_config (inline JSON)model_aliaseskey_vault_name citadel-universal-llm-api-all-models-tests governance_hub_resource_grouplocation citadel-access-contracts-tests governance_hub_resource_grouplocationkeyvault_subscription_id / keyvault_resource_group / keyvault_namefoundry_subscription_id / foundry_resource_group / foundry_account_name / foundry_project_name citadel-model-aliases-tests governance_hub_resource_grouplocationllm_backends_config (inline JSON)model_aliasesdirect_test_model

Multi-environment teams: To point a notebook at a different deployment, change governance_hub_resource_group (and any environment-specific values) in the init cell before running it.

docs.title: 1. LLM Backend Onboarding Runner
docs.text: Notebook llm-backend-onboarding-runner.ipynb Purpose Onboard AI backends into the Citadel Governance Hub and deploy routing logic Run this First — before any other notebook

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text: This notebook automates the full lifecycle of registering LLM backends with your APIM gateway. It extracts the current backend configuration, generates a parameter file with per-model metadata (SKU, capacity, model format, version), deploys the backends and policy fragments, and verifies the deployment through multiple API formats.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text: Step Description 0 Initialize variables — Configure resource group, location, and backend endpoints 1 Verify Azure CLI — Confirm authentication and subscription context 2 Initialize APIM Client — Connect to the existing Governance Hub deployment 3 Extract current backends — Retrieve existing backend pools and routing configuration 4 Discover managed identity — Auto-detect the APIM user-assigned managed identity 5 Generate parameter file — Create a parameter file with full backend definitions 6 Deploy — Run the deployment to create backends, pools, and policy fragments 7 Verify deployment — Confirm backends and policy fragments were created 8 Verify GET /deployments — Test the get-available-models policy fragment for Foundry integration Test Test models — Validate via Universal LLM API, Azure OpenAI API, Python SDK, and streaming

docs.title: Key Configuration
docs.text:
governance_hub_resource_group = "REPLACE"  # Your Governance Hub resource group
location = "REPLACE"                       # e.g., "eastus", "swedencentral"

llm_backends_config = [
    {
        "backendId": "aif-citadel-primary",
        "backendType": "ai-foundry",           # 'ai-foundry' | 'azure-openai' | 'external'
        "endpoint": "https://...",
        "authScheme": "managedIdentity",        # 'managedIdentity' | 'apiKey' | 'token'
        "supportedModels": [
            { "name": "gpt-4o", "sku": "GlobalStandard", "capacity": 100, "modelFormat": "OpenAI", "modelVersion": "2024-11-20" }
        ],
        "priority": 1,
        "weight": 100
    }
]

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
• Deployed APIM backends with circuit breaker support
  • Backend pools with priority/weight-based load balancing
  • set-backend-pools and get-available-models policy fragments
  • Verified model routing through both API formats

docs.title: 2. Universal LLM API — All-Models Tests
docs.text: Notebook citadel-universal-llm-api-all-models-tests.ipynb Purpose Validate the Universal LLM API (/models) against every model exposed by the gateway Run this Immediately after backend onboarding to confirm the full model catalogue is reachable

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text: This notebook provisions a single access contract with allowedModels = "" (no model restriction), then dynamically discovers the live model catalogue via GET /models/models and exercises the appropriate OpenAI v1 operation for each model. It is the fastest way to confirm that every onboarded backend pool is end-to-end reachable through the Universal LLM API surface.

docs.title: Operations Exercised Per Model
docs.text: Model name pattern Operations exercised Contains embedding POST /models/embeddings Contains gpt POST /models/chat/completions and the full Responses API trio: POST /models/responses, GET /models/responses/{response_id}, GET /models/responses/{response_id}/input_items?limit=20 Anything else POST /models/chat/completions

docs.title: Steps
docs.text: Step Description 0 Initialize variables — Configure resource group, location, API versions, and optional model cap 1 Verify Azure CLI — Confirm authentication and subscription context 2 Initialize APIM Client — Discover the Universal LLM API and supported models 3 Provision access contract — Deploy an APIM product + subscription with allowedModels = "" and a generous capacity allocation 4 Retrieve API key — Get the subscription key for the unrestricted product 5 Discover models — Call GET /models/models to enumerate the live model catalogue 6 Per-model operation loop — Auto-classify each model and run chat / embeddings / Responses API operations 7 Summary table — Aggregate per-model pass/fail across all exercised operations Cleanup Delete test products — Optionally remove the unrestricted access contract

docs.title: Key Configuration
docs.text:
governance_hub_resource_group = "REPLACE"
location                      = "REPLACE"

targetInferenceApi    = "models"               # Universal LLM API
inference_api_version = "2024-05-01-preview"
openai_api_version    = "2024-12-01-preview"

# 0 = test every discovered model; set a positive int to cap for quick smoke tests
max_models_to_test = 0

# Delay between POST /responses and the subsequent GET /responses/{id} calls
responses_get_delay_seconds = 0

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
• One APIM product + subscription with no model RBAC restriction
  • Live discovery of every gateway-configured model via GET /models/models
  • Per-model results for chat, embeddings, and (where applicable) Responses API operations
  • Summary table highlighting any model that failed an expected operation

docs.title: 3. Citadel Access Contracts Tests
docs.text: Notebook citadel-access-contracts-tests.ipynb Purpose Create, deploy, and load-test multiple access contracts with different integration patterns Run this After backend onboarding and the Universal LLM all-models smoke test

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text: This notebook provisions three distinct access contracts, each representing a different integration pattern. It generates the parameter files, deploys the contracts as APIM products with subscriptions, performs load testing, and visualizes throttling behavior and token bucket dynamics across all contracts.

docs.title: Access Contracts Created
docs.text: Contract Business Unit Integration Description Sales-Assistant Sales Key Vault only Secrets (endpoint + API key) resolved from Azure Key Vault HR-ChatAgent HR Key Vault + Foundry Optionally creates a Foundry project connection for agent integration Support-Bot Support Direct output No external integrations — uses direct APIM subscription output

docs.title: Steps
docs.text: Step Description 0 Initialize variables — Configure resource group, Key Vault, and Foundry settings 1 Verify Azure CLI — Confirm authentication and subscription context 2 Initialize APIM Client — Discover APIs and supported models 3 Define contracts — Configure three access contracts with varying integration patterns 4 Create parameter files — Generate parameter files with policy XML for each contract 5 Deploy contracts — Run the deployments at subscription scope 6 Retrieve API keys — Extract subscription keys for each deployed product 7 Load test — Send concurrent API requests to each contract and record metrics 8 Visualize results — Compare success/throttled/error rates across contracts 9 Token bucket analysis — Simulate and visualize token bucket refill behavior Cleanup Delete test products — Optionally remove all created APIM products and subscriptions

  • Foundry connection created (if enabled)

docs.title: 4. Citadel Model Aliases Tests
docs.text: Notebook citadel-model-aliases-tests.ipynb Purpose Validate the shared resolve-model-alias policy fragment across the LLM API surfaces (Universal LLM, Azure OpenAI, and — when imported — Unified AI) Run this After backend onboarding (notebook 1). Can be run independently of notebook 3.

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
This notebook re-runs the LLM backend onboarding deployment with a modelAliases parameter populated, which (re)deploys the shared resolve-model-alias policy fragment with the configured aliases inlined. It then provisions an access contract scoped to alias names only (least-privilege RBAC) and exercises the same aliases through the available LLM API surfaces, inspecting the UAIG-* debug response headers to verify the gateway's routing decisions end-to-end.

Two alias strategies are validated:

Alias Strategy Behavior adv-gpt priority First underlying model wins; remaining models act as cross-model fallback (deterministic per-call) gpt-blend weighted Random-weighted picking across underlying models — useful for A/B model swaps

docs.title: Steps
docs.text: Step Description 0 Initialize variables — Fill in resource group / location, paste llm_backends_config, and define the two aliases and a direct-test model 1 Verify Azure CLI & APIM Client — Confirm subscription context and discover the APIM resource + managed identity 2 Generate parameter file — Write a parameter file containing the full backend config + the two aliases 3 Deploy onboarding — Re-run the LLM backend onboarding deployment so the resolve-model-alias fragment is regenerated with the aliases inlined 4 Create access contract — Deploy an APIM product whose allowedModels lists ONLY the alias names + direct_test_model, with enableResponseHeaders=true for UAIG-* debug headers 5 Resolve API key — Pick the subscription created for the contract 6 Discover endpoints — Universal LLM (/models), Azure OpenAI (/openai), Unified AI (/unified-ai, when imported) Discovery GET /deployments honors allowedModels — Aliases appear as type: "alias" entries with descriptions; underlying real models that aren't in allowedModels are filtered out 7 Direct model control test — Call direct_test_model on the available APIs; resolver should be a no-op (no UAIG-Alias header) 8 Priority alias test — Call adv-gpt; resolves deterministically to the first underlying model 9 Weighted alias single call — Call gpt-blend once on each API 10 Weighted distribution test — Send N=30 requests through gpt-blend and tally UAIG-Resolved-Model against configured weights 11 Negative RBAC test — Send a model NOT in allowedModels; expect HTTP 403 unauthorized_model_access Summary Results overview — Cross-API consistency check + alias resolution observations Cleanup Delete access contract — do_cleanup flag (default False); LLM backends and the resolve-model-alias fragment are intentionally preserved

docs.title: UAIG-* Response Headers Inspected
docs.text: Header Meaning UAIG-Model-Id Model that was actually routed to (post alias resolution) UAIG-Alias Original alias name the client sent (only present when alias was used) UAIG-Resolved-Model Real model the alias resolved to UAIG-Backend Backend pool / backend that served the request UAIG-API-Type Detected API type (Unified AI only) UAIG-Final-Path Reconstructed backend path (Unified AI only) UAIG-Auth-Type Auth method enforced by security-handler (Unified AI only) UAIG-Cache-Operation cache-hit / cache-miss for metadata-config UAIG-Request-Id APIM request id for log correlation

docs.title: Key Configuration
docs.text:
governance_hub_resource_group = "REPLACE"
location                      = "REPLACE"
llm_backends_config           = []          # paste your backend config inline (see notebook 1)

model_aliases = [
    { "name": "adv-gpt",   "models": ["gpt-5.2", "gpt-5.4-mini", "gpt-4.1"], "strategy": "priority" },
    { "name": "gpt-blend", "models": ["gpt-5.4-mini", "gpt-4.1"],            "strategy": "weighted", "weights": [70, 30] },
]

direct_test_model     = "gpt-4.1"            # control test (must exist in llm_backends_config)
inference_api_version = "2024-05-01-preview"

docs.title: Output
docs.text:
• Re-deployed resolve-model-alias policy fragment with the two aliases inlined as a static JObject
  • Access contract scoped to alias names (proves alias-name RBAC works without exposing underlying real models)
  • Per-API report of UAIG-* headers showing alias → real-model resolution
  • Distribution table for the weighted alias compared against the configured weights
  • Filtered GET /deployments response showing aliases as first-class entries with properties.capabilities.description
  • 403 negative-test confirmation that unauthorized models are blocked at the gateway

docs.text:
All notebooks import shared helper modules from the ../shared/ directory:
